A linked subsystem has a dashed outline. Its Properties show which library it comes from, and its mask parameters, which you set per instance.

You can You cannot (edit the library instead) set the mask parameter values of each instance add, remove or change blocks inside it open it and look inside change its mask definition or its variants connect it like any block

Break Link in the Properties panel turns a linked copy into an ordinary subsystem that you can change freely. It no longer receives updates from the library.

docs.title: Change a component
docs.text:
Open the .nervlib file with File → Open (or right-click the library in the Library panel → Open Library for Editing), change the component, and save. Models that use it are updated:

  • when they are opened, or
  • right away with File → Update Library Links.

Each instance keeps its own mask values, as long as the library still has a parameter with that name. New mask parameters get their default value from the library.

docs.title: Where the library is stored
docs.text: The model stores the path of the library relative to the model file, so a project folder with models and libraries can be moved or shared as a whole (for example in git). It also stores a copy of each linked subsystem, so the model still opens and simulates when the library is missing. You then get a warning in the Diagnostics panel.

docs.title: Example: two engines from one component
docs.text:
examples/engine_library.py builds examples/library/engine_parts.nervlib with two masked components: a mean-value engine (throttle body, intake manifold, cylinders, torque and crankshaft) and a throttle actuator. examples/engine_comparison.nervus uses each component twice, to compare a 1.6 l and a 2.0 l engine with the same throttle steps. Only the mask values differ: displacement and the inertia J.

Inside, the component uses its mask parameters like workspace variables: the Gain 1 / J, and the parameters of its Python Function blocks ([eta_vol, displacement], read as p[0], p[1] in the code):

At the same throttle opening the larger engine runs slower: the throttle limits how much air gets in, and the larger engine has more friction. Open the library, change the friction model in net_torque, save, and reopen the comparison model: both engines use the new model.

uv run python examples/engine_library.py

docs.title: In Python
docs.text:
from nervus.library import instantiate, refresh_links, save_to_library

save_to_library(engine, "parts.nervlib")  # add or replace the component "engine"
e1 = model.add(instantiate("parts.nervlib", "engine"), name="engine_front")
e1.mask["displacement"] = 2.0e-3  # per-instance value
refresh_links(model)  # update after the library changed

docs.title: Model files
docs.text:
Models are saved as UTF-8 JSON files with the extension .nervus:

{
  "format": "nervus-model",
  "schema_version": 4,
  "name": "first_order",
  "meta": {},
  "settings": {"t_start": 0.0, "t_final": 10.0, "solver": "auto", "step": null,
               "max_step": null, "rtol": 1e-06, "atol": 1e-08},
  "workspace": [
    {"name": "Kp", "value": 1.5, "unit": "%/°", "description": "Proportional gain", "min": 0.0}
  ],
  "blocks": [
    {"name": "u", "type": "sources.step",
     "params": {"time": 0.0, "initial": 0.0, "final": 1.0, "sample_time": 0.0}}
  ],
  "connections": [
    {"src": "u", "src_port": 0, "dst": "err", "dst_port": 0}
  ]
}
  • type is the block's stable type_id (listed in the block reference).
  • Every parameter is written out, including defaults, so a file keeps its meaning if a default changes.
  • Infinite values are written as the strings "inf" / "-inf", so the file stays strict JSON.
  • A parameter given as an expression of workspace variables is stored as the expression string, e.g. "gain": "Kp". See Workspace and calibrations.
  • meta holds GUI data (block positions, view state) and is ignored by the simulator.
  • Output is deterministic, so a small change to the model gives a small git diff.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
schema_version is increased whenever the format changes, and Nervus upgrades older files automatically when it loads them. Version 2 added workspace; version 3 added subsystems (a block entry may contain a nested "system" with its own blocks and connections); version 4 added tests (test cases with inputs, parameters and checks, see Test cases and results). Files from a newer version of Nervus are rejected with a message asking you to upgrade.

Python Function blocks run code

A model containing a Python Function block runs that code when it is loaded and simulated. Only open model files you trust.

docs.title: OBD-II: read live data from a car
docs.text:
Every petrol car since 2001 (EU) / 1996 (US), and every diesel since 2004, has an OBD-II diagnostic port, usually under the dashboard near the steering column. With an ELM327 adapter (USB or Bluetooth) Nervus can read the standard live values that SAE J1979 defines as mode 01 PIDs: engine speed, vehicle speed, temperatures, air flow, throttle position, fuel trims and more.

Use it to:

  • record a real drive and compare it with your model in the Data Inspector, or open a log you made with a scanner app or a CAN logger (below);
  • replay the recording as the input of a test case (for example, real rpm and throttle into your idle controller);
  • check that your plant model behaves like your car.

Read-only

Nervus only sends standard read requests (modes 01, 02, 03, 07, 09 and 0A). It never clears codes, writes to, or reprograms the car's ECUs.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
uv sync --extra obd          # installs pyserial
uv run python -m nervus.obd pids                                 # PIDs Nervus can decode
uv run python -m nervus.obd supported --port /dev/tty.usbserial-1110
uv run python -m nervus.obd record --port /dev/tty.usbserial-1110 \
    --pids rpm,speed,coolant_temp,throttle --duration 120 --out drive.nervres

On Windows the port is called COM3 or similar; on Linux /dev/ttyUSB0 or /dev/rfcomm0 for Bluetooth. Turn the ignition on (or start the engine) before connecting.

Open drive.nervres with File → Open Result in the Data Inspector, or save it as CSV with --out drive.csv.

docs.title: Recording in the editor
docs.text: Tools → Record from OBD-II… does the same as record with live plots. Choose the source: an ELM327 adapter (its serial port), a CAN interface (python-can: SocketCAN, PEAK, Kvaser, Vector, ...) or a simulated ECU (a model with an OBD Responder running in Nervus, see below). Press Connect: PIDs that the car does not report are greyed out. Tick the PIDs, set a duration (or record until Stop) and an interval, and press Record. Each PID gets its own plot while it records. Afterwards, Save… writes a .nervres or .csv file and Open in Data Inspector adds the drive as a run, to compare with a simulation.

docs.title: Logs from scanner apps and CAN loggers
docs.text:
Already have a log? Tools → Open Vehicle Log… (or Load… in the Data Inspector) opens it as a run in the Data Inspector, next to your simulations. Nervus reads:

Log From How it looks CSV, one column per value Torque, OBD Fusion, OBDLink, FORScan, ScanMaster, Nervus's own export, most loggers Device Time,Engine RPM(rpm),Speed (OBD)(km/h) CSV, one row per sample Car Scanner "SECONDS";"PID";"VALUE";"UNITS" CAN log with a DBC file CAN loggers, CANalyzer, PCAN-View, SavvyCAN, candump; trucks (J1939) .asc, .blf, .trc, .log CAN log without a DBC file a CAN log of a scan tool talking to the car the OBD-II answers (0x7E8 to 0x7EF)

For CSV files, Nervus finds the header (lines above it, such as the vehicle name, are skipped), the separator (,, ; or tab), a decimal comma, and the unit in the column name (Engine RPM(rpm) or Fuel rate [l/h] becomes the value Engine RPM in rpm). The time column is the first one called time, seconds, timestamp and the like, in seconds (milliseconds if its name or unit says ms), or as dates and clock times, counted from the first line. Empty cells and - (a value that was not read that time) are filled in from the samples around them; text columns are left out.

For a CAN log, Nervus asks for a DBC file and decodes every signal of every message in it. A truck's J1939 messages are matched by their parameter group, whichever controller sent them, so one J1939 DBC file fits any truck. Cancel the DBC question to decode only the OBD-II answers in the log, with the PIDs Nervus knows.

Every value has its own time stamps (a scanner reads one PID after the other); Nervus puts them on the time stamps of the value with the most samples, linearly interpolated. The units are shown in the plot.

In Python:

from nervus.logs import log_channels, read_log

log_channels("examples/data/obd_scanner_log.csv")  # {'Engine RPM': 'rpm', 'Speed (OBD)': 'km/h', ...}
rec = read_log("examples/data/obd_scanner_log.csv", ["Engine RPM"], raster=0.1)
truck = read_log("truck.blf", dbc="j1939.dbc")
FromWorkspace(time=rec.t, data=rec["Engine RPM"])  # drive a model with the recorded engine speed

docs.title: Trouble codes, freeze frame and VIN
docs.text:
uv run python -m nervus.obd dtc --port /dev/tty.usbserial-1110

VIN: WVWZZZ1KZAW000001
stored trouble codes: 2
  P0133  O2 sensor slow response (bank 1 sensor 1)
  P0300  Random/multiple cylinder misfire detected
pending trouble codes: none
permanent trouble codes: none
freeze frame: rpm=1726, speed=50, coolant_temp=83, engine_load=40.4
Kind OBD mode Meaning stored 03 Confirmed faults; these switch on the check-engine lamp (MIL) pending 07 Seen in the current or last drive cycle, not yet confirmed permanent 0A Stay until the ECU itself sees the fault is gone; a tool cannot clear them freeze frame 02 Snapshot of live values when the first code was stored

A code such as P0133 reads as: letter = system (Powertrain, Chassis, Body, network U), first digit 0/2 = generic SAE code (1/3 = manufacturer specific), then the subsystem (1 = air/fuel metering, 3 = ignition/misfire, 4 = emissions, ...) and the fault number. Nervus knows the descriptions of common generic codes; look up others in the SAE J2012 list or your car's service information.

Nervus does not clear trouble codes (mode 04): clearing also resets the readiness monitors that an emissions inspection checks. Use your car's diagnostic tool for that, once the cause is fixed.

In Python: elm.trouble_codes("stored"), elm.freeze_frame(PIDS["rpm"]), elm.vin().

docs.title: Trouble codes in your own models
docs.text:
The Diagnostic Monitor block (Library → Diagnostics) is the ECU side of a trouble code: it turns the raw result of a monitor (e.g. misfire_rate > limit) into a debounced DTC, the way the diagnostic event manager of an engine ECU does:

  1. Debouncing: a counter goes up by fail_step for each failed sample and down by pass_step for each passed one. At +threshold the test has failed, at −threshold it has passed; short glitches do nothing.
  2. Pending: the first failure makes the code pending immediately.
  3. Confirmed and MIL: after confirm_cycles operation cycles in a row with a failure (2: OBD's two-trip detection) the code is confirmed and the MIL (check-engine lamp) comes on.
  4. Healing: after heal_cycles passed cycles in a row the MIL goes off; the code stays stored as confirmed.
  5. Readiness: the ready output is 1 once the monitor has completed (passed or failed) since the codes were last cleared, which is what an inspection checks; clearing the codes (the optional clear input, like mode 04) sets it back to "not complete".

The optional enable input holds the test while its conditions are not met (e.g. only with a warm engine), and a rising edge on the optional cycle input starts a new operation cycle (key on). The status output is the UDS DTC status byte (ISO 14229), the same bits a scan tool shows. The block generates C code, so the diagnostic logic can run in the ECU code and be tested back to back like the rest of the model.

docs.title: A simulated car: test diagnostic tools without a vehicle
docs.text:
nervus.obd_sim.SimulatedEcu answers OBD requests like a car's engine ECU: live data (mode 01, including PID 01 with the MIL and the number of codes), stored, pending and permanent codes (03, 07, 0A), clearing (04) and the VIN (09). It speaks the ELM327 text protocol, so the Nervus client works with it directly:

from nervus.obd import PIDS, Elm327
from nervus.obd_sim import SimulatedEcu

car = SimulatedEcu({"rpm": 2175, "coolant_temp": 88}, {"P0302": 0x8C}, vin="WVWZZZ1KZAW123456")
elm = Elm327(car)  # instead of a serial port
elm.initialize()
elm.read(PIDS["rpm"])
elm.trouble_codes()
elm.vin()

In a model, the OBD Responder block (Library → Diagnostics) publishes model signals as PIDs and the status of Diagnostic Monitors as trouble codes while the simulation runs. When a tool clears the codes, its clear output resets the monitors in the model. examples/obd_ecu.py is an engine ECU with a misfire monitor (P0302: pending in the first key cycle, MIL in the second) and a lean monitor. Run it in real time, and connect any OBD program to the serial port it prints (a pseudo-terminal, on macOS and Linux):

uv run python -m nervus.obd simulate examples/obd_ecu.nervus
#   ECU 'ecu': ELM327 on /dev/ttys007
uv run python -m nervus.obd dtc --port /dev/ttys007        # in another terminal

docs.title: OBD over CAN, without an ELM327
docs.text:
Cars since about 2008 use CAN for OBD-II (ISO 15765-4: 11-bit identifiers, 500 kbit/s). A request goes to the functional address 0x7DF and the engine ECU answers from 0x7E8. Answers longer than 7 bytes (the VIN, many codes) are split by ISO-TP: a first frame, a flow-control frame from the tool, then consecutive frames. With a CAN interface supported by python-can (PEAK, Kvaser, Vector, SocketCAN on Linux) Nervus talks to the car directly:

uv run python -m nervus.obd dtc --can-interface socketcan --can-channel can0
uv run python -m nervus.obd record --can-interface pcan --can-channel PCAN_USBBUS1 --pids rpm,speed

from nervus.obd_can import CanObd

obd = CanObd(interface="socketcan", channel="can0")
obd.initialize()
obd.read(PIDS["rpm"])
obd.vin()

The simulated ECU answers on CAN too (--can-interface virtual --can-channel test with simulate, or nervus.obd_can.serve_can), which is how the CAN client is tested without hardware.

docs.title: How a PID is decoded
docs.text:
The adapter sends a request such as 010C (mode 01, PID 0x0C = engine speed). The car answers with 41 0C A B, where A and B are data bytes. Each PID has a formula, for example:

\[ n_{\text{engine}} = \frac{256\,A + B}{4}\ \text{rpm}, \qquad T_{\text{coolant}} = A - 40\ \text{°C} \] Name PID Unit Formula engine_load 04 % A·100/255 coolant_temp 05 °C A − 40 stft_b1, ltft_b1 06, 07 % (A − 128)·100/128 map 0B kPa A rpm 0C rpm (256A + B)/4 speed 0D km/h A timing_advance 0E ° A/2 − 64 intake_temp 0F °C A − 40 maf 10 g/s (256A + B)/100 throttle 11 % A·100/255 o2_b1s1 14 V A/200 run_time 1F s 256A + B fuel_level 2F % A·100/255 baro 33 kPa A module_voltage 42 V (256A + B)/1000 lambda_cmd 44 – 2(256A + B)/65536 ambient_temp 46 °C A − 40 pedal_d 49 % A·100/255 oil_temp 5C °C A − 40 fuel_rate 5E L/h (256A + B)/20

Not every car reports every PID; supported asks the car which ones it has.

docs.title: In Python
docs.text:
from nervus.core import Signal
from nervus.obd import Elm327, SerialTransport, record

elm = Elm327(SerialTransport("/dev/tty.usbserial-1110"))
elm.initialize()
drive = record(elm, ["rpm", "throttle"], duration=60)
drive.save("drive.nervres")

rpm_input = Signal(drive.t, drive["rpm"], "linear")  # use as a test-case input

Over an ELM327 each PID takes roughly 30–100 ms, so polling 4 PIDs gives a few samples per second. Planned next (see the plan, Phase 22): OBD directly over a CAN interface, and a live recording window in the editor.

docs.title: Physical modelling
docs.text:
Signal blocks compute an output from their inputs: information flows one way. Physical systems are not like that: in a circuit, the current through a resistor depends on everything else connected to it. Nervus models electrical circuits, rotating shafts and heat paths with physical blocks whose ports are joined by links, like Simscape. Kirchhoff's laws are assembled automatically.

Domain Across (at a port) Through (in a component) Library electrical voltage [V] current [A] Electrical: Resistor, Capacitor, Inductor, Voltage/Current Source, Switch, Diode, Battery, DC Motor, H-Bridge, sensors rotational angular velocity [rad/s] torque [N·m] Rotational: Inertia, Spring, Damper, Torque/Speed Source, Ideal Gear, sensors thermal temperature [°C] heat flow [W] Thermal: Thermal Mass, Thermal Resistance, Heat Source, Temperature Source, sensors hydraulic pressure [bar] volume flow [L/min] Hydraulic: Tank, Pump (Flow Source), Pressure Source, Orifice, Relief Valve, Volume, sensors

docs.title: Drawing circuits in the editor
docs.text:
Physical blocks are in the library under Electrical, Rotational and Thermal. Their physical ports are small squares on the left and right sides, in the colour of their domain (blue electrical, green rotational, orange thermal); signal inputs (a controlled source) are on the top and signal outputs (sensors) at the bottom. Drag from one square to another to link them: a link is a plain line without an arrow, because current can flow both ways. Several links on one port join at one node. Ports of different domains cannot be linked. Select a link and press Delete (or right-click → Delete Link) to remove it; deleting a block removes its links, and everything can be undone.

To put part of a circuit into a subsystem, add Connection Port blocks inside (Library → Ports & Subsystems): each one becomes a physical port along the bottom edge of the subsystem.

docs.title: A first circuit
docs.text:
from nervus import Diagram, simulate
from nervus.blocks import Capacitor, ElectricalReference, Resistor, Scope, VoltageSensor, VoltageSource

d = Diagram("rc")
supply = d.add(VoltageSource(V=10.0), name="supply")
r = d.add(Resistor(R=1000.0), name="R")
c = d.add(Capacitor(C=1e-3), name="C")
gnd = d.add(ElectricalReference(), name="gnd")
vc = d.add(VoltageSensor(), name="vc")
d.link((supply, "p"), (r, "p"))  # physical links: no direction
d.link((r, "n"), (c, "p"))
d.link((c, "n"), (gnd, "p"))
d.link((supply, "n"), (gnd, "p"))
d.link((vc, "p"), (c, "p"))
d.link((vc, "n"), (gnd, "p"))
d.connect(vc, d.add(Scope()))  # a sensor's output is an ordinary signal
res = simulate(d, 3.0)
res["vc"]  # 10 (1 - e^(-t/RC)), RC = 1 s

Every circuit needs an Electrical Reference (ground). Sensors turn physical quantities into signals; controlled sources (controlled = on) turn signals into voltages, currents, torques or heat flows. So a controller built from signal blocks can drive a physical plant: a PI controller that reads a Speed Sensor and sets a Voltage Source driving a DC Motor.

docs.title: Automotive electrics
docs.text:
The Automotive Electrics library has components with their typical behaviour built in:

Block What it models Solenoid a coil (R, L) whose armature pulls in above a current and drops out below a lower one Fuel Injector a solenoid injector: the needle opens a little after the ECU switches it on (the opening delay); outputs lift and fuel flow Relay coil plus a contact that closes while the armature is pulled in Glow Plug a heater whose resistance rises with its temperature, so it limits its own current; thermal port to the cylinder head Alternator the regulated generator: holds 14.2 V up to a current limit that depends on its speed, and loads the engine with the electrical power divided by its efficiency

The opening delay of an injector, for example, follows from its coil: the current rises as \(i(t) = \frac{V}{R}\left(1 - e^{-tR/L}\right)\), so a 12 Ω, 10 mH injector at 12 V reaches its 0.6 A pull-in current after \(-\frac{L}{R}\ln(1 - 0.6) = 0.76\) ms. With a weaker battery the delay grows; ECUs correct the injection time for the battery voltage for this reason.

docs.title: Hydraulics
docs.text: Pressure in bar (above the tank) and volume flow in L/min. A Hydraulic Volume (a fuel rail, a hose) stores fluid: \(\frac{V}{\beta}\frac{dp}{dt} = q\), with the bulk modulus β. An Orifice is a turbulent restriction, \(q \propto \sqrt{\Delta p}\), with a laminar region near zero so the equations stay smooth. A Relief Valve opens above its cracking pressure, like the pressure regulator of a fuel system: a pump feeding a rail with a 4 bar regulator and injectors settles just above 4 bar, with the excess returning to the tank.

docs.title: Electronic circuits: semiconductors, like SPICE
docs.text:
The Semiconductors library has SPICE-like device models: Diode (Shockley equation, with reverse breakdown for Zener diodes; LEDs with their own Is and N), Bipolar Transistor (NPN/PNP, Ebers-Moll), MOSFET (N/P, SPICE level 1) and Op-Amp (high gain, output limited to its rails). The Ideal Diode in the Electrical library is a faster piecewise-linear switch.

These devices are nonlinear, so the network is solved the way SPICE does it: around the last solution each device is replaced by a conductance and a current source (its companion model), the linear system is solved, and this is repeated (Newton-Raphson) until the solution no longer changes. Junction voltages are limited between iterations (SPICE's pnjlim), so the exponentials converge from any starting point. For a diode:

\[ i = I_s\left(e^{v/(N V_T)} - 1\right) \quad\Rightarrow\quad i \approx i_0 + g_0 (v - v_0), \qquad g_0 = \frac{I_s}{N V_T} e^{v_0/(N V_T)} \]

Circuits with more than 80 unknowns are solved with sparse matrices, so circuits with hundreds of nodes stay fast. The voltage-controlled sources E and G of SPICE are the blocks Voltage-Controlled Voltage/Current Source.

docs.title: Analyses
docs.text:
SPICE Nervus .tran (transient) an ordinary simulation (▶ Run, or simulate) .op (operating point) nervus.circuit.operating_point(model): every node voltage at the steady state .dc (DC sweep) nervus.circuit.dc_sweep(model, "Vin", "V", values, ["vout"]) .ac (small-signal) Linear Analysis: an In block on a controlled source, an Out block on a sensor → Bode plot 
from nervus.circuit import dc_sweep, operating_point

op = operating_point(model)
print(op.table())  # R1.n  0.6291, D1.p 0.6291, ...
curve = dc_sweep(model, "Vin", "V", np.linspace(0, 5, 51), ["vd"])

docs.title: SPICE netlists (LTspice)
docs.text:
File → Import SPICE Netlist… opens a netlist as a model, and Export SPICE Netlist… writes one. In LTspice, View → SPICE Netlist shows the netlist of a schematic; save it as a .cir file. Nervus reads R, C, L, V, I (DC, SIN, PULSE), D, Q, M, E and G, .model, .param and .tran. Every node gets a Voltage Sensor named like SPICE's probes, so res["V(out)"] is the voltage of node out:

* Half-wave rectifier with a smoothing capacitor
V1 in 0 SIN(0 10 50)
D1 in out D1N4007
C1 out 0 100u
R1 out 0 1k
.model D1N4007 D(IS=7n N=1.8 BV=1000 IBV=5u)
.tran 50u 100m
.end

from nervus.spice import read_netlist, write_netlist

d = read_netlist("rectifier.cir")
res = simulate(d)  # V(out): about 9 V with 1.8 V of ripple
write_netlist(d, "back.cir")

The rise and fall times of PULSE sources are ignored (ideal edges), subcircuits (.subckt) and behavioural sources (B) are not read yet; a list of elements that were left out is shown after the import.

docs.title: How it is solved
docs.text:
Ports that are linked share a node. At every node the through values add up to zero (Kirchhoff's current law), and every component relates the across values of its nodes to its through values. Nervus collects these equations with modified nodal analysis:

\[ A\,z = b \]

where z holds the across value of every node and the through value of every voltage-source-like branch. Elements with energy storage have states: a capacitor's voltage, an inductor's current, an inertia's speed, a spring's torque, a thermal mass's temperature. At every evaluation the states are known, so a capacitor acts as a voltage source and an inductor as a current source; one linear solve gives all voltages and currents, and from them the derivatives, e.g.

\[ C\,\frac{dv}{dt} = i, \qquad L\,\frac{di}{dt} = v, \qquad J\,\frac{d\omega}{dt} = \tau \]

The states are integrated by the same solver as the rest of the model. Diodes and switches change mode; the solve is repeated until the modes are consistent, and variable-step solvers stop exactly where they switch.

In the compiled model a network is split into a part that owns the states (sensor outputs that depend on states only, such as a motor's speed) and a part for outputs that react instantly to input signals (the current through a resistor fed by a controlled source). So a speed control loop around a motor is not an algebraic loop, while a loop around a purely resistive circuit is reported as one.

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• Two elements may not fix the same across value. A capacitor directly across an ideal voltage source, or two inertias joined rigidly (directly or through an Ideal Gear), have no unique solution; Nervus reports the network as unsolvable. Add the resistance or the shaft stiffness that the real system has (a Resistor, a Rotational Spring), or merge the inertias (reflect one through the gear: J/n²).
  • Inertias, springs and thermal masses are measured against the fixed frame (the reference), so a shaft or a heat path needs no reference block; a Rotational Reference fixes a port (a housing).
  • Temperatures are in °C. Only differences and derivatives enter the equations, so °C and K give the same results.
  • A physical block has no C code: physical blocks are the plant. Generate code for the controller subsystem.

docs.title: Example: speed control of a DC motor
docs.text:
from nervus.blocks import PID, Constant, DCMotor, Inertia, RotationalDamper, RotationalReference, SpeedSensor, Sum

motor = d.add(DCMotor(R=2.0, L=0.01, k=0.1), name="motor")  # k: N·m/A and V·s/rad
rotor = d.add(Inertia(J=1e-4), name="rotor")
friction = d.add(RotationalDamper(d=1e-4), name="friction")
housing = d.add(RotationalReference(), name="housing")
speed = d.add(SpeedSensor(), name="speed")
for part, port in ((rotor, "a"), (friction, "a"), (speed, "a")):
    d.link((motor, "shaft"), (part, port))
d.link((friction, "b"), (housing, "a"))
drive = d.add(VoltageSource(controlled=True), name="drive")  # the voltage is an input signal
...

At a constant voltage the motor settles where the torque balances the friction:

\[ \omega = \frac{k\,V}{R\,d + k^2} \]

for 12 V, 117.6 rad/s (1120 rpm). The tests (tests/test_physical.py) check this, an RC and an RLC circuit, a gear, a cooling body, a battery, an H-bridge and a rectifier against their analytical solutions.

docs.title: Roadmap to Nervus 1.0
docs.text:
Nervus 0.1 models, simulates and tests ECU software, and generates its C code. Nervus 1.0 closes the loop to the real vehicle: it also reads from and writes to a real ECU, measuring and calibrating it while it runs, flashing its software and reading its diagnostics, like ETAS INCA or Vector CANape. A car or truck function can then be developed in one tool from the first model to the calibrated ECU in the vehicle.

The detailed task list is plan.md; this page groups it into releases. Each release is usable on its own.

docs.title: 0.1: model, simulate, generate (released)
docs.text: Block diagrams, physical models, state charts, test cases with coverage and MC/DC, requirements, CAN and OBD-II, C code generation (MISRA C, fixed point, integer-only code, reusable functions, FMI), an XCP slave in the model, A2L export, Simulink .slx import, 33 tutorials. Changelog.

docs.title: 0.2: reach (released)
docs.text:
• Standalone applications for macOS, Windows and Linux (no Python needed), on every release page.
  • Versioned documentation: one site per release.
  • Simulink import of the older .mdl text format; coverage of the generated C code by the test cases; MC/DC for state chart guards; Help ▸ About Nervus with the contributors.

docs.title: 0.3: real hardware (released; tests on real boards still open)
docs.text:
• Development-board targets with CAN (an STM32 Nucleo and an ESP32 first): the generated code with a scheduler template and a small hardware layer per board, built and flashed from Nervus. The model stays the same; only the target changes. Done: board projects with an XCP slave in C; open: tests on real boards.
  • Processor-in-the-loop (PIL): the generated code runs on the board, the plant in Nervus, compared step by step with the simulation.
  • Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL): the plant model in real time on the PC, talking CAN to a real ECU.
  • The XCP slave on the board, so the board can be measured and calibrated like a production ECU (done for polling; DAQ to follow).
  • Simulink import of Stateflow charts as State Chart blocks (needs sample models from MATLAB: help wanted).
  • Faster simulation for large models: accelerated mode, the model as compiled C (done; physical networks still run in Python).
  • What users report: bugs, missing blocks, unclear tutorials.

docs.title: 0.4 to 0.6: measurement and calibration (the first INCA part; most of it is in 0.3)
docs.text:
• A2L import of any ECU's description (not only Nervus's own): measurements, characteristics (values, curves, maps with their axes), conversion methods, record layouts, memory segments.
  • XCP master over CAN, CAN FD and Ethernet (UDP and TCP), and CCP for older ECUs: connect, seed and key, read and write memory, DAQ lists with time stamps at several rates.
  • Measurement windows: oscilloscope, numeric, bar and state displays of the ECU's variables while it runs; recording to MDF4 with triggers; the recordings open in the Data Inspector next to simulations.
  • Calibration editors: values, curves and maps as tables and 3-D surfaces, changed live in the ECU, with working and reference pages (switch between the calibration under test and the safe one in one click).
  • The same windows work against the model (simulation), the development board and a production ECU.
  • Done in 0.3: the Calibration window with A2L import of any ECU, the XCP master on CAN, CAN FD, UDP and TCP with DAQ lists, seed and key, working and reference pages, value/curve/map editors, recording to MDF4, and a virtual ECU. Still open: CCP, 3-D map views, bar and state displays, triggers.

docs.title: 0.7 and 0.8: data sets, flashing and diagnostics
docs.text:
• Calibration data sets: read and write HEX and S19 files and calibration files (DCM, CDF/CDFX); compare and merge two data sets; a history of changes with who changed what and why.
  • Flashing over UDS (ISO 14229) through the ECU's bootloader: program, verify, checksums, and back to a known software if something goes wrong.
  • Diagnostics over UDS and KWP2000: read and clear trouble codes with their freeze frames, read data by identifier, run routines.

docs.title: 0.9: release candidate
docs.text:
• Experiments saved as files: the ECU connection, the windows, the variables and their layout, so a session can be opened again on the next day or by a colleague.
  • A stable Python API for scripting measurements, calibrations and tests against the real ECU (automated calibration and end-of-line style tests).
  • Safety: write-protection per memory area, plausibility limits for every calibration value (from the A2L file), a confirmation before flashing, and a log of every write.
  • Tutorials on a bench: a development board with a small plant (a DC motor or a throttle), measured, calibrated and flashed from Nervus.
  • Feedback from users who try it on their own benches.

docs.title: 1.0: what it means
docs.text:
Nervus 1.0 is released when:

  1. A real ECU can be read and written: measurement (DAQ) and calibration over XCP on CAN, CAN FD and Ethernet, and flashing and diagnostics over UDS, tested against at least two different ECUs or boards.
  2. The file formats are stable: models (.nervus), experiments and calibration data sets from 1.0 open in every later 1.x release.
  3. The Python API is stable: it follows semantic versioning, so scripts written for 1.0 keep working in 1.x.
  4. Everything is documented in the user guide and the in-app help, with tutorials from the first model to the calibrated ECU on a bench.
  5. It installs without Python on macOS, Windows and Linux.

docs.title: Decided along the way
docs.text:
• Inside Nervus or a separate application? Decided: inside Nervus, as a Calibration workspace, because the same windows then work against the model, a board and the real ECU, and a calibration found on the vehicle can go back into the model in one step.
  • Which hardware? CAN interfaces through python-can (PEAK, Kvaser, Vector, SocketCAN, CANable and others). Decided: not one development board but several, through a small hardware layer per board, so users can take the board they have. What to buy: Hardware.
  • Signed applications? Postponed: signing costs a yearly fee. The unsigned applications open with right-click ▸ Open (macOS) or More info ▸ Run anyway (Windows).

docs.title: Safety and the law
docs.text: Writing to an ECU changes how a vehicle behaves. Nervus's calibration and flashing features are for development work on test benches and test vehicles by people who know what they change. Changing the software or calibration of a vehicle used on public roads can make it unsafe, and changes that affect emissions or safety systems are illegal in most countries. Nervus will warn, limit and log, but the responsibility stays with the user.

docs.title: Help wanted
docs.text: Contributions are welcome at every step: try a release on your own hardware and report what happens, add a block or a tutorial, or take on one of the items above. See CONTRIBUTING.md; merged contributions are credited in Help ▸ About Nervus ▸ Contributors.

docs.title: State machines
docs.text: Operating modes, start sequences and fault handling are naturally described as state machines. In Simulink they are Stateflow charts; in Nervus they are State Chart blocks (Library → State Machines → State Chart).

docs.title: The chart editor
docs.text:
Double-click a State Chart block to open the chart editor:

  • States are boxes. Double-click empty space (or press Add state) to add one; drag it to move it. Select a state to edit its name and its entry, during and exit actions on the right. Add child state puts a state inside the selected one (a nested state); Make initial marks the state entered first at its level (the dot and arrow).
  • Transitions are arrows. Select the source state, press Add transition and click the target state. Select an arrow to edit its guard and action. When several transitions leave the same state, the number on the label is the order in which they are checked: Check earlier and Check later change it.
  • With nothing selected, the panel shows the chart's inputs, outputs, locals, parameters and events.
  • The Text tab shows the same chart in the chart language below; edit either one.
  • Apply or OK writes the chart to the block, as one step you can undo (Ctrl+Z). A chart that is not valid (an unknown name in a guard, say) shows the reason at the bottom and cannot be applied.

The positions of the states are saved in the model file. A chart without positions (written as text) is laid out automatically, from the initial state on the left; Tidy up does that again. Comments in the chart text are not kept when the chart is edited graphically.

docs.title: Writing a chart as text
docs.text:
Charts are stored in a short text language. Besides the chart editor's Text tab, you can select the block and edit its definition in the Properties panel, then press Apply code:

# Engine operating modes
input rpm, key
output mode = 0, fuel = 0
local starts = 0

state off
  entry: mode = 0; fuel = 0

state cranking
  entry: mode = 1; starts += 1
  during: fuel = 1

state running
  entry: mode = 2; fuel = 1

transition off -> cranking: key > 0.5
transition cranking -> running: rpm > 600
transition cranking -> off: after(300) / fuel = 0
transition running -> off: key < 0.5 or rpm < 300
Line Meaning input a, b input ports, in this order output y = 0, z = 1 output ports with initial values local n = 0 variables kept between steps, not visible outside state NAME a state; the first one is the initial state (or write initial NAME) entry: ... actions when the state is entered during: ... actions every period the state stays active exit: ... actions when the state is left transition A -> B: guard / action leave A for B when guard is true; the action is optional

Actions are assignments separated by ; (y = 1; n += 1). Guards and actions can use + - * / **, comparisons, and or not, abs min max sqrt exp log sin cos floor ceil, pi and e.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
• after(n) is true once the state has been active for n sample periods.
  • t_in_state is the time in seconds since the state was entered. One period has passed at the first step after entering.

docs.title: Semantics
docs.text:
The chart runs at its sample time (set sample_time, or let it inherit a discrete rate). Every period:

  1. The transitions leaving the active state are checked in the order they are written. The first with a true guard fires: the source's exit actions run, then the transition action, then the target's entry actions.
  2. If none fires, the active state's during actions run.

With state_output on, an extra last output gives the active state's number (0, 1, 2, ... in the order the states are written). It's handy for plotting.

docs.title: Nested states, parallel states, history and events
docs.text:
Larger charts are easier to read with hierarchy. Indent a state under another one to nest it:

input key, rpm, fault
output mode = 0, mil = 0, stalls = 0
event stalled

state off
  entry: mode = 0
state on parallel             # two regions, both active while 'on' is
  state engine
    state cranking            # the first child is the initial one
      entry: mode = 1
    state running
      entry: mode = 2
  state diagnosis
    state ok
      entry: mil = 0
    state failed
      entry: mil = 1

transition off -> on: key > 0.5
transition on -> off: key < 0.5                  # leaves every state inside 'on'
transition cranking -> running: rpm > 600
transition running -> cranking: rpm < 300 / stalls += 1; send(stalled)
transition ok -> failed: fault > 0.5 or stalled
transition failed -> ok: fault < 0.5 and after(30)
  • Nested (OR) states: a state with child states has exactly one active child. Entering it enters its initial child: the first one, or the one named by an indented initial NAME.
  • Parallel (AND) states: state NAME parallel makes all its children active at the same time, as independent regions (here the engine and its diagnosis). There are no transitions between regions; they communicate through variables and events.
  • History: an indented history line makes a state remember which child was active when it was left; entering it again goes back to that child instead of the initial one.
  • Events: event NAME declares an event. An action send(NAME) broadcasts it: after the current pass the chart runs once more with NAME true in the guards. Here the stall in the engine region sets the diagnosis region to failed in the same sample. At most 8 events are processed per sample.
  • Transitions across levels: a transition may connect any two states (not in different parallel regions). It exits the states it leaves from the inside out (exit actions, innermost first), runs its action, and enters the states down to the target from the outside in (entry actions), then the target's initial children.

Priority: outer transitions are checked first: while on is active, on -> off is checked before anything inside it. If no transition of a state fires, its during actions run and then its active children are processed in the order they are written. after(n) and t_in_state count the time in the state whose transition or during action is being evaluated. The state output gives the innermost active state of the first region.

Hierarchical charts are generated as C code like flat ones (the same algorithm, unrolled over the states), and back-to-back tests check them sample by sample. The Model Advisor knows that initial children and parallel regions are entered by default.

docs.title: Calibration parameters in a chart
docs.text:
Thresholds and times in an ECU's mode logic are calibrated like any other value. Declare them with param: the chart reads them, but cannot change them, and their values come from the model workspace (or from the mask of a subsystem around the chart):

input rpm, pedal
output fuel = 1
param rpm_cut_on, rpm_cut_off          # model workspace variables

state run
state fuel_cut
  entry: fuel = 0
  exit: fuel = 1

transition run -> fuel_cut: pedal < 1 and rpm > rpm_cut_on
transition fuel_cut -> run: pedal > 2 or rpm < rpm_cut_off

Change rpm_cut_on in the Model Workspace (or in a parameter set or test case) and the chart follows. In generated C, param names become calibration parameters in <model>_P, with the variable's data type, and they appear in the A2L file.

docs.title: Example: engine operating modes
docs.text:
examples/engine_modes.py is the mode logic of an engine ECU: off, crank (starter on, with a 3 s starter protection into crank_fail), idle (idle speed control on), run, fuel_cut (overrun fuel cut-off while coasting) and stalled (no automatic restart). All thresholds are params. Four test cases drive the key, engine speed and pedal with scenarios: a normal start, a failed start, fuel cut-off, and a stall.

Coasting from 3000 rpm with the pedal released, the chart switches the fuel off (no fuel is needed: the car's momentum turns the engine) and back on at 1100 rpm, before the engine could stall, and goes to idle control.

docs.title: Example: gear-shift logic
docs.text: examples/gear_shift.py has one state per gear. Each transition compares the vehicle speed with the shift speed read from a map for the current gear and pedal, speed > up_speed and after(min_gear_time); the minimum time in a gear and the hysteresis between the up- and downshift maps keep it from hunting. See the gear-shift tutorial.

docs.title: C code
docs.text: Charts are generated as C code (the transitions of each state as if / else if, and the entry and exit actions inlined), so they can be part of the ECU code. A back-to-back test in the test suite checks the generated chart against the simulation sample by sample, with zero tolerance.

docs.title: Subsystems
docs.text:
A subsystem is a block that contains its own diagram. Subsystems structure a model the way functions structure code. In ECU work, each subsystem is typically one software function (throttle control, fuel, ignition), and the generated C code will follow that structure.

Here the throttle example is grouped so that everything running on the ECU (sensor sampling, error and PI controller) is inside one subsystem:

Double-click it to open it. The breadcrumb bar shows the path back to the model:

docs.title: In the editor
docs.text:
Action How Group blocks into a subsystem select them, Edit → Create Subsystem from Selection (⌘G / Ctrl+G) Open a subsystem double-click it Go back up click a breadcrumb, or View → Up to Parent (⌘↑ / Ctrl+Up) Add an empty subsystem Library → Ports & Subsystems → Subsystem

Lines crossing the selection boundary become In/Out ports. Undo works across levels and opens the subsystem where the change is undone.

docs.title: Atomic subsystems: one ECU task
docs.text:
An ECU's operating system runs its software in tasks with fixed periods, such as a 10 ms task for idle speed and throttle control and a 100 ms task for temperatures. In Nervus, a subsystem with a sample_time is such a task:

  • Every block inside that inherits its sample time (-1, e.g. Gain, Sum, Counter, Discrete PID with sample_time = -1) runs at the task period. Blocks with their own sample time keep it, and an inner task keeps its own period.
  • The inputs are sampled at the start of each period and the outputs held until the next one, as if the task read its inputs from RAM when it starts.
  • Blocks with continuous states (Integrator, Transfer Function) are not allowed inside. Use their discrete versions.
  • The block shows its period (⏱ 10 ms). In generated C the multirate scheduler runs each task's blocks at its rate, or, with one function per task, each task becomes its own C function (see C code generation).

So you set the period in one place, and every block in the task follows it: change sample_time to "Ts_fast" and the whole task moves with the workspace variable.

docs.title: Enabled subsystems
docs.text:
Tick enable_port in a subsystem's Properties to give it an extra last input, ⏻ enable. While the enable is ≤ 0 nothing inside runs: outputs and discrete states are held, and continuous states stop. Typical use: a function that only runs in one operating mode, with the enable coming from a State Chart's mode output.

when_enabled Discrete states when enabled again held (default) continue from where they stopped reset restart from their initial values

The enable is decided once per time step (when the blocks inside execute) and held during solver sub-steps. The generated C wraps the subsystem's blocks in if (enabled) and resets their states the same way, which the test suite checks against the simulation with zero tolerance.

docs.title: Triggered subsystems
docs.text:
Set trigger to rising, falling or either to give the subsystem a last input, trigger. The subsystem then runs only when that signal has an edge, and holds its outputs and states in between. Use it for event-driven functions: counting crank teeth, latching a value when a button is pressed, or running a task each time a CAN message arrives.

trigger Runs when the trigger signal goes rising from ≤ 0 to > 0 falling from > 0 to ≤ 0 either either way

The trigger is checked each time the blocks inside would execute, so drive it with a discrete signal of the same rate as those blocks. The first execution only records the trigger value, so nothing runs before the first real edge. Blocks with continuous states (integrators, transfer functions) are not allowed inside; use their discrete versions. A subsystem can have both an enable and a trigger input (data inputs first, then enable, then trigger). It then runs on an edge only while it is enabled. The generated C checks the edge the same way, and the tests compare it with the simulation with zero tolerance.

docs.title: Variant subsystems: several implementations of one component
docs.text:
A subsystem can have variants: alternative implementations with the same inputs and outputs. Typical uses: a petrol and a diesel engine model, a simple and a detailed sensor model, or the controller for two vehicle versions. Only the active variant is simulated and turned into C code.

Select a subsystem and press Create Variants… (or Variants…) in the Properties panel:

  • Add (copy of active) creates a new variant as a copy of the active one; open the subsystem and change it.
  • Condition chooses the variant from model workspace variables, e.g. ENGINE == 2. Comparisons (==, !=/~=, <, <=, >, >=) and and/&&, or/||, not/~ are allowed. A variant with an empty condition is the default, used when no condition is true. It is an error if several conditions are true at once.
  • Without any conditions, you pick the active variant by hand.

The block shows the active variant (◆ petrol). Opening the subsystem shows and edits the active variant; switch variants to edit another. A parameter sweep can switch variants too: simulate(model, 10, params={"ENGINE": 2}).

engine = Subsystem(system=petrol_engine)
engine.active_variant = "petrol"
engine.add_variant("diesel", diesel_engine, condition="ENGINE == 2")
engine.variants["petrol"].condition = "ENGINE == 1"

docs.title: Function-call subsystems
docs.text:
Sometimes logic, not a clock, decides when a function runs: store a value each time the engine is switched off, or run a learning routine once per drive cycle. Set trigger to function_call: the subsystem then runs once every time the trigger value changes. The caller, usually a State Chart, increments a counter output whenever it wants the function to run:

input u
output calls = 0

state low
state high
  entry: calls = calls + 1      # call the subsystem once, every time we enter "high"

transition low -> high: u > 0.5
transition high -> low: u < -0.5

Connect calls to the subsystem's trigger input (marked ƒ()). The subsystem runs in the same time step as the call, after the chart, and holds its outputs and states between calls. In generated C it becomes if (call counter changed) { ... } around its blocks.

docs.title: Masks: reusable components with parameters
docs.text:
A masked subsystem has its own parameters, like a function's arguments. The blocks inside use them in their expressions, and each copy of the subsystem can have different values. This is how you build reusable components such as an engine model with a displacement parameter.

Select a subsystem and press Create Mask… (or Edit Mask…) in the Properties panel:

  • Mask parameters: name, value, unit and description. Values can be numbers, vectors, or expressions of model workspace variables (3 * base).
  • Icon text: shown on the block; \n starts a new line.
  • Description: shown in the Properties panel.

The parameters then appear in the Properties panel of the subsystem, like the parameters of any block:

Names are looked up from the inside out: a block sees the parameters of the nearest mask first, then those of outer masks, then the model workspace. In generated C, mask parameters are per-instance values. Only bare model workspace variables become shared calibration parameters.

from nervus.core import Variable

engine = Subsystem(system=engine_diagram)
engine.mask.add(Variable("displacement", 1.6e-3, "Swept volume", "m³"))
engine.mask_icon = "Engine\\n1.6 l"

docs.title: In Python
docs.text:
from nervus import Diagram, simulate
from nervus.blocks import Gain, Inport, Integrator, Outport, Scope, Step, Subsystem, Sum

plant = Diagram("plant")
u = plant.add(Inport(port=1), name="u")
e = plant.add(Sum(signs="+-"), name="e")
k = plant.add(Gain(gain="1/tau"), name="k")  # uses the model workspace
y = plant.add(Integrator(), name="y")
plant.connect(u, (e, 0))
plant.connect(y, (e, 1))
plant.chain(e, k, y, plant.add(Outport(port=1), name="y_out"))

model = Diagram("model")
model.workspace["tau"] = 0.5
sub = model.add(Subsystem(system=plant), name="plant")
model.chain(model.add(Step(time=0.0)), sub, model.add(Scope()))

res = simulate(model, 2.0)
res["plant/y"]  # blocks inside subsystems are named by path

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Before simulation, the compiler flattens the hierarchy. The In and Out blocks inside subsystems become identity nodes, so sorting, signal widths and sample times work across subsystem boundaries exactly as in a flat model. Every block keeps its path name for results and error messages.

In model files, a subsystem block carries its diagram in a nested "system" entry (schema version 3).

docs.title: Test cases, scenarios and results
docs.text:
Model-based development lives on reproducible tests: the same scenario, run after every change, with clear pass/fail criteria. In Nervus a test case is saved with the model and contains:

  • inputs: time signals for the model's top-level In blocks (the scenario),
  • parameters: workspace overrides and/or a parameter-set file (the calibration under test),
  • a stop time,
  • checks: what must be true about the results.

docs.title: In the editor
docs.text:
Open the Test Manager tab (next to Diagnostics):

Button Does New / Edit… opens the test case editor: inputs, parameter overrides, parameter set, stop time, checks Duplicate / Delete as named; every change is undoable and saved with the model Run selected / Run all runs the tests in the background (Simulation → Run All Tests, ⌘T)

The Result column shows ✓ pass / ✗ fail. Details names the failing check and why ("reached at t = 0.41"). Double-click a result to open it in the Data Inspector.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
In the test case editor, every top-level In block has a row. Enter points as time: value pairs:

0: 5, 0.2: 60, 1.2: 20

With interpolation hold this is a staircase (5 until 0.2 s, then 60, then 20); with linear it ramps between the points. Vector inputs use [ ]: 0: [1 2], 1: [3 4]. Leave a row empty to use the In block's own value.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
Check Arguments Passes when bounds lower, upper, optional t_from, t_to the signal stays within [lower, upper] (in the time window) final_value value, tolerance the last value is value ± tolerance reaches value, before, optional direction=below the signal reaches the value before the given time max / min value the maximum is at most / the minimum is at least the value baseline path, tolerance the signal matches a saved result file within the tolerance (regression test)

Signals are named as in results: plate_angle, ECU/throttle_pi, mux:1.

docs.title: Drawing test signals: the Signal Builder
docs.text:
For signals that are easier to draw than to type, put a Signal Builder block (Library → Sources) in the model and double-click it:

  • Each signal is a plot and one output of the block (Add signal, Rename, Remove). Drag a point to move it, double-click in a plot to add one, select a point and press Delete to remove it. The table on the right shows the selected signal's points exactly; type in it for precise values.
  • Between two points the signal is a straight line. Two points at the same time make a jump (the pedal pressed in one instant); after the last point the value is held. The solver stops exactly at every point, so jumps are sharp.
  • Groups are scenarios with the same signals: a tip-in, a panic stop, a cold start. Add copies the current group as a starting point. Play this group chooses the one the simulation uses (the block's group parameter, also in the Properties panel).
  • The Text tab shows the same signals as text, e.g. pedal: 0 0, 1 0, 1 80, 6 80 (pairs of time and value); Apply writes them to the block, as one step you can undo.

Test cases set the model's In blocks; a Signal Builder lives inside the model, so it suits scenarios you switch by hand while you develop, and models without top-level inputs.

docs.title: Test suites as files
docs.text: Export… in the Test Manager saves the selected test cases (or all of them) to a .nervtest file, and Import… adds the test cases of such a file to the open model. Use it to share a test suite between model variants, or to keep the tests of a component in its own file next to the library.

docs.title: Test report
docs.text:
After a test run, Report… saves a self-contained HTML page with every test case, its parameters and every check with its result, plus the model coverage when it was measured. It works in light and dark mode and can be attached to a review or archived with a release.

from nervus.testing import load_suite, run_tests, save_html_report, save_suite

save_suite(model.tests, "throttle_tests.nervtest")
results = run_tests(model, load_suite("throttle_tests.nervtest"))
save_html_report(results, "report.html", "Throttle controller tests")

docs.title: Parameter sweeps and Monte Carlo runs
docs.text:
To see how a design behaves over a range of parameters, or with production tolerances, run it many times from Python and collect a few numbers (metrics) per run:

from nervus.sweep import monte_carlo, sweep

# Every combination: 3 × 2 = 6 runs.
table = sweep(
    model,
    {"Kp_stft": [0.05, 0.1, 0.2], "n_exh": [8, 20]},  # the lambda control example
    metrics={"lambda_min": lambda r: r["lambda_cyl"].min()},
)
print(table.summary())

# Tolerances: 100 runs with random parameters (normal, uniform or choice). Here, for the lambda control
# example: injectors that deliver up to a few percent more or less fuel than their nominal flow.
table = monte_carlo(
    model,
    {"injector_error": ("normal", 0.0, 0.02), "tau_sensor": ("uniform", 0.08, 0.12)},
    runs=100,
    metrics={"ltft_end": lambda r: r["ECU/ltft_pct"][-1]},
    seed=1,
)
table.to_csv("monte_carlo.csv")  # one row per run: parameters, metrics, error
lowest = table.column("ltft_end").min()

A metric is any function of the result that returns one number. Runs that fail (for example a parameter value that makes the model invalid) are kept with their error message, so they show up in the table.

docs.title: In the editor
docs.text:
Analysis → Parameter Sweep / Monte Carlo… (Ctrl+Shift+W) does the same without code. Add the workspace variables to vary and their values: a list (0.5, 1, 1.5, 3) or linspace(0.5, 3, 6) for a sweep over every combination, or normal(mean, std) / uniform(low, high) with a number of runs and a seed for Monte Carlo. Choose a signal (an Out block or any block) and a metric of it: final value, max, min, mean, RMS, peak-to-peak or the time of the maximum. Run simulates in the background (the model is locked meanwhile; Stop ends early) and shows:

  • Signal: the signal of every run on top of each other; with many runs (Monte Carlo) in one transparent colour, so where the runs bunch up is darker;
  • Metric: the metric against the first variable, one line per value of the second (sweep), or a histogram (Monte Carlo);
  • Table: one row per run, with Export CSV….

Ready-made metrics are also available in Python: metric("plate_angle", "max") from nervus.sweep.

docs.title: Data Inspector
docs.text: Simulation → Data Inspector (⌘I) keeps the last 20 runs, both normal simulations and test results. Check runs and signals to overlay them. With two runs selected it shows the largest difference, and Difference to first run plots the deviation directly. Save run… writes a .nervres file (use it as a baseline), Load… reads one (or an MDF4 measurement, or a vehicle log), and Export writes CSV, MATLAB .mat or MDF4.

docs.title: MDF4 measurement files
docs.text:
MDF4 (.mf4, ASAM MDF) is the file format of INCA, CANape, vehicle data loggers and test benches (uv sync --extra mdf). Load… also reads MDF4 files, so a vehicle measurement can be overlaid on a simulation, and Export writes a run as MDF4 to open it in the calibration tool. An MDF file keeps every channel group at its own rate (a logger records each CAN message at its own period); on loading, all channels are put on the time base of the group with the most samples, the others linearly interpolated. Text and byte-array channels are skipped.

from nervus.mdf import mdf_channels, read_mdf, write_mdf

mdf_channels("drive.mf4")  # {'n_engine': 'rpm', 'T_coolant': 'degC', ...}
rec = read_mdf("drive.mf4", ["n_engine", "T_coolant"], raster=0.01)
write_mdf(res, "simulation.mf4", units={"rpm": "rpm"})

A recorded channel can drive a model: FromWorkspace(time=rec.t, data=rec["n_engine"]), or an In block in a test case.

docs.title: In Python
docs.text:
from nervus import load, simulate
from nervus.core import Check, Signal, TestCase
from nervus.testing import compare_results, run_tests

model = load("examples/throttle_ecu.nervus")
for result in run_tests(model, base_dir="examples"):  # the tests stored in the model
    print(result.summary())

# A scenario for a top-level In block called "pedal":
res = simulate(model, inputs={"pedal": Signal.steps([(0, 5), (0.2, 60)])})

# Results
res.save("baseline.nervres")
res.to_mat("run.mat")  # for MATLAB users
old = type(res).load("baseline.nervres")
print(compare_results(res, old))  # max |difference| per signal

# A new test case
case = TestCase(
    "tip-in",
    parameter_set="throttle_tight.nervcal",
    checks=[Check("reaches", "plate_angle", {"value": 59.0, "before": 0.35})],
)
model.tests.append(case)

Because tests are plain Python objects, the same checks work inside pytest, which is how you run model regression tests in CI. The Nervus repository does exactly that for the examples.

docs.title: Signals from logged data
docs.text: Signal.from_csv("drive_log.csv", "rpm") reads a column of a CSV file (first column = time), for example data exported from a vehicle logger, to replay a real drive as a test input. For scanner app logs and CAN logs use read_log, for MDF4 files read_mdf (above).

docs.title: Verification: coverage, requirements and the Model Advisor
Model coverage
docs.text:
Passing tests only say something if they exercise the model. Model coverage measures which decision outcomes the tests reached:

Block Outcomes Switch input 0 passed, input 2 passed Relational Operator, Compare To Constant, Logical Operator true, false Saturation, Dead Zone below, within, above Integrator, PID (with limits) at upper limit, at lower limit, between limits Relay on, off Rate Limiter rising limited, falling limited, not limited 1-D Lookup Table each interval between breakpoints, below and above the range State Chart every state, every transition

The Test Manager measures coverage on every run and shows it next to the buttons (Coverage 50 %). Coverage report opens an HTML report listing every block with its outcomes, exercised (green, with counts) or never reached (red). A red outcome usually means a missing test case. For example, the idle speed example's tests never drive the controller to its upper limit, so no test checks full-throttle authority.

From Python:

from nervus import load
from nervus.coverage import Coverage
from nervus.testing import run_tests

model = load("examples/idle_speed_control.nervus")
cov = Coverage()
run_tests(model, coverage=cov)
print(cov.summary())  # Decision coverage: 4/8 outcomes (50 %) ...
cov.save_html("coverage.html")

simulate(model, coverage=cov) measures a single run. One Coverage object can collect several runs.

docs.title: Condition coverage and MC/DC
docs.text:
Decisions with several conditions, the Logical Operator block with two or more inputs (enable AND speed_ok AND no_fault), are measured more strictly as well:

Measure Satisfied when condition coverage every condition was true at least once and false at least once MC/DC (modified condition/decision coverage) for every condition, two evaluations that differ only in that condition gave different results: each condition is shown to change the decision on its own

MC/DC is what ISO 26262 recommends for the most critical software (ASIL D) and DO-178C requires for level A. It finds tests that look complete but are not: 000 and 111 make every condition of a three-input AND true and false (100 % condition coverage) but show none of them independently (0 % MC/DC). The minimal set for an AND of n conditions is n + 1 evaluations: all true, and each condition false on its own (111, 011, 101, 110).

The Test Manager shows MC/DC next to the coverage, and the coverage report lists each decision with the conditions shown (green) and, for the others, the evaluation a test still needs, for example:

permit: condition 2: needs (1, 0, 1) → 0 (the pair (1, 1, 1) → 1 / (1, 0, 1) → 0)

State chart transition guards with several conditions count as decisions too, named after the transition (modes: crank -> idle); nested guards such as a > 0.5 and (b > 0.5 or not c > 0.5) are evaluated exactly, so masking is taken into account (with c false, b cannot change the result, and the report asks for an evaluation with c true).

From Python: cov.mcdc_percent, cov.condition_percent, cov.mcdc_missing().

docs.title: Requirements traceability
docs.text:
ECU software is written against requirements ("the engine idles at 800 ± 50 rpm when warm"), and a review asks for each one: which part of the model implements it, and which test shows that it works? The Requirements tab (next to the Test Manager) keeps that link.

  1. Add requirements: press Add and type the id, title and text in the table, or Import CSV… a file exported from Excel, DOORS, Polarion or Jira. The file needs an id column; title (or name), text (or description) and source are optional, and both , and ; separators work.
  2. Link blocks: right-click a block (usually an ECU subsystem) ▸ Requirements… and tick the requirements it implements.
  3. Link test cases: in the Test Manager's test editor, list the ids in the Requirements field.
  4. Run the tests (Ctrl+T). Each requirement's status updates:
Status Meaning verified it has test cases and all of them passed failed a test case linked to it failed not run it has test cases that have not run yet not tested a block implements it, but no test case checks it not implemented no block is linked to it

Report… writes the traceability matrix as an HTML page for reviews; double-click a row to show its block. Renaming a requirement's id updates the links in blocks and test cases. The Model Advisor warns about requirements without blocks or tests, and about links to ids that do not exist. Requirements are saved in the model file.

from nervus.core.requirements import Requirement, read_csv, trace, write_report
from nervus.testing import run_tests

for req in read_csv("requirements.csv"):
    model.requirements.add(req)
model.block("ECU").meta["requirements"] = ["IDLE-01", "IDLE-02"]
model.tests[0].requirements = ["IDLE-02"]
results = {r.case.name: r.passed for r in run_tests(model)}
for row in trace(model, results):
    print(row.requirement.id, row.status)
write_report(model, "traceability.html", results)

docs.title: Model Advisor
docs.text:
Analysis → Model Advisor (⇧⌘A / Ctrl+Shift+A) checks the model for practices that often cause bugs in ECU software. Click a finding to open the block.

Rule Checks for float-equality == / != on floating-point signals division Product blocks that divide (possible division by zero) antiwindup PI controllers with output limits but no anti-windup, or an integral term without limits implicit-sampling discrete blocks that read a continuous signal without a Zero-Order Hold chart-unreachable chart states that can never become active chart-shadowed chart transitions that come after an always-true transition lookup-extrapolation lookup tables that extrapolate linearly beyond the calibrated range workspace-docs workspace variables without a unit or description (they end up in the A2L file) workspace-unused workspace variables no block uses default-names blocks inside subsystems that still have default names 
from nervus.advisor import advise

for finding in advise(model):
    print(finding)

docs.title: Model workspace and calibrations
docs.text: Engine control software is code plus calibration. Nervus keeps the two apart: block parameters can refer to named workspace variables, and the values of those variables can be saved and loaded as parameter sets (.nervcal files).

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Each variable has a name, a value, and optional unit, minimum, maximum and description. A value can be:

  • a number: 1.5
  • a vector or matrix: [1 2 3], [1 2; 3 4] (MATLAB style) or [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
  • an expression of variables defined above it: Kp / Ti, 2*pi*f_c

Values outside [min, max] are reported as warnings in Diagnostics. These ranges will also go into the A2L calibration file once that exists (see the roadmap).

docs.title: Block parameters as expressions
docs.text:
Any numeric parameter (numbers, vectors, matrices, sample times) can be an expression of workspace variables:

from nervus import Diagram
from nervus.blocks import DiscretePID, Gain, ZeroOrderHold
from nervus.core import Variable

d = Diagram()
d.workspace.add(Variable("Kp", 1.5, "Proportional gain", "%/°", min=0))
d.workspace["Ti"] = 0.04
d.workspace["Ts"] = 0.01
pid = d.add(DiscretePID(P="Kp", I="Kp/Ti", sample_time="Ts"))

Expressions are stored in the model file exactly as written and evaluated every time the model is compiled. In the editor, the canvas shows the expression (e.g. Kp) instead of the number:

Expressions may use + - * / ** %, the functions sqrt, exp, log, sin, cos, abs and the constants pi, e, inf, true and false. Comparisons (==, !=, <, <=, >, >=) and and, or, not give 1 (true) or 0 (false), so Kp * (MODE == 2) works. The MATLAB spellings ~=, &&, || and ~ are accepted too.

docs.title: Autocompletion and Find Usages
docs.text:
While you type a parameter in the Properties panel, the names of the variables the block can see (the model workspace and the masks around it) pop up; Enter or a click completes the word under the cursor, so Kp / T becomes Kp / Ti.

Select a variable in the Model Workspace and press Find Usages to list every place that uses it: block parameters (gain = 1 / r_wheel), State Chart param declarations, mask variables, variant conditions and other workspace variables. Double-click a row to open the subsystem and select the block. Inside a masked subsystem whose mask defines the same name, the mask's own variable is meant, so those blocks are not listed. From Python: d.usages("r_wheel").

docs.title: Calibration maps over shared axes
docs.text:
ECU software is full of curves and maps over the same few axes: engine speed, load, coolant temperature. For one map, use a 1-D or 2-D Lookup Table. When several maps share an axis, use a Prelookup block per axis and an Interpolation using Prelookup block per map: the breakpoint search runs once, and every map reuses its result (index k and fraction f).

Put the axes and tables in the workspace, so they can be calibrated and swapped with parameter sets:

d.workspace["speed_axis"] = [800, 1500, 3000, 6000]  # rpm
d.workspace["load_axis"] = [0.2, 0.5, 1.0]
d.workspace["ign_map"] = [[10, 8, 5], [20, 16, 10], [30, 25, 18], [35, 30, 22]]  # ° before TDC
speed = d.add(Prelookup(breakpoints="speed_axis"))
load = d.add(Prelookup(breakpoints="load_axis"))
ign = d.add(Interpolation(dimensions=2, table="ign_map"))  # inputs: k1, f1, k2, f2

The result is identical to a 2-D Lookup Table with linear interpolation, in the simulation and in the generated C. Hover over the Interpolation block's ports to see which input is which.

docs.title: Data types and constants for the ECU
docs.text:
Two columns of the Model Workspace control how a variable ends up in generated C code:

Column Meaning Example Type the storage type in C: double (default), single, int8 … uint32, boolean, or fixed point fixdt(signed, bits, fraction_bits) an ignition map as fixdt(1,16,7): 2 bytes per value, steps of 1/128 ° Cal. ticked: calibratable, in RAM and in the A2L file. Unticked: a constant in ROM (flash), not in the A2L file a sensor's fixed conversion factor

Smaller types matter on an ECU: a 16 × 16 map takes 2 KB as double but 512 bytes as int16. The simulation uses exactly the value the type can hold (hover over the value to see it), so the model and the generated C stay bit-true. In C, the parameter is stored as integers and scaled where a block reads it:

/* ign_map: fixdt(1,16,7): value = 0.0078125 * stored + 0 */
int16_T ign_map[12];
...
y = ((real_T)ign_P.ign_map[(r) * 3u + (c)] * 0.0078125 + 0.0) ...

The A2L file describes the stored type (e.g. SWORD) and the scaling (COEFFS_LINEAR), so a calibration tool such as INCA or CANape shows and edits physical values. Typed parameters work for scalar parameters (gains, limits, thresholds) and for lookup tables and their breakpoints. Matrix parameters (matrix gains, state-space matrices) must stay double.

from nervus.core import Variable

ws.add(Variable("ign_map", ign, "Ignition advance", "°", data_type="fixdt(1,16,7)"))
ws.add(Variable("speed_axis", [800, 1500, 3000, 6000], unit="rpm", data_type="uint16"))
ws.add(Variable("k_sensor", 0.0125, "ADC to volts", "V", calibratable=False))  # const, in ROM

docs.title: Data dictionary: signal objects
docs.text:
Workspace variables describe parameters; the Data Dictionary (a tab next to the Model Workspace) describes signals. A signal object has a name, a data type (inherit = any), a unit, a range and a description. Right-click a wire and choose Name Signal… to give the source output a name; the name is shown under the wire and binds the output to the signal object of that name. Then:

  • the data type is checked when the model is compiled (an output that must be uint16 but is double is an error naming the block);
  • the range is checked after every simulation: values outside [min, max] are reported as warnings, e.g. signal engine_speed is above its maximum 7000 from t = 7 s (up to 8000 rpm);
  • results can be read by the name: res["engine_speed"], also for a subsystem's output;
  • the generated A2L file lists the signal as a measurement with its name, description, unit and limits, so INCA or CANape show engine_speed [rpm] instead of an internal variable name.

Each name can be given to one output. Double-click a row to show the block that drives the signal; names without an object are listed too, so Add with such a row selected creates the object. Signal objects are saved with the model, and every change can be undone.

from nervus.core.dictionary import SignalObject

model.signals.add(SignalObject("engine_speed", "double", "rpm", 0, 7000, "Crankshaft speed"))
model.name_signal("engine", 0, "engine_speed")
simulate(model)["engine_speed"]

docs.title: Parameter sets
docs.text:
from nervus import ParameterSet, load, simulate

d = load("examples/throttle_pi.nervus")
ParameterSet.from_workspace(d.workspace, "baseline").save("baseline.nervcal")

d.workspace.apply(ParameterSet.load("examples/throttle_tight.nervcal").values)
res = simulate(d)

res = simulate(d, params={"Kp": 2.0})  # temporary override for a single run

A .nervcal file is plain JSON:

{
  "format": "nervus-parameters",
  "schema_version": 1,
  "name": "tight",
  "description": "Higher gains: less overshoot",
  "values": {"Kp": 3.0, "Ki": 80.0}
}

In the editor, use Load set… / Save set… in the Model Workspace panel. Loading is a single undo step.

docs.title: Linear analysis
docs.text:
Analysis → Linear Analysis… (⌘L / Ctrl+L) linearizes the model from a top-level In block to an Out block.

  1. Add an In block where the input of the system is (e.g. the throttle command) and an Out block at the output (e.g. engine speed).
  2. Choose the operating point: the initial states, or the steady state (trim) for the In blocks' values.
  3. Press Linearize.

You get the transfer function, the poles (and whether the system is stable), the DC gain, a Bode plot, the gain and phase margins, and the step response.

The margins treat G(s) as the open loop of a unity-feedback system. To analyse a control loop, put the In block at the controller input (the error), the Out block at the plant output, and leave the loop open. A rule of thumb for a robust loop: a phase margin of at least 45° and a gain margin of at least 6 dB.

The Step response tab shows G and the closed loop G / (1 + G). Nyquist draws G(jω) (solid for positive, dashed for negative frequencies): for a stable open loop, the closed loop is stable when the curve does not encircle −1. Root locus shows the closed-loop poles of k·G(s) as k grows from 0: from the open-loop poles (×) to the zeros (○) or infinity.

docs.title: PID tuning
docs.text:
The PID Tuning tab needs no In or Out blocks. Choose a PID Controller (or Discrete PID) block, PI or PID, and a phase margin, then press Tune. Nervus opens the loop at the block's output, linearizes the plant the controller sees, and shapes the loop: a PI has its zero at ωc/4 (Ti = 4/ωc), a PID also a derivative with Td = Ti/4 filtered at 10·ωc. It picks the fastest crossover ωc that keeps the phase margin, at least 6 dB gain margin and a stable closed loop, limited to 2π/(20·Ts) for a discrete controller; spare margin is used for faster integral action. The plot compares the closed-loop step responses with the current and tuned gains.

Apply to Block writes the gains; a gain given as a workspace variable (P = Kp) changes the variable. The tuned gains are a robust starting point. Discrete blocks with state (filters, delays) cut the loop while the plant is linearized.

From Python: nervus.analysis.linearize, trim, LinearModel.bode() / .margins() / .nyquist() / .root_locus(), and plant_at + tune_pid for PID tuning.

docs.title: Development boards
docs.text:
Code → Board Project… turns the generated code of a model (usually its ECU subsystem) into a complete project for a development board with CAN. The board then runs the code like an ECU, and the Calibration window measures and calibrates it over XCP on CAN, as it would a production ECU. What to buy: Hardware.

Board CAN pins Tools to build and flash STM32 Nucleo-G474RE FDCAN1: PA12 (TX), PA11 (RX) arm-none-eabi-gcc, STM32CubeG4, STM32CubeProgrammer (flashes over the Nucleo's USB cable) ESP32 (ESP-IDF) TWAI: GPIO 5 (TX), GPIO 4 (RX) ESP-IDF (idf.py build flash) This computer none: a test drives the CAN frames your C compiler and make (for trying a project without hardware)

Every board needs a 3.3 V CAN transceiver between its CAN pins and the bus.

Not tested on hardware yet: The board layers follow ST's and Espressif's published APIs, and the portable parts (the main loop, the XCP slave, the generated code) are tested on this computer. They have not run on a real board yet. If you try one, please report what happens (Help wanted).

docs.title: What a project contains
docs.text:
File What it does ECU.c, ECU.h the generated code (as in C code generation) main.c initialises the board, CAN and the model; calls the step function every base period; answers XCP io.c yours to edit: reads the sensors into the model's inputs and drives the actuators from its outputs. Nervus never overwrites it. board.c, nervus_target.h the board's hardware layer: the clock, CAN send and receive nervus_xcp.c, nervus_xcp.h a small XCP-on-CAN slave in portable C: the tool can read the model's signals and states and change its calibration parameters, and nothing else ECU.a2l the A2L file with the board's XCP CAN identifiers and bit rate Makefile / CMakeLists.txt the board's build

Build runs the board's build tool and then writes the addresses of the built program into the A2L file, so the Calibration window (or INCA and CANape) finds every variable. Flash programs the board over USB. The buttons are enabled when the tools are installed.

docs.title: Steps for a board
docs.text:
1. Install the board's tools (see the table above) and connect the board with a USB data cable.
  2. Code → Board Project…: choose the subsystem, the board, the CAN bit rate and the XCP identifiers, and a folder. Press Create project.
  3. Edit io.c: which ADC channel is the throttle sensor, which PWM drives the motor. Until you do, the inputs stay at their initial values.
  4. Build, then Flash.
  5. Connect the transceiver to the bus and a CAN adapter to the laptop. In Tools → Calibration… choose XCP on CAN, the project's A2L file and your adapter, and Connect.

docs.title: In Python
docs.text:
from nervus.codegen.boards import create_project, build, fill_a2l_addresses

create_project(model.block("ECU"), "esp32", "ecu_esp32", request_id=0x7E0, response_id=0x7E8, bitrate=500000)
build("ecu_esp32", "esp32")
fill_a2l_addresses("ecu_esp32")

docs.title: Still to come
docs.text: The XCP slave on the board answers polling (read and write); DAQ lists and the working and reference pages are already in the virtual ECU and will follow on the boards. Processor-in-the-loop (the board runs the code, the plant runs in Nervus, step by step) and hardware-in-the-loop (the plant in real time against a real ECU) come next, once a board has been tested.

docs.title: Measurement and calibration
docs.text:
Tools → Calibration… measures and calibrates an ECU while it runs, like ETAS INCA or Vector CANape: it reads the ECU's variables (measurements) and changes its parameters (characteristics: values, curves and maps) over XCP. What the ECU contains, and where, comes from its A2L file.
