Only on a bench or a test vehicle: Changing an ECU's calibration changes how the vehicle behaves. Use it on test benches and test vehicles, never on a vehicle on public roads. Changes to emissions or safety functions are illegal in most countries. Nervus refuses values outside the limits in the A2L file and logs every write, but you are responsible for what you change.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
Choose the target:

Target For Address Virtual ECU of this model trying everything without hardware: the generated C code of the model (or of a subsystem such as ECU) runs in real time on your computer the subsystem XCP on UDP / XCP on TCP ECUs and development boards on Ethernet host:port, e.g. 192.168.1.10:5555 XCP on CAN ECUs on CAN, through a CAN adapter (Hardware) interface:channel:bitrate:request id:response id, e.g. pcan:PCAN_USBBUS1:500000:0x7E0:0x7E8

For a real ECU, choose its A2L file first. If the A2L file describes the connection (the CAN identifiers and baud rate, or the IP address and port in its IF_DATA XCP), the address is filled in from it. Press Connect.

ECUs that protect calibration ask for seed and key: the ECU sends a random seed, and the tool must answer with the key computed by the supplier's algorithm. Put that algorithm in a Python file with a function key(seed: bytes) -> bytes and choose it with Seed & key… before you connect.

The virtual ECU needs a C compiler (as for software-in-the-loop tests). Nervus generates the code, compiles it, takes the addresses of the variables from the compiled code and writes them into the A2L file, so it behaves like a real ECU: the same windows, the same protocol, the same file.

docs.title: Measure
docs.text:
Tick measurements in the list on the left. They appear in the plot (the last 10 seconds) and in the table with their current value. Nervus asks the ECU to send them by itself at every cycle of its task (DAQ lists, with the ECU's time stamps). If the ECU cannot (no DAQ, or a value is too big for a CAN packet), Nervus reads them in turn (polling); the status line says which.

● Record records the ticked measurements until you press it again. The recording opens in the Data Inspector, next to simulations, and can be saved as MDF4 (for INCA, CANape and other tools) or as a Nervus result.

docs.title: Calibrate
docs.text:
Click a characteristic to read it from the ECU:

  • a value: one cell;
  • a curve: its values over the axis points, with a plot;
  • a map: a table with the X axis down the side and the Y axis across the top, coloured by value, and a plot with one line per column.

Edit a cell and press Enter: Nervus checks the value against the limits in the A2L file, converts it to the ECU's raw value (with the conversion method of the A2L file), writes only the bytes that change, and reads the characteristic back. Every write is listed in the write log with the old and the new value.

Working page / Reference page. ECUs keep two copies of their calibration: the working page in RAM, which you change, and the reference page with the original, safe values. Switching to the reference page puts the safe calibration back in one click (it cannot be changed); switching back restores your changes.

docs.title: A2L files
docs.text:
Nervus reads the A2L files of any ECU (ASAM MCD-2 MC): measurements (also arrays and bit masks), characteristics of type VALUE, VAL_BLK, CURVE and MAP, axis points stored in the record (STD_AXIS), computed (FIX_AXIS) or shared with other maps (COM_AXIS and AXIS_PTS), conversion methods (IDENTICAL, LINEAR, RAT_FUNC, tables with and without interpolation, verbal tables), record layouts with alignment and static layouts, byte order, memory segments (only DATA segments are written), and the XCP connection.

from nervus.a2l import load_a2l
from nervus.xcp import UdpTransport, XcpMaster

a2l = load_a2l("ecu.a2l")
master = XcpMaster(UdpTransport("192.168.1.10", 5555))
master.connect()
ign = a2l.characteristics["ign_map"]
record = master.upload(ign.address, ign.size(a2l))
table = ign.decode(record, a2l)  # {"values": [[...], ...], "axes": [[rpm...], [load...]]}
table["values"][2][3] += 1.5  # one more degree of ignition advance at one point
master.download(ign.address, ign.encode(table["values"], a2l, record))

docs.title: XCP from Python
docs.text:
nervus.xcp.XcpMaster is the same tool without the window, for scripts and automated tests:

from nervus.xcp import CanTransport, REFERENCE_PAGE, XcpMaster

master = XcpMaster(CanTransport(bus, 0x7E0, 0x7E8), a2l="ecu.a2l")
master.connect()
master.unlock(my_key_function)  # if the ECU is protected
master.start_daq(["engine_speed", "lambda"], event=0)
samples = master.read_daq()  # {"engine_speed": [(t, value), ...], ...}
master.set_page(REFERENCE_PAGE)  # the safe calibration

A virtual ECU from the command line, for INCA, CANape or a script:

uv run python -m nervus.vecu examples/throttle_ecu.nervus --subsystem ECU --udp 5555

It writes ECU.a2l with the real addresses and serves XCP on UDP port 5555 (and on CAN with --can).

docs.title: Against the simulation
docs.text: A model with an XCP Slave block can be calibrated while it simulates: give its CAN Bus block an interface (for example virtual), set pacing to real time, and connect with XCP on CAN to the same interface and channel (see the XCP tutorial).

docs.title: CAN communication
docs.text:
ECUs exchange signals over CAN. Which bits of a frame carry which signal, and how to convert them to physical units, is described in a DBC file. Nervus reads DBC files (uv sync --extra can). Two blocks in the CAN library convert between signals and bytes; the others simulate whole CAN buses (below):

Block Input Output CAN Unpack the frame's data bytes (a vector: 8, or up to 64 for CAN FD) one output per signal, in physical units CAN Pack one input per signal, in physical units the data bytes (uint8)

Set dbc_file (relative paths are relative to the model file), choose the message from the drop-down, and optionally list the signals to use (empty = all, in DBC order).

docs.title: Conversion
docs.text:
Each signal occupies length bits starting at start bit:

\[ \mathrm{physical} = \mathrm{raw} \cdot \mathrm{factor} + \mathrm{offset} \]
  • Intel byte order (@1 in the DBC): the start bit is the signal's least significant bit; bytes are in little-endian order.
  • Motorola byte order (@0): the start bit is the signal's most significant bit; bytes are in big-endian order.
  • Signed signals (-) are two's complement.

CAN Pack rounds to the nearest raw value (half away from zero) and saturates to the bit field, so an out-of-range value is sent as the closest representable one.

docs.title: Bit-exact and generatable
docs.text: Packing and unpacking use the same 64-bit integer arithmetic in the simulation and in the generated C code. The test suite checks the decoding against the cantools library for random frames, and checks the generated C against the simulation with zero tolerance. A typical use is an ECU subsystem with a CAN Unpack at its inputs and a CAN Pack at its outputs; the generated step() function then reads and writes raw frames.

docs.title: CAN FD, multiplexing and value tables
docs.text:
CAN FD frames carry up to 64 data bytes, and the data part is sent at a faster bit rate (e.g. 2 Mbit/s after arbitration at 500 kbit/s). Messages that the DBC file marks as FD (VFrameFormat) work everywhere: CAN Pack outputs and CAN Unpack expects as many bytes as the message has, the bus computes the frame time with both bit rates (data_bitrate on the CAN Bus block), and the trace and log files mark them as FD frames.

Multiplexed messages reuse the same bytes for different signals, chosen by a multiplexer signal (M in the DBC; the multiplexed ones are m1, m2, ...). For example Diagnostics in examples/data/chassis.dbc sends the oil temperature and pressure when Page = 1 and the battery voltage and ambient temperature when Page = 2. CAN Pack writes a multiplexed signal only when the multiplexer value selects it; CAN Unpack outputs it when it is in the frame and holds the last value otherwise.

Signals with a value table (VAL_, e.g. GearSelector: 0 Park, 1 Reverse, 2 Neutral, 3 Drive) are shown with their names in the CAN Bus Trace (GearSelector=3 (Drive)).

How each signal's bits are spread over the bytes (both byte orders, any frame length) is computed once from the DBC file; the simulation and the generated C code extract the same runs of bits, so FD and multiplexed messages are bit-exact in C too.

docs.title: DBC signals in the workspace
docs.text:
Model Workspace ▸ Import DBC… adds the signals and value tables of a DBC file as workspace variables:

  • every value-table entry as a constant <Signal>_<Name>, e.g. GearSelector_Drive = 3, so the model compares with GearSelector_Drive instead of a magic 3;
  • every signal as a variable with its initial value, unit, range and comment: a data dictionary of the bus.

They are constants (not calibratable); names that already exist are kept, and one Undo removes the whole import. In Python: nervus.can.dbc_variables("chassis.dbc").

docs.title: Simulated CAN buses
docs.text:
Pack and Unpack turn signals into bytes; the blocks below put those bytes on a simulated bus, so several ECUs can talk to each other with realistic timing, and faults can be injected.

Block What it does CAN Transmit sends a message: periodic (its sample_time; 0 = the DBC's GenMsgCycleTime), on_change or on_trigger; signals or raw bytes (payload); fault injection CAN Receive the last received frame: one output per signal (or the 8 bytes), then new (a frame arrived this sample) and age (seconds since the last frame) CAN Bus bit rate of a bus, its load as an output, and optionally a real interface CAN Rest Bus sends every message of the ECUs that are not modelled, at their DBC cycle times CAN Gateway forwards chosen identifiers from one bus to another E2E Protect / E2E Check AUTOSAR-style end-to-end protection: CRC-8 and alive counter (with C code)

Buses are identified by name (bus, default can0); blocks anywhere in the model, also inside ECU subsystems, that use the same name share the bus.

docs.title: Timing and arbitration
docs.text:
A standard data frame with n data bytes has \(44 + 8n\) bits (from the start bit to the end of frame) plus stuff bits (after five equal bits the sender inserts an opposite one), plus 3 bits of inter-frame space. The simulation counts the stuff bits of the real bit pattern, including the CRC-15. At 500 kbit/s an 8-byte frame takes about 0.25 ms.

When the bus becomes idle, every waiting frame starts at once and the lowest identifier wins the arbitration; the others wait. Low-priority messages therefore see the longest delays, which grow quickly with the bus load:

A frame reaches the CAN Receive blocks when its last bit has been sent; the receiver's task reads it at its next sample, like a mailbox. The CAN Bus block outputs the load (the share of time the bus was busy); keep a real bus below about 50 to 70 %.

docs.title: Fault injection
docs.text: CAN Transmit can make its frames misbehave from fault_time on: drop (probability that a frame is lost), delay (extra latency), corrupt (probability of a flipped data bit: an error behind the CAN CRC, e.g. in a gateway, which only an E2E check detects) and bus_off (the node stops sending). A receiver sees lost frames as a growing age; this is how timeout monitors and U-codes (lost communication) are tested.

docs.title: End-to-end protection (E2E)
docs.text: Safety-relevant signals carry their own check, independent of the bus: E2E Protect writes an alive counter (0 to 14, one step per frame) and a CRC-8 (SAE J1850, polynomial 0x1D) over a 16-bit data ID and the other bytes. E2E Check at the receiver reports ok, no_new_data, wrong_crc, repeated (stuck sender) or wrong_sequence (more than max_delta frames lost) and a valid flag. Put Protect between CAN Pack and CAN Transmit (payload = bytes), and Check after CAN Receive (payload = bytes). Both generate C code that matches the simulation bit for bit.

docs.title: Rest-bus simulation and gateways
docs.text: An ECU under test expects all the messages of its bus. CAN Rest Bus sends the messages of the nodes you do not model (every sender in the DBC file if empty) at their cycle times, with signal values from values (e.g. VehicleSpeed=50). CAN Gateway routes identifiers from one bus to another, as the central gateway does between powertrain and body CAN; it adds up to one task period of latency.

docs.title: Trace and log files
docs.text:
Tools ▸ CAN Bus Trace lists every frame of the last simulation: time, identifier, message, sender, bytes and the decoded signals, with the bus load. Export to ASC (text) or BLF (binary), the Vector log formats that CANalyzer, CANoe, SavvyCAN and python-can read. In Python:

from nervus.canbus import bus

b = bus("powertrain")  # after a simulation
b.load(0.0, 1.0)  # 0.037
b.latency(0x100)  # queue-to-receive time of each frame
b.write_asc("powertrain.asc")

docs.title: Real hardware
docs.text:
Set interface on the CAN Bus block (socketcan, pcan, kvaser, vector, slcan; needs python-can and the vendor driver) and channel (e.g. can0 or PCAN_USBBUS1). Every frame the model sends also goes out on the interface, and frames from it reach the CAN Receive blocks. With real-time pacing (Simulation ▸ Settings) the model can act as the rest of the car for a real ECU on the bench (HIL-style).

See the tutorial a vehicle network (CAN) in the help contents.

docs.title: Pack and unpack in Python
docs.text:
from nervus.can import load_dbc, pack, unpack

msgs = load_dbc("examples/data/vehicle.dbc")
engine = msgs["EngineData"]
frame = pack(engine, {"EngineSpeed": 812.3, "CoolantTemp": 90})
unpack(engine.signal("EngineSpeed"), frame)  # 812.25 (0.25 rpm resolution)

docs.title: XCP: live measurement and calibration
docs.text:
XCP (ASAM MCD-1) is how calibration tools such as INCA and CANape read and change an ECU's memory while it runs. The tool (the master) sends a command in one CAN frame (request_id, e.g. 0x7F0) and the ECU (the slave) answers in one frame (response_id, e.g. 0x7F1). The tool knows where each variable is from the A2L file. Nervus implements the basic commands (CONNECT, DISCONNECT, GET_STATUS, SET_MTA, UPLOAD, SHORT_UPLOAD, DOWNLOAD, SHORT_DOWNLOAD): enough for polled measurement and for calibration. Event-driven measurement (DAQ lists) is not implemented.

The simulation as a slave. The XCP Slave block makes a running model reachable. Its inputs are measurements (measurements: their names) and its outputs are calibration values (calibrations: workspace variables), which start at the variables' values and change when the tool writes them, like an ECU's calibration RAM. Wire the outputs where the tunable value is needed. write_a2l("slave.a2l") on the block writes the matching A2L file (8-byte doubles: calibrations from 0x10000, measurements from 0x20000). Connect the CAN Bus block to an interface and turn on real-time pacing (Simulation ▸ Settings), and a calibration tool on a real CAN adapter can measure and tune the model.

Nervus as the tool. nervus.xcp.XcpMaster connects to any XCP-on-CAN slave, the simulated one or a real ECU, through python-can, and reads and writes variables by name from an A2L file (the one Nervus generates with the C code, after fill_addresses, or the ECU supplier's):

import can
from nervus.xcp import CanTransport, XcpMaster

ecu = can.Bus(interface="pcan", channel="PCAN_USBBUS1", bitrate=500000)
tool = XcpMaster(CanTransport(ecu, request_id=0x7F0, response_id=0x7F1), a2l="ecu.a2l")
tool.connect()
tool.read("engine_rpm")  # polled measurement
tool.write("Kp_idle", 0.8)  # calibration

docs.title: C code generation
docs.text: Nervus turns the discrete-time part of a model into plain C code for an ECU.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Put the ECU software in a subsystem. Its In/Out blocks are the interface: sensors in, actuators out.
  2. Give the controller blocks a sample time (e.g. the workspace variable Ts = 0.01).
  3. Select the subsystem and choose Code → Generate C Code… (⌘B / Ctrl+B). With nothing selected, the whole model is generated.
  4. Press Run SIL check. The code is compiled and run side by side with the model on the same inputs, and the largest difference is shown. It should be about 1e-15.
  5. Save to folder… writes the files; Open report shows which lines belong to which block.

docs.title: Using the code
docs.text:
Call <name>_initialize() once, then every <NAME>_BASE_PERIOD seconds:

  1. write the inputs into <name>_U,
  2. call <name>_step(),
  3. read the outputs from <name>_Y.

main_example.c shows the pattern. Only <name>.h and <name>.c go into the ECU project.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text: Parameters are in the struct <name>_P. A parameter written as a workspace variable (Kp) becomes one shared field <name>_P.Kp that a calibration tool can change while the code runs.

docs.title: Typed parameters and constants
docs.text: Workspace variables can be stored as integer or fixed-point types and as constants in ROM (the Type and Cal. columns of the Model Workspace, see Workspace and calibrations). Calibratable parameters are in <name>_P, ordered by size (8, 4, 2, 1 bytes) so the struct has no padding and the A2L offsets are exact. Constants are in const <name>_C, which the linker puts in flash, and they are not in the A2L file.

docs.title: Calibration file (A2L)
docs.text: The code generator also writes <name>.a2l, the file calibration tools such as INCA or CANape read. It lists the tunable parameters, with units and limits from the model workspace, and the block signals for measurement.

docs.title: One function per task (RTOS)
docs.text:
On a real ECU an operating system (an RTOS, e.g. AUTOSAR OS or FreeRTOS) runs the software in periodic tasks, and a faster task interrupts a slower one. Tick One function per task (for an RTOS) in the Generate C dialog (or generate_c(model, tasks=True)) to get one function per rate:

void ecu_task_10ms(void);   /* call every 10 ms, highest priority */
void ecu_task_100ms(void);  /* call every 100 ms */

main_example.c then shows one OS task per rate, with the priorities to use. ecu_step() still exists: called every base period, it runs the due tasks fastest first, which is what the SIL check compares with the simulation.

Signals between tasks need a Rate Transition block. If the 10 ms task read the 100 ms task's output directly, it would see the old or the new value depending on whether the slow task had finished, so the result would depend on timing. A Rate Transition makes the transfer deterministic, in the simulation and on the target:

Direction Set Behaviour fast_to_slow sample_time = the slow rate the slow task gets the fast signal as it was at the start of its period slow_to_fast sample_time = the slow rate, output_sample_time = the fast rate the fast task gets the slow signal one slow period later

The code generator checks the model: a signal that goes from one task to another without a Rate Transition is reported with both block names. Blocks that get the model's In ports directly must have a rate of their own: sample the inputs with a Zero-Order Hold, or put each task in an atomic subsystem (see Subsystems) with its own sample_time.

docs.title: What can be generated
docs.text: Everything that is discrete-time or has no state: gains, sums, lookup tables, logic, relays, filters, counters, delays, discrete PID, and more. Not generated: blocks with continuous states (Integrator, Transfer Fcn, PID Controller, ...) and time-based sources (Step, Sine, ...). Keep those in the plant, outside the subsystem. If something cannot be generated, Diagnostics lists the blocks.

docs.title: Integer-only code (no floating point)
docs.text:
Small ECUs often have no floating-point unit. Tick Integer arithmetic only in the code generation dialog (or generate_c(model, integer_only=True)) and the generated code has no double or float at all: every signal stays its stored integer (int16_T for fixdt(1, 16, 7), uint8_T for a boolean), and every block computes in an int64 accumulator. Moving the binary point is an integer multiplication, or a division rounded exactly as the simulation rounds (nv_div_nearest, half away from zero; floor, ceil, zero), then the block's overflow handling (nv_sat or nv_wrap). The results are the simulation's, bit for bit; the back-to-back test checks it at zero tolerance.

/* scale (Gain): 5/128 °C per ADC count, into fixdt(1, 16, 7) */
temp_B.scale[0] = (int16_T)nv_sat(((int64_T)5 * (int64_T)temp_B.z[0]), (int64_T)-32768, (int64_T)32767);

What it needs:

Rule Why every signal has an integer, boolean or fixed-point type with binary-point scaling (slope 2^-n, no bias): set the types from the In blocks on other scalings need real multiplications a gain is an exact binary fraction (0.75, 0.0390625), or a workspace variable with a fixed-point type (then it is calibratable as a stored integer) 0.0123 is neither: the simulation would use a value the integer code cannot blocks: In/Out, Constant, Sum, Gain, Product (*), Bias, Abs, MinMax, Relational Operator, Compare To Constant, Logical Operator, Switch, Saturation, Unit Delay, Integer Delay, Zero-Order Hold, Data Type Conversion, subsystem ports the blocks of integer ECU code; others (a PID, a filter, a chart) need floating-point code

A model that breaks a rule gets a message that names the block and the rule. Results that the simulation's double arithmetic could round (more than 52 bits) are refused too, so the two always agree.

docs.title: Reusable functions for subsystems
docs.text:
Normally every block of a subsystem is written into the model's code (inline). When the same subsystem appears several times, for example one injector or cylinder controller per cylinder, give the subsystems a function name (the function_name parameter in the Properties panel). Subsystems with the same function name then share one C function, called once per subsystem:

/* cyl_trim.h: generated once */
void cyl_trim_initialize(cyl_trim_B_t *B, cyl_trim_DW_t *DW);
void cyl_trim_output(const cyl_trim_U_t *U, cyl_trim_Y_t *Y, cyl_trim_B_t *B, cyl_trim_DW_t *DW,
                     const cyl_trim_P_t *P);
void cyl_trim_update(cyl_trim_B_t *B, cyl_trim_DW_t *DW, const cyl_trim_P_t *P);

/* engine.c: each cylinder has its own signals, states and calibration */
cyl_trim_output(&in, &out, &engine_cyl0_B, &engine_cyl0_DW, &engine_cyl0_P);

Each subsystem keeps its own data: signals (_B), states (_DW) and calibration parameters (<model>_<subsystem>_P, for example different trims per cylinder from a mask). The model calls _output where the subsystem's blocks would compute their outputs and _update where they would update their states, so the code does exactly what the inline code does; the back-to-back test compares it with the simulation.

The subsystems must have the same contents (blocks and wiring; their parameter values may differ), run at one rate (their own sample_time) and have no enable or trigger port. The functions are in their own files (cyl_trim.c, cyl_trim.h), which the ECU project builds with the model's code. Each instance's calibration parameters are in the A2L file as <model>_<subsystem>_P.<name>.

docs.title: Coverage of the generated code
docs.text:
nervus.codegen.c_coverage.coverage_of_tests(model, model.block("ECU")) runs every test case of the model, records the signals that enter the code at each of its steps, replays them into the generated C compiled with --coverage, and reads gcov's counts: which lines and branches of the ECU code the tests execute (with each test's calibration).

cov = coverage_of_tests(model, model.block("ECU"))
print(cov.summary())  # C code coverage: lines 100 % (25/25), branches 75 % (6/8) in 3 run(s), and what never ran
cov.save_html("ecu_coverage.html")

Many blocks become one-line conditionals (a Switch, a Saturation), so a missing test shows as a branch never taken rather than a line. Needs a C compiler and gcov. In the editor: C coverage (tests) in the code generation dialog shows the percentages and opens the annotated report.

docs.title: MISRA C
docs.text:
MISRA C:2012 is the coding standard for safety-related C in the automotive industry: ISO 26262 asks for a coding standard, and most ECU projects choose MISRA. The generated code follows it, and MISRA check in the code generation dialog checks it with the free checker cppcheck and its MISRA addon (install it with brew install cppcheck or apt install cppcheck). From Python:

from nervus.codegen.misra import misra_check

findings = misra_check(generate_c(model.block("ECU")))  # [] : no findings

What the generated code does for it:

Rule In the generated code 10.4, 7.2 unsigned loop counters and index constants (for (i = 0u; i < 4u; i++)) 12.1 explicit parentheses: (Kp * err) + x, (a != 0.0) && (b != 0.0) 14.4 conditions are comparisons: if ((st & 0x02u) != 0u), never if (st & 0x02u) 15.7 every if … else if chain ends with an else 2.2, 2.3 no + 0 in index expressions; only the type aliases the model uses 8.9 data used by one function only is declared in it (e.g. the rate periods) 12.3 one declaration per line

The check analyses <name>.c and <name>.h (with main_example.c, so the calls of the step function count, but its own findings are not reported). Three rules are deviations, as a MISRA compliance report records them:

Rule Why 2.5 (advisory) <MODEL>_BASE_PERIOD is part of the interface, for the scheduler that calls the step function 8.7 (advisory) <model>_P has external linkage so the calibration tool (XCP, A2L) and other ECU code reach the parameters 7.3 a false positive of the addon: the last letter of an identifier like pedal taken for an l suffix

The test suite checks the code of every block with a C template and several example ECUs this way, and compiles it with -std=c99 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pedantic. cppcheck checks the rules a tool can decide; a MISRA compliance claim for a project also needs a review of the rules no tool can decide, and a compliance report. Many projects use a commercial checker (PC-lint, Polyspace, QA-C) as well.

docs.title: FMI export
docs.text:
Code ▸ Export FMU… packs the generated code of the selected subsystem (or the whole model) as an FMI 2.0 co-simulation FMU, the standard format for exchanging models between tools (Simulink, Dymola, OpenModelica, SimulationX, CANoe, fmpy). The FMU contains:

  • modelDescription.xml: the inputs and outputs (In and Out blocks), the tunable parameters (the calibratable parameters of the _P struct, with their start values) and the default communication step (the base period);
  • binaries/<platform>/: the library compiled for this computer (darwin64, linux64 or win64), with the FMI functions (fmi2Instantiate, fmi2DoStep, fmi2GetReal, ...) around the generated step function;
  • sources/: the generated C files and the FMI wrapper, so other platforms can build it.

Each fmi2DoStep runs the step function once per base period; the communication step must be a whole number of base periods. The generated code keeps its state in global variables, so one process runs one instance. In Python: nervus.codegen.fmu.export_fmu(model.block("ECU"), "ECU.fmu").

The FMU block imports FMUs from other tools into a model (co-simulation, needs fmpy: uv sync --extra fmi). See the tutorial Exchanging models with FMI.

docs.title: Coming from Simulink
docs.text: Nervus uses the same ideas as Simulink, and most defaults match, so moving between the two is easy. This page maps Simulink names to Nervus names.

docs.title: Models and simulation
docs.text: Simulink Nervus model (.slx) Diagram, saved as a .nervus JSON file (Model files) Model Configuration Parameters Simulation → Settings, diagram.settings (SimulationSettings) sim('model') simulate(diagram), or ▶ Run in the editor out.logsout, To Workspace SimResult: res["block"]; every block output is logged. ToWorkspace(variable=...) Simulation Data Inspector Data Inspector (Ctrl+I): runs, signals, comparisons sample time -1, 0, inf, [T, o] the same ode45 / ode23 / ode15s RK45 / RK23 / BDF or LSODA ode4 / ode1 (fixed step) rk4 / euler zero-crossing detection the same, per block, with a chattering (Zeno) guard Model Workspace, Simulink.Parameter Model Workspace variables with unit, min, max, description (Workspace) parameter sets / data dictionary .sldd parameter sets (.nervcal files) .mat results res.to_mat("run.mat"); results also save as .nervres

docs.title: Blocks
docs.text: Simulink Nervus Notes Constant, Step, Ramp, Sine Wave, Pulse Generator, Clock same names Sine frequency in rad/s, as in Simulink From Workspace From Workspace arrays or a CSV file Gain, Sum, Product, Abs, Saturation, Math Function same names Sum signs as "+-", Product ops as "*/" Integrator, Derivative, Transfer Fcn, State-Space same names Integrator: limits, external reset, x0 input, saturation port; Derivative is filtered (see its help) Unit Delay, Zero-Order Hold, Discrete-Time Integrator, Discrete Transfer Fcn same names Discrete-Time Integrator has an external reset PID Controller (continuous/discrete) PID Controller, Discrete PID Controller parallel form, filter coefficient N, anti-windup Scope, To Workspace, Terminator, Stop Simulation, Assertion same names Mux, Demux, Switch same names Switch control input is the middle port 1-D / 2-D Lookup Table 1-D Lookup Table, 2-D Lookup Table interpolation linear/nearest/flat; extrapolation clip/linear Prelookup, Interpolation Using Prelookup Prelookup, Interpolation using Prelookup 1-D to 4-D tables over shared axes (n-D lookup) Relational Operator, Logical Operator, Compare To Constant same names booleans are 1.0 / 0.0 Relay, Dead Zone, Rate Limiter, Quantizer same names Relay and Rate Limiter run at a discrete rate Delay / Integer Delay, Counter Limited, Detect Rise/Fall Integer Delay, Counter, Edge Detect Discrete Filter (first order), Moving Average, debouncing Discrete Filter (PT1), Moving Average, Debounce MinMax, Bias, Ground, Data Type Conversion, IC same names (IC: Initial Condition)

docs.title: Importing a Simulink model
docs.text:
File ▸ Import Simulink Model… opens an .slx file, or an .mdl file (Simulink's older text format), as a new Nervus model (save it as .nervus). From Python: model = nervus.simulink.read_model("controller.slx").

  • The common blocks are translated with their parameters and positions: sources (Constant, Step, Sine Wave, Ramp, Clock), math (Gain, Sum, Product, Bias, Abs, MinMax), continuous and discrete blocks (Integrator, Transfer Fcn, State-Space, Unit Delay, Memory, Zero-Order Hold, Discrete-Time Integrator, Discrete Transfer Fcn), discontinuities (Saturation, Dead Zone, Rate Limiter, Relay, Quantizer), logic (Relational Operator, Logical Operator, Compare To Constant), routing (Switch, Mux, Demux, Data Type Conversion), lookup tables (1-D, 2-D), PID controllers, sinks, ports and subsystems with their masks.
  • Parameters stay expressions with their workspace variables (Kp, 2*pi, [1 2 3]); MATLAB's ^ becomes ** and 0:0.5:2 becomes a list. The variables the model uses are added to the Model Workspace with the value 1: give them their values (they live in a MATLAB script or data dictionary that the .slx does not contain).
  • A block that is not translated (an S-Function, a Stateflow chart, a block from another toolbox) becomes an empty subsystem with the same ports, named like the Simulink block, so the wiring stays and you can rebuild it there.
  • The import report lists the blocks that were not translated and the workspace variables.

Compare the results: run the same scenario in both tools, export Simulink's results to a CSV or MAT file, and load them in the Data Inspector next to Nervus's.

docs.title: Differences
docs.text:
• Unconnected inputs are errors, not warnings. Simulink silently treats them as zero; Nervus makes you decide (use a Constant 0 or Ground).
  • Everything is logged. Every block output is available in the result; Scopes only mark what the editor plots.
  • Models are text. .nervus files are JSON and diff well in git.
  • Charts are also text. State charts are drawn in the chart editor and stored in a small text language, which diffs well and can be edited directly.
  • Stateflow charts are not imported. .slx and .mdl models are (see above); charts become empty subsystems and have to be rebuilt as State Chart blocks.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text: Every signal is a vector of floating-point numbers. A scalar signal has width 1. Widths are worked out automatically when the model is compiled. Most math blocks work elementwise, and a scalar combines with a vector by scalar expansion (a scalar gain of 2 doubles every element).

docs.title: Blocks
docs.text:
A block is a small dynamic system with inputs u, outputs y and optionally states x:

Function Meaning Called outputs(t, u, xc, xd) output equation \(y = g(t, u, x)\) whenever outputs are needed derivatives(t, u, xc, xd) continuous states \(\dot x_c = f(t, u, x_c)\) by the solver update(t, u, xc, xd) discrete states \(x_d[k+1] = f(t, u, x_d[k])\) at the block's sample hits

Direct feedthrough means that outputs uses u directly (Gain, Sum). Blocks whose output only depends on their state (Integrator, Unit Delay) are not direct feedthrough.

docs.title: Execution order and algebraic loops
docs.text:
Before simulating, Nervus sorts the blocks so that each direct-feedthrough block runs after the blocks that drive it. A feedback loop made only of direct-feedthrough blocks has no valid order. That is an algebraic loop: \(y = u - 2y\) defines y in terms of itself. Nervus reports these as errors and lists the blocks involved:

AlgebraicLoopError: algebraic loop: s -> g -> s. Every feedback loop needs a block with state ...

Put an Integrator (continuous) or a Unit Delay (discrete) in the loop. In a real control system that delay always exists anyway.

docs.title: Solving algebraic loops
docs.text:
Some models are naturally algebraic: a voltage divider with a load that depends on its own voltage, a mass-flow balance, a controller with a direct feedthrough on purpose. For these, set Simulation ▸ Settings ▸ Algebraic loops to Solve iteratively (in Python: model.settings.algebraic_loops = "solve"). Nervus then

  1. finds each loop (a group of blocks that depend on each other directly),
  2. chooses tear blocks in it, whose outputs it guesses, so that the rest of the loop can be computed in order,
  3. adjusts the guess with Newton's method until computing the loop from the guess gives the guess back: for \(y = u - 2y\) it finds \(y = u/3\), and for \(x = \cos x\) it finds 0.739085.

Each evaluation of the model then solves the loop, which is slower; the simulation reports every solved loop as a warning, with its tear blocks. A loop without a solution (e.g. \(y = u + y\) with \(u \ne 0\)) stops the simulation with an error naming the blocks. A loop must run at one rate and outside enabled or triggered subsystems, and a model with a solved loop cannot become C code: an ECU cannot iterate in its tasks, so break the loop with a Unit Delay before generating code.

docs.title: Sample times
docs.text:
Each block runs at a sample time, using the same values as Simulink:

Value Meaning 0 continuous: computed at every solver step T > 0 discrete: computed every T seconds, held in between [T, offset] discrete with an offset -1 inherited from the blocks that drive it inf constant: computed once

Inherited blocks take the sample time of their inputs: a Gain after a 10 ms Zero-Order Hold also runs every 10 ms. If its inputs have mixed rates it becomes continuous.

Discrete outputs are computed only at sample hits and held between them. That is how code on an ECU behaves: a 10 ms task computes a value and it stays put until the next run.

Use a Zero-Order Hold where a continuous signal (a sensor) enters a discrete controller.

docs.title: Solvers
docs.text:
Solver Type Use for auto / RK45 variable step the default; smooth, non-stiff models RK23 variable step low accuracy needs, quick DOP853 variable step high accuracy Radau, BDF, LSODA variable step, implicit stiff models (very fast and very slow dynamics together) rk4 fixed step models that will become code; deterministic step size euler fixed step the simplest method; matches simple embedded code

Variable-step solvers pick their own step size from rtol/atol, up to max_step. They also stop exactly at discontinuities that blocks announce (the time of a Step, the edges of a Pulse), so these are captured accurately.

Fixed-step solvers use step everywhere. The step must divide every discrete sample time. If you don't set it, Nervus picks one.

docs.title: Zero crossings and discontinuities
docs.text:
Switching inside a model, such as a Saturation hitting its limit, a Switch changing input, an Integrator reaching its limit or a comparison flipping, makes the equations discontinuous. Variable-step solvers cannot step across a discontinuity accurately, so Nervus uses zero-crossing detection (like Simulink):

  1. Each such block declares a zero-crossing signal that changes sign exactly at the discontinuity, e.g. u − upper for a saturation.
  2. During integration the block's branch (its mode, e.g. "saturated at the upper limit") is frozen, so the equations stay smooth.
  3. The solver stops exactly where a zero-crossing signal changes sign, and the modes are re-evaluated there.

The result is exact switching times and accurate integrals, e.g. ∫ clip(sin t) to 1e-8 with large steps. If a signal keeps crossing back and forth very rapidly (the system chatters along a limit), detection is switched off for that block and the run reports a warning in Diagnostics.

Turn it off in Simulation Settings (Locate discontinuities exactly) or with d.settings.zero_crossing = False. Fixed-step solvers never use it: on an ECU the code also just steps.

Blocks with zero crossings: Saturation, Dead Zone, Abs, Sign (Math Function), Switch, Relational Operator, Compare To Constant, Integrator (with limits), PID Controller (with limits). Stop Simulation stops a run at the exact moment its input becomes true, and Assertion fails it when its input becomes false.

docs.title: Simulation loop
docs.text: At each major step Nervus (1) computes all outputs, (2) logs them, (3) updates discrete states with a sample hit, and (4) integrates the continuous states to the next major step. With a variable-step solver, the major steps are the discrete sample hits and the breakpoints. The solver's own steps in between are logged too.

docs.title: Accelerated simulation
docs.text:
Simulation Settings → Simulation mode → Accelerated runs the whole model as compiled C: Nervus generates C code for every block, compiles it, and runs the simulation loop in C. Large models run 30 to 700 times faster. The first run of a model (and the first run after a parameter change) takes a moment longer to compile; later runs use the compiled code again.

Normal Accelerated Blocks all blocks with C code: the ECU blocks, Integrator, Transfer Fcn, State-Space, Derivative, PID, the time sources (Step, Sine, Pulse, Ramp, From Workspace, Drive Cycle, Clock) and Python Function blocks written in simple Python Solver the one you chose the fixed-step solver you chose; a variable-step solver is replaced by rk4 (the step is the max step, else 1/1000 of the time span) Needs nothing a C compiler (on macOS: xcode-select --install; on Linux: gcc; on Windows: MinGW or clang)

The results are the same as a normal run with the same fixed-step solver (to about 1e-12). Models with blocks that have no C code (physical networks, FMUs, CAN buses, OBD Responder), algebraic loops, or coverage collection run normally, and Diagnostics says why. A Python Function is translated if it uses numbers, if/elif/else, arithmetic, math/np functions, min/max/abs, np.clip and np.interp with lists of numbers; loops and arrays keep the model in normal mode. In Python:

d.settings.mode = "accelerated"
res = simulate(d)
print(res.stats.solver)  # "rk4 (accelerated, compiled C)"

docs.title: Data types and fixed point
docs.text: Most ECU software does not use double. Sensor values arrive as integers, memory is scarce, and many microcontrollers have no floating-point unit, so signals are integers or fixed point. Nervus simulates these types bit-true: the simulation gives exactly the values the generated C code computes.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Type Meaning double, single 64- and 32-bit floating point boolean 0 or 1 int8, uint8, int16, uint16, int32, uint32 integers fixdt(s, w, f) fixed point: signed (s=1) or unsigned, w bits, f fraction bits (resolution 2⁻ᶠ) fixdt(s, w, slope, bias) fixed point with arbitrary scaling inherit take the type from the inputs

A fixed-point signal stores an integer Q and represents the real value

\[ V = \mathrm{slope} \cdot Q + \mathrm{bias} \]

For example fixdt(1, 16, 8) covers −128 … 127.996 in steps of 1/256, and fixdt(0, 8, 0.5, -40) is a temperature from −40 °C to 87.5 °C in 0.5 °C steps, in one byte. On wires the editor uses the short names sfix16_En8 and ufix8_S0.5_B-40.

docs.title: Setting types
docs.text:
• Data Type Conversion (Signal Attributes) converts a signal to a type, with a choice of rounding (nearest, floor, ceil, zero) and overflow (saturate or wrap):
  • In, Constant, Gain, Sum, Product, Bias and the lookup tables have an output_type parameter.
  • Everything else inherits. A block outputs the common type of its inputs (or double if they differ). Logic and comparison blocks output boolean. Continuous-time blocks, PID controllers and charts always use double.

Turn on View → Show Data Types to label every wire that carries a non-double type (Show Signal Widths and Sample Time Colours are next to it).

docs.title: How it is simulated
docs.text: Each block computes in double precision and its output is then converted to its type, with the block's rounding and overflow mode (default: nearest and saturate). Doubles represent every 32-bit integer and fixed-point value exactly, so this is bit-true.

docs.title: Generated code
docs.text:
• The input and output structs use real C types (int16_T, uint8_T, boolean_T, ...). Fixed-point ports carry the stored integer, and the header comment states the scaling.
  • Inside the step function, signals are converted with small generated helper functions (nv_q_int16_nearest_saturate, ...) that use exactly the same rounding and overflow as the simulation. The test suite checks this with a back-to-back test at zero tolerance.
  • The floating-point code computes in double between the conversions. For targets without an FPU, integer-only code (C code generation) keeps every signal a stored integer and computes with integers only, bit-true too.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: examples/fixed_point_sensor.py runs a pressure sensor chain twice: a 12-bit ADC (uint16 counts), scaling to kPa, a PT1 filter and a limit check, once in double and once in fixdt(0, 16, 6). The largest difference is 0.010 kPa, within the fixed-point resolution of 1/64 kPa (see the tutorial on fixed point).

docs.title: Window layout
docs.text:
Area What it does Library (left) All blocks, grouped by category. Type in the search box to filter. Drag a block onto the canvas or double-click it. Hover for a short description. Canvas (centre) The diagram. Properties (right) Parameters of the selected block. Press ? for the block's help. Model Workspace (bottom, tab) Named parameters that blocks can use. See Workspace and calibrations. Diagnostics (bottom) Problems in the model, such as unconnected inputs or algebraic loops. Click an entry to select the blocks involved.

Panels can be moved, closed and reopened from the View menu.

docs.title: Blocks
docs.text:
• Select: click, or drag a rectangle on empty canvas. Shift-click adds to the selection.
  • Move: drag. Blocks snap to a 10-pixel grid.
  • Rename: edit Name in the Properties panel, or right-click → Rename…. Names must be unique.
  • Delete: Delete or Backspace.
  • Copy / cut / paste: ⌘C / ⌘X / ⌘V (Ctrl on Windows and Linux). Lines between copied blocks are copied too.
  • Double-click: opens a subsystem, the plot window of a Scope, or the Properties panel for other blocks.
  • Flip: Ctrl+Shift+F swaps the input and output sides (see below).

docs.title: Lines (signals)
docs.text:
• Drag from an output port (right side, ▸) to an input port (left side). You can also start from an input and drag backwards to an output.
  • An output can feed many inputs (a dot marks the branch). An input has exactly one source. Connecting a new line to an input that is already used replaces the old line.
  • Click a line to select it; Delete (or right-click → Delete Wire) removes it.
  • Lines are routed automatically with right angles. When the direct route would pass through a block, the line goes around the blocks (the shortest route with the fewest bends).
  • Drag a line segment to place it yourself: the middle segments move sideways; the short segments at the ports follow the blocks. Lines from the same output move together at a shared segment, so dragging the segment at a branch moves the branch point. Manually placed lines keep their corners when blocks move (the ends follow the ports) and are saved with the model. Right-click → Reset Route returns to automatic routing.
  • Hover over a port to see which input it is, e.g. input 2: reset (rising) on a Discrete-Time Integrator with an external reset, or k1, f1 on an Interpolation block.

docs.title: Right-click menus
docs.text:
Right-click a block, a wire or the empty canvas for the actions that fit it:

On Actions a block Rename, help, cut / copy / delete, create a subsystem from the selection; Open Scope for scopes a subsystem also Open Subsystem, Edit Mask…, Variants…, Save Subsystem to Library…, Generate C Code… (or Break Library Link when it is linked) a wire Delete Wire the canvas paste, select all, auto layout, fit to window, up to the parent system

Right-clicking a block that is part of a selection keeps the selection, so Delete or Create Subsystem act on all selected blocks.

docs.title: Flipping blocks for feedback paths
docs.text:
Feedback paths, such as a sensor signal going back to the controller, are easier to read when they run from right to left. Select blocks and press Ctrl+Shift+F (Edit → Flip Block, or right-click → Flip Block): their inputs move to the right side and their outputs to the left. Flipping only changes the drawing, and it is saved with the model.

In Python, set block.meta["flipped"] = True.

docs.title: Rotating, resizing and nudging blocks
docs.text:
Ctrl+Shift+R (Edit → Rotate Block, or right-click → Rotate Block) turns the selected blocks a quarter turn clockwise: the signal then flows down (inputs on top, outputs at the bottom), then to the left, then up, then right again. Use it for signal chains drawn top to bottom, like a sensor path. Flipping a rotated block swaps top and bottom.

To make a block bigger, select it and drag the grip in its lower right corner; blocks never get smaller than their natural size. Edit → Reset Block Size undoes it. The arrow keys move the selected blocks by one grid step, Shift+arrow by five. All of these can be undone and are saved with the model.

In Python: block.meta["vertical"] = True (with flipped for upwards), block.meta["size"] = [140, 80].

docs.title: Sample times, widths and data types on the canvas
docs.text:
The View menu can annotate the diagram with what the compiler found out:

View → Shows Show Data Types the data type on every wire that is not double (int16, fixdt(1,16,8), ...) Show Signal Widths [3] on vector wires, which are also drawn thicker Sample Time Colours blocks and wires coloured by their sample time, with a legend in the status bar

The discrete rates get colours from fastest to slowest (orange, green, blue, amber, ...); continuous blocks keep the normal colour and constant blocks are pink. A subsystem whose blocks all run at one rate takes that colour. Use it to check that every block of an ECU task really runs in that task, and to find where a Rate Transition is needed. The annotations update while you edit, once the model compiles.

docs.title: Editing parameters
docs.text:
Numeric fields accept:

You type Meaning 0.5, -1e-3 numbers 2*pi, 1/0.05, sqrt(2) arithmetic; pi, e, inf are known [1 2 3] or [1, 2, 3] vectors [1 2; 3 4] matrices (rows separated by ;, as in MATLAB) Kp, 1/tau, 2*Kp workspace variables and expressions of them Kp * (MODE == 2), A > 1 && B ~= 0 comparisons and logic give 1 or 0 (MATLAB ~=, &&, \|\|, ~ work too)

Press Enter or leave the field to apply. If a value is invalid the field turns red and the old value is kept.

docs.title: Tidying up
docs.text: Edit → Auto Layout (⇧⌘L / Ctrl+Shift+L) arranges the blocks of the shown diagram from left to right in signal-flow order. It can be undone like any other edit.

docs.title: Scripting console
docs.text:
View ▸ Console (a tab next to the Model Workspace) runs Python with the open model and its results in scope:

Name What it is model the open model (a Diagram): model.block("pid").params, model.workspace["Kp"] res, runs the last result and all runs in the Data Inspector: res["speed"].max() simulate, load, save run, open and save models block classes, blocks model.add(Gain(gain=2), name="k") np, plt NumPy and Matplotlib window the main window, for scripting the app itself

Statements over several lines work as in the Python prompt (finish with an empty line); ↑ and ↓ recall earlier lines. Errors are printed in the console. Changes a statement makes to the model appear in the editor at once and are one undo step (Edit ▸ Undo reverts them). Assigning another model to model (e.g. model = load("examples/drive_cycle.nervus")) opens it.

docs.title: Undo
docs.text: Every change, including moves, can be undone with ⌘Z and redone with ⇧⌘Z (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y).

docs.title: Zoom and pan
docs.text:
• Zoom: ⌘/Ctrl + mouse wheel, trackpad pinch, or ⌘+ / ⌘−. Fit to window: ⌘0.
  • Pan: two-finger scroll on a trackpad, the middle mouse button, or hold Space and drag.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text: View → Theme switches between light and dark, or follows the system setting.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Nervus models a system as a block diagram: blocks are small dynamic systems (a gain, an integrator, a PID controller), and the lines between them carry signals.

New here? Help ▸ Editor Tour shows the parts of the editor in a minute, and Help ▸ Welcome offers the first tutorial (a cruise control, built step by step) and the beginner examples, each with its tutorial.

docs.title: Build your first model in 5 steps
docs.text:
1. Add blocks. Drag a block from the Library (left) onto the canvas, or double-click it in the library. Add a Step, a Transfer Fcn and a Scope.
  2. Connect them. Press on a block's output port (the small triangle on its right side) and drag to another block's input port (left side). Releasing on the body of a block connects to its first free input.
  3. Set parameters. Select a block and edit its parameters in the Properties panel (right). Values accept expressions like 2*pi, 1/0.05 and matrices like [1 2; 3 4].
  4. Run. Press ▶ Run (⌘R / Ctrl+R or F5). The stop time is in the toolbar.
  5. Look at the result. Scope windows open after the first run. Double-click a Scope block to reopen it. Hover over the plot to read values.

docs.title: What Nervus can do
docs.text:
Every feature has a page in this Help window (the list on the left):

Area Features Help page Editor block library, wires, undo, copy/paste, right-click menus, flip blocks, auto layout, themes Using the editor, Keyboard shortcuts Simulation continuous, discrete and multirate models, solvers, zero crossings, stop and assertion blocks Running simulations, Concepts Parameters model workspace, expressions, parameter sets (.nervcal) Workspace and calibrations Structure subsystems, masks, enabled/triggered subsystems, atomic tasks, variants, component libraries Subsystems, Component libraries Logic State Chart block State machines ECU code C code, A2L file, fixed-point data types, software-in-the-loop check C code generation, Data types and fixed point Testing test cases, Test Manager, Data Inspector, coverage, Model Advisor Test cases and the Data Inspector, Coverage and Model Advisor Analysis linearisation, trim, Bode, margins Linear analysis Vehicle networks CAN with DBC files; OBD-II live data and trouble codes CAN communication, OBD-II live data Simulink users how Simulink names map to Nervus Coming from Simulink Files what is stored in a .nervus file Model files

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Using the editor: selecting, moving, copying and undoing.
  • Running simulations: solvers, sample times and what to do when something goes wrong.
  • Block reference: every block, its equation and parameters (the last section in the list on the left). Select a block and press F1 to jump to its page.
  • Tutorials: idle speed control, lambda control and fuel trims, and a car on a drive cycle.

Complete example models come with Nervus: File → Open Example lists the model of every tutorial by topic, and All examples… opens the folder. To run and change the example scripts, copy them to a folder of your own with nervus --copy-examples ~/nervus-examples. The examples:
