docs.title: Tutorial: Level control of coupled water tanks
docs.text:
You will learn a nonlinear process, linearization at an operating point, PI design for a second-order process, gain scheduling, actuator limits Before this DC motor speed and position control Level and time intermediate, about 40 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/coupled_tanks.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Control engineering ▸ Classic lab experiments (all tutorials)

examples/coupled_tanks.py is the process-control experiment of many lab courses: a pump fills an upper tank, the water runs through an orifice into a lower tank and out through a second orifice, and a PI controller holds the level of the lower tank. Unlike the motor, this process is nonlinear: a controller designed at one level behaves differently at another. The dimensions are those of a common lab rig.

uv run python examples/coupled_tanks.py

docs.title: The plant
docs.text:
Water flows out of a tank through an orifice at Torricelli's speed \(\sqrt{2 g h}\), so the outflow grows with the square root of the level:

\[ A \frac{dh_1}{dt} = K_{pump} V - a_1 \sqrt{2 g h_1}, \qquad A \frac{dh_2}{dt} = a_1 \sqrt{2 g h_1} - a_2 \sqrt{2 g h_2} \]

with the tank cross-section \(A = 15.5\) cm², the orifices \(a_1 = 0.32\) cm² and \(a_2 = 0.18\) cm², and a pump that delivers 3.3 cm³/s per volt (0 to 22 V). In the model each tank is an Integrator limited to 0-30 cm (the tank height) with a square-root block for the outflow.

Operating point: for the lower tank at 15 cm, the outflow is \(a_2\sqrt{2g \cdot 15} = 30.5\) cm³/s; the pump needs 9.26 V for that, and the upper tank settles at 4.74 cm. Linearized around this point, each tank is a first-order system with the time constant \(\tau_i = \frac{A}{a_i}\sqrt{\frac{2 h_i}{g}}\): 4.8 s for the upper tank and 15.2 s for the lower one. The steady-state gain from pump voltage to the lower level is \(\frac{dh_2}{dV} = \frac{K_{pump}\, q}{g\, a_2^2} = 3.2\) cm/V.

docs.title: Step 1: the open-loop step
docs.text: Set closed_loop = 0 and V_open = 10.25 (1 V more than the equilibrium) and run 400 s. The lower level rises from 15 to 18.4 cm: 3.4 cm/V, a bit more than the linear 3.2 cm/V, because the process is nonlinear. It takes 23 s to reach 63 % of the change: the two time constants in series (15.2 + 4.8 s) make an S-shaped response.

docs.title: Step 2: the PI controller
docs.text:
With closed_loop = 1 the PI controller drives the pump. The design cancels the slow lower tank: the integral time \(T_i = 15.2\) s equals its time constant, so the loop is \(L(s) = \frac{K_c \cdot 3.2}{T_i s (4.8 s + 1)}\). For a crossover of 0.1 rad/s (a closed loop about ten times faster than the tank) \(K_c = 0.1 \cdot 15.2 / 3.2 = 0.47\) V/cm, with a phase margin of about 65°.

The reference steps to 17 cm at 50 s: the level follows with 0.12 cm overshoot and settles within 2 % in 44 s; the step down to 13 cm takes 38 s.

docs.title: Step 3: the nonlinearity
docs.text: At 250 s the reference drops to 5 cm, far from the design point. The controller still works, but it takes 62 s to settle, half as fast. The process gain \(dh_2/dq\) is proportional to \(\sqrt{h_2}\): at 5 cm it is only 58 % of the gain at 15 cm, so the loop crosses over at a lower frequency. Industrial controllers solve this with gain scheduling: the gain is made a function of the operating point. Try Kc = 0.94 (twice the gain): the step to 5 cm then settles in 30 s, at the price of more overshoot around 15 cm.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Try What you will see Kc = 0.94 twice the gain: 2.2 % overshoot at 17 cm, and the step to 5 cm settles in 30 s instead of 62 s Kc = 0.235 half the gain: no overshoot, but 52 s near 15 cm and 121 s at 5 cm Ti = 5 too much integral action: the level shoots to 18 cm and drops to 3.4 cm after the step to 5 cm Kc = 5 the pump runs into its limits (0 V on the way down); with anti_windup on none (block pi in Properties) the level undershoots to 3.2 cm instead of reaching 5 cm cleanly

docs.title: Tutorial: DC motor speed and position control
docs.text:
You will learn system identification from a step response, PI design by pole-zero cancellation, PD design from damping and natural frequency, a physical motor model and a 1 kHz controller Before this Position control of a mass-spring-damper Level and time intermediate, about 45 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/dc_motor_speed.nervus, examples/dc_motor_position.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Control engineering ▸ Classic lab experiments (all tutorials)

examples/dc_motor_lab.py is the servo experiment of control lab courses: a small DC motor with an inertia disk, a ±10 V amplifier, an encoder, and a controller running at 1 kHz. You will identify the motor from a step response, design a PI speed controller by pole-zero cancellation, and a PD position controller from a damping specification. The motor data are those of a typical teaching rig.

uv run python examples/dc_motor_lab.py    # builds dc_motor_speed.nervus and dc_motor_position.nervus

docs.title: The plant
docs.text:
The motor is built from physical blocks: the amplifier is a controlled voltage source, the DC motor block has the armature resistance \(R = 8.4\) Ω, inductance \(L = 1.16\) mH and torque constant \(k_m = 0.042\) N·m/A, and the shaft drives an inertia \(J = 2.1 \cdot 10^{-5}\) kg·m². The encoder (an angle sensor) and a speed sensor feed the 1 ms controller through Zero-Order Holds. Neglecting the small inductance, voltage to speed is a first-order system:

\[ \frac{\omega(s)}{V(s)} = \frac{K}{\tau s + 1}, \qquad K = \frac{1}{k_m} = 23.8 \ \tfrac{\text{rad/s}}{\text{V}}, \qquad \tau = \frac{R J}{k_m^2} = 0.10 \text{ s} \]

docs.title: Step 1: identify the motor
docs.text: Open dc_motor_speed.nervus, set closed_loop = 0 in the Model Workspace and run: the amplifier gets a 5 V step at 0.1 s. In the scope, read the final speed (119 rad/s, so \(K = 119 / 5 = 23.8\) rad/s/V) and the time at which the speed reaches 63 % of it: 0.1 s after the step, so \(\tau = 0.10\) s. This is how you would identify the real rig, and the numbers match the formulas above.

docs.title: Step 2: PI speed control
docs.text:
Set closed_loop = 1. A PI controller \(C(s) = K_p + K_i/s = K_p (1 + \frac{1}{T_i s})\) with \(T_i = \tau\) cancels the motor's pole; the loop then behaves like an integrator \(K K_p / (\tau s)\), and the closed loop is first order with the time constant \(\tau_{cl} = \tau / (K K_p)\). For \(\tau_{cl} = 33\) ms:

\[ K_p = \frac{\tau}{K \tau_{cl}} = 0.122 \ \tfrac{\text{V}}{\text{rad/s}}, \qquad K_i = \frac{K_p}{\tau} = 1.26 \ \tfrac{\text{V}}{\text{rad}} \]

Run it: the speed follows the 50 rad/s step like a first-order system (63 % after 34 ms), without overshoot, and the amplifier needs 6.1 V at most. Set Ki_w = 0 to see why the I term is there: with P alone the motor settles at 37.2 rad/s, because the steady state needs a voltage and P only gives one when there is an error (\(50 \cdot K K_p / (1 + K K_p)\)).

docs.title: Step 3: PD position control
docs.text:
Open dc_motor_position.nervus. From voltage to angle the motor adds an integrator, \(\theta(s)/V(s) = K / (s(\tau s + 1))\). With a PD controller \(V = K_p e + K_d \dot e\) the closed loop is

\[ \tau s^2 + (1 + K K_d) s + K K_p = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \omega_n^2 = \frac{K K_p}{\tau}, \qquad 2 \zeta \omega_n = \frac{1 + K K_d}{\tau} \]

For \(\omega_n = 40\) rad/s and \(\zeta = 0.7\): \(K_p = 6.5\) V/rad and \(K_d = 0.186\) V·s/rad. The 1 rad step overshoots by 4.3 % (the textbook value for ζ = 0.7 is 4.6 %) and is settled within 2 % after 0.14 s. The step makes the D term kick the amplifier to its 10 V limit for a moment. Set Kd_th = 0 to see the undamped servo: 70 % overshoot and a long ringing.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Try What you will see speed: Kp_w = 0.5, Ki_w = 5.15 faster (63 % after 14 ms), but the amplifier saturates at 10 V speed: J = 4.2e-5 (a heavier disk) the cancellation no longer fits: slower (57 ms) and 8 % overshoot position: Kd_th = 0.05 too little damping: 42 % overshoot position: Kp_th = 20 faster but 25 % overshoot; the amplifier limits the acceleration position: J = 4.2e-5 17 % overshoot: a controller tuned for one load does not fit another

docs.title: Tutorial: From continuous to discrete: sample times
docs.text:
You will learn what running a controller every T milliseconds does to a loop, the zero-order hold, choosing a sample time, discrete poles and stability, aliasing and anti-aliasing filters Before this Your first model: a cruise control; read Sample times first Level and time beginner, about 30 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/discrete_control.nervus, examples/aliasing.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic ECU software, communication and diagnostics ▸ From model to ECU code (all tutorials)

A controller on an ECU does not run continuously. A task wakes up every few milliseconds, reads its sensors, computes a new output and writes it to the actuator, and that output then stays put until the next run. This tutorial shows what that does to a control loop. Below some sample time, nothing changes. Above it, the loop overshoots, then rings, then goes unstable. It also shows the trap in the other direction: a signal that is too fast for the sample time turns into a slow one that isn't there.

uv run python examples/discrete_control.py

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
discrete_control.nervus holds the same control loop twice. The plant is the speed of a DC motor, a first-order lag with gain \(K = 2\) rad/s per volt and time constant \(\tau = 0.1\) s:

\[ G(s) = \frac{K}{\tau s + 1} \]

The controller is a PI controller. Its gains are chosen to cancel the motor's pole (\(K_i / K_p = 1/\tau\)), which makes the closed loop a clean first-order lag with the time constant we ask for, \(\tau_{cl} = 20\) ms:

\[ K_p = \frac{\tau}{K \tau_{cl}} = 2.5, \qquad K_i = \frac{K_p}{\tau} = 25 \]

All of this is in the Model Workspace: Kp and Ki are expressions of K, tau and tau_cl, so they follow when you change the motor.

  • The top loop uses the continuous PID Controller block. This is the controller on paper.
  • The bottom loop is the controller as an ECU runs it: a Zero-Order Hold (sensor) reads the speed every T seconds, and a Discrete PID Controller with the same gains computes the voltage at the same moments and holds it until the next one. T is a workspace variable, 10 ms to start with.

Turn on View ▸ Sample Time Colours: the discrete blocks change colour, and the legend in the status bar shows which colour is which rate. Blocks with an inherited sample time (-1) take the colour of the rate that drives them.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Press ▶ and open the scope. At \(T = 10\) ms the two loops are almost on top of each other: the discrete one overshoots by 0.4 %, and the continuous one not at all.

Now change T in the workspace and run again. The figure shows four runs:

T T / τcl Overshoot What happens 1 ms 0.05 0 % the same as continuous 10 ms 0.5 0.4 % hardly different 20 ms 1 1.6 % a visible step in the curve, still fine 30 ms 1.5 30 % overshoot, then an oscillation that dies out 50 ms 2.5 97 % the loop rings for a long time 60 ms 3 — unstable: the speed grows, flipping direction every sample

The rule of thumb that comes out of this: sample at least 5 to 10 times faster than the closed-loop time constant, here 2 to 4 ms. Then the discrete controller behaves like the one you designed. ECU tasks of 1, 5, 10 and 100 ms exist for this reason. Fast loops, such as current control or throttle position, run at 1 ms. Slow ones, such as coolant temperature, run at 100 ms.

docs.title: Why it goes wrong
docs.text:
Between two samples the controller is blind. It computed its output from the speed at the last sample, and it keeps applying that output while the motor moves on. The longer the gap, the more the controller acts on old news. On average a held output lags the signal by half a sample period, \(T/2\), and a lag in a feedback loop eats phase margin. With too little margin the loop overshoots, and with none it oscillates.

Because the discrete loop has a closed form, the limits are exact. The motor seen from the controller, sample to sample, is

\[ y[k+1] = a\,y[k] + b\,u[k], \qquad a = e^{-T/\tau}, \quad b = K (1 - a) \]

With the discrete PI controller, the closed-loop poles are the roots of

\[ (z - 1)(z - a) + b \left( K_p (z - 1) + K_i T \right) = 0 \]

A discrete loop is stable when every pole is inside the unit circle, \(|z| < 1\). A pole on the negative real axis makes the output flip sign from sample to sample: the ringing in the figure. For this loop:

  • for \(T < 23\) ms both poles are positive: no ringing, only a small overshoot;
  • at \(T = 23\) ms one pole goes negative, and the loop rings;
  • at \(T = 58\) ms that pole leaves the unit circle at \(z = -1\), and the loop is unstable.

The script examples/discrete_control.py computes the overshoot for each sample time with a sweep, as in Scripting and testing models from Python.

Retuning helps, up to a point: A slower design tolerates a slower controller. With tau_cl = 0.1 the 50 ms controller overshoots by 2.9 % instead of 97 %, but the loop is then five times slower. Sample time and bandwidth are traded against each other. You cannot make a slow task control a fast plant.

docs.title: Aliasing: the other trap
docs.text:
Sampling also fails when the signal is too fast for the sample time. Open aliasing.nervus: a sensor signal with a 45 Hz vibration (a sine) is read every 20 ms, that is at 50 Hz.

The samples trace a smooth 5 Hz wave, and nothing in the samples tells it apart from a real 5 Hz signal. That is aliasing. A frequency \(f\) above half the sample rate (the Nyquist frequency, \(f_s/2\)) shows up at \(|f - n f_s|\) for the nearest whole \(n\): here \(|45 - 50| = 5\) Hz. A controller would react to it as if it were real.

No software after the sampler can undo this. The cure is in hardware, before the ADC: an anti-aliasing filter, a low-pass (often a simple RC network on the ECU's input pin) that removes everything above the Nyquist frequency. An NTC temperature sensor interface has one.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Try What you will see T = 0.023 the edge of ringing: 2.7 % overshoot and no undershoot yet; at 0.03 the undershoot appears T = 0.06 unstable; the Diagnostics panel stays quiet, because unstable is not an error T = 0.05, tau_cl = 0.1, stop time 1.5 the slow design copes with the slow controller: 2.9 % overshoot, settled in about 1 s in aliasing.nervus, f_signal = 55 also 5 Hz: 45 Hz and 55 Hz are indistinguishable at 50 Hz in aliasing.nervus, f_signal = 50 0 Hz: a constant, because every sample hits the sine at the same phase T = 0.01, and set sample_time of pi_discrete to 0.02 mixed rates: the colours show the controller now runs slower than its sensor

docs.title: Tutorial: A car on a drive cycle
docs.text:
You will learn vehicle longitudinal dynamics, a driver model, standard drive cycles (ECE-15, WLTC, FTP-75), where the energy goes, fuel consumption Before this Your first model: a cruise control Level and time beginner, about 40 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/drive_cycle.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Vehicle dynamics and energy ▸ Longitudinal dynamics and energy (all tutorials)

This tutorial follows examples/drive_cycle.py: a car with a driver model drives the ECE-15 urban cycle. You will see where the energy for city driving goes, and how vehicle mass changes it.

uv run python examples/drive_cycle.py      # simulates, saves drive_cycle.nervus, runs the tests
uv run nervus examples/drive_cycle.nervus  # open it in the editor

docs.title: Drive cycles
docs.text: A drive cycle is a speed-over-time profile that every car of a type approval test has to drive on a dynamometer. Fuel consumption and emissions figures come from such cycles. The ECE-15 urban cycle (the city part of the old European NEDC, also called UDC) is 195 s long, reaches 50 km/h and covers 994 m. Today's WLTP cycle is more dynamic: 30 minutes, up to 131 km/h. The official WLTC class 3b and FTP-75 tables come with Nervus: use the Drive Cycle block (Sources), or build("wltc3b") in the example (see below).

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
driver: like a test driver following the speed trace on a screen, a PI controller acts on the speed error. A feed-forward term adds the pedal needed for the cycle's acceleration, \(a_{ref}\,m/F_{max}\). The pedal is limited to −1 (full brake) … +1 (full throttle).

vehicle: Newton's second law along the road:

\[ m\,\frac{dv}{dt} = F_{wheel} - \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}\rho\,c_d A\,v^2}_{\text{aerodynamic drag}} - \underbrace{m\,g\,c_{rr}}_{\text{rolling resistance}} \]

The wheel force comes from the pedal. Traction is limited by the maximum force (wheel slip, first gear) and by the engine power, \(F \le P_{max}/v\), and the brakes provide up to \(F_{brake,max}\). The rolling resistance uses \(\tanh(10\,v)\) instead of a sign function, so it fades out smoothly at standstill. The block wheel_energy_J integrates the positive wheel power: the energy the engine must deliver.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
1300 kg 1800 kg distance 993 m 992 m max. speed error 0.75 km/h 1.0 km/h energy at the wheels 340 kJ = 9.5 kWh/100 km 460 kJ = 12.9 kWh/100 km

Where does the energy go? For the 1300 kg car:

Estimate accelerating: \(\tfrac{1}{2} m v^2\) for the three accelerations to 15, 32 and 50 km/h ≈ 188 kJ lost again as heat in the brakes (the negative power) rolling resistance: \(m g c_{rr} \times 994\) m ≈ 152 kJ the simulation gives the same aerodynamic drag: \(\int F_{aero}\,v\,dt\) from the simulation ≈ 39 kJ small at city speeds

These add up to 379 kJ, a bit more than the 340 kJ the engine delivers: while the car slows down, part of the rolling and drag losses is paid from its kinetic energy instead of by the brakes. Both big terms grow with the mass. That is why mass matters so much in city driving, and why hybrids and electric cars, which recover braking energy, gain most in the city.

The example also prints a rough fuel estimate: wheel energy / (25 % average efficiency × 43 MJ/kg) gives about 4.3 l/100 km. A real car uses clearly more in the city. It burns fuel while idling (almost a third of this cycle is standstill), and its efficiency at light load is much lower than 25 %. Modelling that needs an engine efficiency map: a 2-D lookup table over speed and torque, the next step.

docs.title: WLTP and FTP-75
docs.text:
build("wltc3b") and build("ftp75") replace the ECE-15 by the Drive Cycle block with the official second-by-second tables (WLTC class 3b from UNECE GTR No. 15, FTP-75 from the US EPA); its second output, the cycle's acceleration, is the driver's feed-forward. The same car and driver:

Cycle distance max. speed error energy at the wheels fuel (25 % efficiency) ECE-15 0.99 km 0.75 km/h 9.5 kWh/100 km 4.3 L/100 km FTP-75 17.77 km 1.3 km/h 11.3 kWh/100 km 5.1 L/100 km WLTC class 3b 23.26 km 1.3 km/h 13.0 kWh/100 km 5.8 L/100 km

The WLTC needs more energy per kilometre: its extra-high phase runs at up to 131 km/h, where the drag grows with the square of the speed. Use nervus.cycles.cycle_stats("wltc3b") for the cycle's own figures.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
To try one: change the value in the Model Workspace tab (double-click it), or for a block parameter select the block and edit it in Properties; press ▶ and compare with the previous run in the Data Inspector (Ctrl+I). Ctrl+Z undoes the change.

Try What you will see m = 1800 about 35 % more energy: accelerating and rolling grow with the mass, only drag does not cd_A = 0.9 (a van) only 3 % more energy: drag matters at motorway speeds, not at 50 km/h P_max = 30e3 still enough power for this gentle cycle; on the WLTC the car falls behind in the extra-high phase Kp_driver = 0.1 a lazier driver: the speed error reaches 2.1 km/h, just enough to fail the tracking test

The test cases in the Test Manager check the tracking, the distance and the energy of both masses.

docs.title: Tutorial: Engine operating modes
docs.text:
You will learn an ECU's mode logic as a State Chart: cranking, starter protection, idle, fuel cut-off, stall; calibration parameters in a chart; behaviour specified by test cases Before this Your first model: a cruise control Level and time beginner, about 30 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/engine_modes.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Powertrain and engine control ▸ Engine management (all tutorials)

examples/engine_modes.py models the mode logic at the heart of every engine ECU: is the engine off, cranking, idling, running, coasting with the fuel cut off, or stalled? It is a State Chart running every 10 ms, and its behaviour is specified by test cases that drive the key, engine speed and pedal.

uv run python examples/engine_modes.py

docs.title: The modes
docs.text:
Mode When What the ECU does off key off no fuel, no ignition crank key on, engine below 600 rpm starter on, fuel on (cranking enrichment) crank_fail cranking for more than 3 s starter off to protect it, until the key is turned off idle engine runs, pedal released the idle speed controller holds the speed run pedal pressed torque follows the driver fuel_cut coasting above 1500 rpm with the pedal released injectors off: no fuel is needed to coast stalled the engine stopped while the key is on no fuel and no automatic restart

The thresholds are param names in the chart, so they are calibration parameters in the Model Workspace: rpm_started (600 rpm), crank_limit (300 samples of 10 ms = 3 s), rpm_cut_on (1500 rpm), rpm_cut_off (1100 rpm) and so on.

Double-click the modes block: the chart editor shows the modes as states and the conditions as arrows. Click the arrow from crank to idle to see its guard, rpm > rpm_started; the number in front of it, 1, means it is checked first of the three transitions leaving crank. See the chart editor.

docs.title: Follow the scenarios
docs.text:
The model has no sources of its own: its inputs come from the four test cases. Open the Test Manager tab and press Run All (Ctrl+T); all four pass. Double-click a result to see its signals in the Data Inspector.

  • normal start: key on at 0.5 s; the engine cranks at 250 rpm and catches at 1.8 s (crank → idle).
  • failed start protects the starter: the engine never starts; after exactly 3 s of cranking the chart goes to crank_fail and switches the starter off.
  • overrun fuel cut-off: the driver lifts the pedal at 4 s with the engine at 3000 rpm. The chart cuts the fuel (fuel_cut) and gives it back at 7.6 s, when the speed falls below 1100 rpm, early enough that the engine does not stall:

  • stall: the speed drops below 300 rpm at 2.4 s: stalled, no fuel, and the chart stays there until the key is turned off.

The order of the transitions matters: in run, run -> fuel_cut is written before run -> idle, so coasting at high speed cuts the fuel instead of going to idle. The Model Advisor (Analysis ▸ Model Advisor) checks charts for states that can never be reached and for transitions that can never fire.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
Change a value in the Model Workspace and press Run All in the Test Manager:

Try What you will see crank_limit = 100 (1 s) two tests fail: normal start (this engine needs 1.3 s of cranking, the chart gives up at 1.5 s) and failed start (it specifies 3 s of cranking): the tests are the specification rpm_cut_off = 800 overrun fuel cut-off fails: the speed never falls below 800 rpm in the scenario, so the fuel never comes back (in a car the engine would stall) rpm_cut_on = 3500 no fuel cut-off at all: the chart stays in run until 7.4 s and then goes to idle; the fuel is never switched off in the chart editor, select crank → off (key < 0.5) and press Check earlier twice no change in these scenarios: the key stays on while cranking. The order matters only when two guards are true at the same time

The chart can be generated as C code (Code ▸ Generate C Code), and a back-to-back test checks the code against the simulation; see C code generation.

docs.title: Tutorial: Electric vehicle range on the WLTP cycle
docs.text:
You will learn the energy chain of an electric car, drivetrain efficiency, regenerative braking, the winter heater, consumption in kWh/100 km and range Before this A car on a drive cycle Level and time beginner, about 30 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/ev_range.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Vehicle dynamics and energy ▸ Longitudinal dynamics and energy (all tutorials)

How far does an electric car get on one charge, and why so much less in winter? examples/ev_range.py drives an electric version of the car from the drive-cycle tutorial over the official WLTC (the cycle of the WLTP type approval) and follows the energy from the battery to the wheels and back.

uv run python examples/ev_range.py

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
The vehicle, driver and road loads are those of the drive-cycle model, with the WLTC class 3b from the Drive Cycle block: 30 minutes, 23.3 km, up to 131 km/h. The car weighs 1800 kg and has 150 kW. The new part is the battery power (a Python Function on the wheel power):

\[ P_{bat} = \begin{cases} P_{wheel} / \eta_{drive} & P_{wheel} \ge 0 \ \text{(driving)} \\ P_{wheel} \cdot \eta_{regen} \cdot s_{regen} & P_{wheel} < 0 \ \text{(braking)} \end{cases} \; + P_{aux} + P_{heater} \]

with the drivetrain efficiency \(\eta_{drive}\) = 0.88 (inverter, motor, gearbox), the recovery efficiency \(\eta_{regen}\) = 0.75, the share of the braking done by the motor \(s_{regen}\) = 1, and 0.3 kW for the auxiliaries. Integrated over the cycle, it gives the energy taken from the battery.

docs.title: Where the energy goes
docs.text:
Over the 23.3 km of the WLTC:

kWh energy delivered to the wheels (rolling resistance, air drag, accelerating the mass) 3.72 + drivetrain losses (12 %) 0.51 − braking energy recovered (75 % of 1.05 kWh) −0.78 + auxiliaries 0.15 = from the battery 3.60

That is 15.5 kWh/100 km, and with 60 kWh usable a WLTP range of 387 km, typical for a mid-size electric car. The negative spikes in the battery power are the decelerations, where the motor charges the battery.

docs.title: Winter
docs.text:
In winter the cabin must be heated, and an electric car has no waste heat from an engine. A resistive heater takes about 3 kW, the whole time: on the 30-minute cycle that is 1.5 kWh, more than a third of the driving energy.

Situation kWh/100 km Range summer 15.5 387 km no regenerative braking 18.8 318 km winter, heat pump (1.2 kW) 18.1 332 km winter, resistive heater (3 kW) 21.9 274 km

The heater costs more range than the whole regenerative braking gains; a heat pump gets most of it back. And the slower the driving, the larger the heater's share, because it takes power per hour, not per kilometre: in a traffic jam the heater can use more energy than the driving.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Try What you will see regen_share = 0.5 half the braking with the friction brakes: 17.2 kWh/100 km m = 2200 (four passengers and luggage) 17.4 kWh/100 km: the mass costs on every acceleration and on the rolling resistance cd_A = 0.55 instead of 0.66 (a sleeker car) 14.5 kWh/100 km and 415 km: air drag dominates the WLTC's fast extra-high phase P_aux = 1000 a hot day with the air conditioning: 17.0 kWh/100 km, 353 km instead of 387

docs.title: Tutorial: Your first model: a cruise control
docs.text:
You will learn the editor, blocks and wires, workspace variables, scopes, the Data Inspector, PI control and integrator windup Before this nothing: start here (the editor needs uv sync --extra gui) Level and time beginner, about 30 minutes Follow along build the model yourself, step by step below; the finished model is examples/cruise_control.nervus Topic Getting started (all tutorials)

We build a cruise control: a controller that adjusts the engine force so the car holds a set speed. On the way you meet the most common effect in control engineering, integrator windup, and fix it.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
The car accelerates with the engine force \(F\) and is slowed by the drag, which we take as proportional to the speed \(v\) (in km/h):

\[ m \frac{dv}{dt} = F - c \cdot v \]

The controller compares the set speed with the actual speed and computes the force. In a block diagram, the equation becomes a loop: set speed → error → controller → force → car → speed → back to the error.

docs.title: Step 1: start the editor and add the blocks
docs.text:
uv run nervus

You get an empty model. Add these 8 blocks. To add a block, type its name in the search box above the library (top left) and drag it onto the canvas (or double-click it in the library). Then give it the name in the table: select the block and edit Name at the top of the Properties panel (right).

Library block Name it What it does Step (Sources) set_speed the driver sets 100 km/h at t = 1 s Sum (Math Operations) error set speed − speed PID Controller (Control) cruise_control the controller Sum net_force engine force − drag Gain (Math Operations) accel force → acceleration Integrator (Continuous) speed acceleration → speed Gain drag speed → drag force Scope (Sinks) scope shows the result

Arrange them roughly like this, with drag below the main line:

docs.title: Step 2: connect the blocks
docs.text:
Drag from an output port (the small arrow on the right side of a block) to an input port (left side). Make these 10 connections:

  1. set_speed → error input 1, and set_speed → scope input 1
  2. error → cruise_control → net_force input 1
  3. net_force → accel → speed
  4. speed → error input 2 (the feedback), speed → drag, and speed → scope input 2
  5. drag → net_force input 2

drag points the wrong way for a feedback path: select it and press Ctrl+Shift+F (⌘⇧F on a Mac) to flip it, so its input is on the right. The lines route themselves around the blocks:

Check your work: The Diagnostics tab at the bottom says No problems found when every input is connected. If it lists an unconnected input, click the message: the block is selected for you.

docs.title: Step 3: set the parameters
docs.text:
First the model workspace: open the Model Workspace tab at the bottom, press Add four times and fill in the table (double-click a cell to edit it):

Name Value Unit m 1500 kg c_drag 8 N/(km/h) Kp 300 N/(km/h) Ki 0 N/(km/h·s)

Now select each block and set its parameters in the Properties panel. Parameters can use the workspace names, so you can tune later without touching the blocks:

Block Parameters set_speed time 1, final 100 error, net_force signs +- (the first input is added, the second subtracted) cruise_control P Kp, I Ki, upper 4000, lower -6000 (the engine's and the brakes' limits in N) accel gain 3.6 / m (the 3.6 converts m/s to km/h) drag gain c_drag scope num_inputs 2

Press Enter after typing a value. Click in a field (or hover over it) to see what you can write there, e.g. for signs that +- subtracts the second input; press F1 for the block's help page.

Finally set the Stop time in the toolbar to 40.

docs.title: Step 4: run and look at the result
docs.text:
Press ▶ (or Ctrl+R), then double-click the scope:

The car accelerates at full force (the controller output is at its 4000 N limit), but it settles at 97.4 km/h, not 100. Why? At 100 km/h the drag is 800 N, and a P controller only produces force when there is an error: it needs \(800 / (300 + 8) \approx 2.6\) km/h of error to push 800 N. This steady-state error is typical of P control.

docs.title: Step 5: add integral action, and meet windup
docs.text:
The integral term keeps increasing the force as long as there is any error, so it removes the steady-state error. In the Model Workspace set Ki = 30 and run again.

Now open Simulation ▸ Data Inspector (Ctrl+I). Tick both runs and the signal speed:

Run 2 (orange) reaches 100 km/h, but only after shooting up to 139 km/h. While the car was accelerating at the 4000 N limit, the integrator kept adding up the large error ("winding up"). When the speed finally reached 100 km/h, the integrator held so much that the controller kept pushing, and it took many seconds to unwind. This is integrator windup, and it happens in every controller with an output limit: throttle, idle speed, boost pressure.

docs.title: Step 6: fix it with anti-windup
docs.text:
Select cruise_control and set anti_windup to clamping: the integrator stops integrating while the output is at its limit. Run again. Run 3 (green) reaches 100 km/h with no overshoot and settles in about 15 s.

Run Controller Highest speed After 40 s 1 P 97.4 km/h 97.4 km/h 2 PI 138.6 km/h 104.1 km/h 3 PI with anti-windup 100.0 km/h 100.0 km/h

docs.title: Step 7: save, and make it a test
docs.text:
Save with Ctrl+S (for example as cruise_control.nervus). The file is plain JSON, so it works well with Git.

To make sure nobody breaks the controller later, add a test case: in the Test Manager tab press Add, set the stop time to 40 and add a check bounds on speed with upper limit 101. Press Run All (Ctrl+T): it passes now, and it fails if someone removes the anti-windup. See Test cases.

docs.title: The same in Python
docs.text:
Every model can also be built and run from Python, for scripts, sweeps and CI. examples/cruise_control.py builds this model and runs the three versions:

from nervus import simulate
from cruise_control import build  # in examples/

for ki, aw in ((0, "none"), (30, "none"), (30, "clamping")):
    res = simulate(build(ki=ki, anti_windup=aw))
    print(ki, aw, res["speed"].max())

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
Change a value in the Model Workspace, press ▶, and compare with the earlier runs in the Data Inspector.

Try What you will see m = 2500 (a loaded car) slower acceleration and a small overshoot (100.4 km/h); the controller still settles at 100 Kp = 1000 P only: the steady error shrinks to 0.8 km/h, but never disappears Ki = 200 with anti-windup a stronger integral action: the speed overshoots to 103 km/h before settling cruise_control upper = 2000 a weaker engine: it takes twice as long to get close to 100 km/h

docs.title: Tutorial: A sensor signal chain in fixed point
docs.text:
You will learn fixed-point data types (word length, fraction bits, resolution, range), an ADC model, quantization error, and the silent failure of a badly chosen range Before this From model to ECU C code; read Data types and fixed point first Level and time intermediate, about 30 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/fixed_point_sensor.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic ECU software, communication and diagnostics ▸ From model to ECU code (all tutorials)

Many ECU microcontrollers have no floating-point unit, or the code must be fast and deterministic, so signals are stored as integers with a scale. examples/fixed_point_sensor.py runs a manifold pressure sensor chain twice, in double and in fixed point, so you can see what the integers cost in accuracy and what happens when the scaling is chosen badly.

uv run python examples/fixed_point_sensor.py

docs.title: The signal chain
docs.text:
Stage Block Data type pressure sensor and ADC: 20 kPa reads 0 counts, 0.0763 kPa per count Bias, Gain double (physics) 12-bit ADC: truncate to whole counts, sample every 10 ms Data Type Conversion (floor), Zero-Order Hold uint16 counts counts → kPa Gain (0.0763 kPa/count), Bias (+20 kPa) double or fixdt(0, 16, 6) smoothing Discrete Filter (PT1, 50 ms) inherited over-pressure check Compare to Constant (> 150 kPa) boolean

fixdt(0, 16, 6) means unsigned, 16 bits, 6 fraction bits: the stored integer \(q\) represents \(q / 2^6\), so the resolution is 1/64 = 0.0156 kPa and the range 0 to 1024 kPa. The scaling Gain sets this type with its output_type; the Bias and the filter after it inherit it, exactly as in generated C code, where the blocks become integer arithmetic with shifts.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text: The true pressure swings between 40 and 160 kPa. The fixed-point chain follows the double chain within 0.010 kPa (10 Pa), less than one resolution step: every value it produces is a multiple of 1/64 kPa (turn on View ▸ Data Types to see the types on the wires). That is far below the sensor's own accuracy, so the 16-bit format is a good choice.

docs.title: What can go wrong: the range
docs.text: More fraction bits mean finer resolution but a smaller range. fixdt(0, 16, 10) has a resolution of 1/1024 kPa but can only hold values up to 64 kPa. Select scale_fix, set output_type to fixdt(0, 16, 10) and run: the pressure saturates at 64 kPa, and the over-pressure check never fires, although the real pressure reaches 160 kPa. Nothing crashes and no error is reported: this is why fixed-point formats are chosen from the signal's physical range, and why production code is tested with the extreme values.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
Select the scale_fix block and change its output_type in Properties:

Try What you will see fixdt(0, 16, 2) resolution 0.25 kPa: the error grows to 0.15 kPa, still small for a pressure sensor uint8 whole kPa only (and at most 255): the error is up to 0.7 kPa, visible as steps fixdt(0, 16, 9) the range ends at 128 kPa: the signal is cut off there and the check never fires fixdt(0, 16, 10) saturates at 64 kPa, as above

See Data types and fixed point for the rules (rounding, overflow, how types are inherited) and the code-generation tutorial for turning such a chain into C.

docs.title: Tutorial: Exchanging models with FMI
docs.text:
You will learn FMI 2.0 co-simulation FMUs: exporting a subsystem, running it in another tool (fmpy, Simulink), importing an FMU as a block, and the communication-step delay of co-simulation Before this From model to ECU C code Level and time intermediate, about 30 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/fmi_plant.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic ECU software, communication and diagnostics ▸ From model to ECU code (all tutorials)

FMI (Functional Mock-up Interface) is the standard for exchanging simulation models between tools. A model is packed as an FMU, a zip file with a description of its variables and compiled code, and almost every simulation tool can run one: Simulink (the FMU block), Dymola, OpenModelica, SimulationX, CANoe, AMESim, and Python with fmpy. This is how a Nervus model reaches a colleague's Simulink model, and how a supplier's plant model gets into Nervus.

uv sync --extra fmi
uv run python examples/fmi_exchange.py

docs.title: Step 1: export an FMU
docs.text:
Open examples/throttle_ecu.nervus, select the ECU subsystem and choose Code ▸ Export FMU…. Nervus generates the C code (as in the code-generation tutorial), adds the FMI 2.0 functions around it, compiles it for this computer and writes ECU.fmu:

In the FMU From the model inputs target_deg, tps_deg the subsystem's In blocks output duty_pct the Out block tunable parameters Kp, Ki, ... the calibratable workspace variables and block parameters default communication step 0.01 s the ECU's task period binaries/darwin64 (or linux64, win64) the compiled library for this computer sources/ the C code, so the FMU can be built on other platforms

It is a co-simulation FMU: the importing tool calls it every communication step (a whole number of 10 ms periods), and the FMU runs the generated step function. The generated code keeps its state in global variables, so one program can run one instance of it at a time.

docs.title: Step 2: run it without Nervus
docs.text:
The example runs the FMU in fmpy, without any Nervus code: a step of the target angle from 5° to 60° gives a duty cycle of 0 % before the step and 82 % after it, the same numbers as the model. In Simulink, drag an FMU block into a model and pick ECU.fmu; in Python:

from fmpy import simulate_fmu

result = simulate_fmu("ECU.fmu", stop_time=1.0, input=signals, start_values={"Kp": 3.0})

docs.title: Step 3: import an FMU
docs.text:
The FMU block (Ports & Subsystems library) runs any FMI 2.0 co-simulation FMU in a Nervus model. Its ports are the FMU's inputs and outputs; parameters sets the FMU's parameters, for example Kp = 3.0; sample_time is the communication step (0: the FMU's default). examples/fmi_plant.nervus is the throttle model with the ECU subsystem replaced by the FMU:

The responses differ during the fast tip-in by up to 13°, and peak and steady state are the same. The reason is the co-simulation itself: the FMU's output is available at the end of a communication step, so the controller acts 10 ms later than the inline subsystem. That is true for every co-simulation FMU, also in Simulink; a shorter communication step (when the FMU allows it) makes the difference smaller.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
Try What you will see ECU_fmu parameters = Kp = 3.0 a stiffer controller inside the FMU: a faster rise parameters = Kq = 1 an error: the FMU has no such parameter ECU_fmu sample_time = 0.02 the FMU runs two internal steps per communication step: a 20 ms lag, and the difference grows to 25° uv run python -c "from fmpy import dump; dump('examples/generated/ECU.fmu')" the FMU's description: variables, value references, platforms

See C code generation for the details of the export.

docs.title: Tutorial: Wall wetting and learned fuel trims
docs.text:
You will learn fuel film dynamics (x-tau) and transient compensation, a switching lambda sensor, long-term trims learned per load cell (Adaptive Map) Before this Lambda control and fuel trims Level and time intermediate, about 30 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/fuel_film.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Powertrain and engine control ▸ Engine management (all tutorials)

This tutorial follows examples/fuel_film.py and continues lambda control with three things every production fuel system has.

uv run python examples/fuel_film.py

docs.title: Wall wetting (x-tau)
docs.text:
Part of the fuel injected into the intake port lands on its wall and evaporates later. With the share X that deposits and the evaporation time constant τ:

\[ \frac{dm_{film}}{dt} = X\,q_{inj} - \frac{m_{film}}{\tau}, \qquad q_{cyl} = (1 - X)\,q_{inj} + \frac{m_{film}}{\tau} \]

On a tip-in (air flow 5 → 20 g/s) the film first has to grow, so the cylinders get too little fuel and the engine runs lean, then rich on the tip-out. Without compensation lambda jumps by 28 %. The ECU runs the same model with its own film estimate and injects

\[ q_{inj} = \frac{q_{cyl,desired} - m_{film,est}/\tau}{1 - X} \]

which cuts the excursion to 10 % here (the rest comes from the manifold filling and the 10 ms task).

docs.title: A switching lambda sensor
docs.text: A narrow-band (zirconia) sensor only says rich (about 0.8 V) or lean (about 0.1 V). The short-term trim therefore jumps by 2 % when the sensor switches and ramps by 8 %/s in between: lambda oscillates in a small limit cycle around 1, which is also what the catalyst needs to store and release oxygen.

docs.title: Long-term trims per load cell
docs.text: The injectors in this model deliver 8 % too little at low flow (an injector non-linearity at short pulses). The long-term trim is an Adaptive Map over the air flow: it learns the average short-term trim in the cells around the current operating point. At idle it learns +8.8 %; at 20 g/s it stays near 0 %, and when the engine comes back to idle, the idle correction is still there, so the short-term trim does not have to start over. A single long-term trim would be pulled back and forth between the two regions.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
To try one: change the value in the Model Workspace tab (double-click it), or for a block parameter select the block and edit it in Properties; press ▶ and compare with the previous run in the Data Inspector (Ctrl+I). Ctrl+Z undoes the change.

Try What you will see xtau_comp = 0 28 % lean and rich spikes on every tip-in and tip-out X_film = 0.5 and xtau_comp = 0 (a cold engine, no compensation) 46 % spikes; a real ECU makes X and τ depend on the coolant temperature ltft_rate = 0.1 the map learns slowly: after 20 s it has 6.7 % and the short-term trim still carries the rest

docs.title: Tutorial: Gear-shift logic
docs.text:
You will learn an automatic gearbox's shift schedule, hysteresis, a State Chart in its own ECU task, kickdown and hills, fuel consumption per gear Before this Your first model: a cruise control, A car on a drive cycle; read State machines first Level and time intermediate, about 60 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/gear_shift.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Powertrain and engine control ▸ Transmission and driveline (all tutorials)

This tutorial follows examples/gear_shift.py: the shift logic of an automatic gearbox, running in its own ECU (the TCU, transmission control unit), and a car to try it on. You will see how a shift schedule works, why it needs hysteresis, and how it reacts to the driver and to a hill.

uv run python examples/gear_shift.py      # simulates, saves gear_shift.nervus, runs the tests
uv run nervus examples/gear_shift.nervus  # open it in the editor

docs.title: The model
docs.text: The pedal and the road grade come from From Workspace blocks. The tcu subsystem reads the vehicle speed and the pedal and decides the gear; the car subsystem turns the gear and the pedal into speed and engine speed.

docs.title: The shift schedule
docs.text:
A TCU decides the gear from two maps over (gear, pedal position):

Upshift speed [km/h] pedal 0 % 50 % 100 % 1 → 2 15 25 40 2 → 3 30 45 70 3 → 4 45 65 100 4 → 5 60 85 130 Downshift speed [km/h] pedal 0 % 50 % 100 % 2 → 1 10 15 30 3 → 2 22 32 55 4 → 3 35 50 85 5 → 4 50 68 110

With more pedal both thresholds rise. The engine revs further before each upshift, so there is more power when the driver asks for it. With a light foot the gearbox shifts up early, and the engine runs at low speed, where it uses less fuel. Pressing the pedal fully at speed raises the downshift speed above the current speed, and the gearbox drops a gear or two: kickdown.

In the TCU, two 2-D Lookup Tables (up_map, down_map) read the maps for the current gear and the pedal. The current gear comes from the chart through a Unit Delay: the maps for this step use the gear of the last step, which also breaks the loop between the chart and the maps. The maps are workspace variables (upshift_map, downshift_map), so they are calibration data in the generated C code and in the A2L file.

docs.title: The chart
docs.text:
input speed, up_speed, down_speed
output gear = 1, shifting = 0
param min_gear_time, shift_time

state g1
  entry: gear = 1; shifting = 0
state g2
  entry: gear = 2; shifting = 1
  during: shifting = 1 if t_in_state < shift_time else 0
...
transition g1 -> g2: speed > up_speed and after(min_gear_time)
transition g2 -> g3: speed > up_speed and after(min_gear_time)
transition g2 -> g1: speed < down_speed and after(min_gear_time)
...

One state per gear. Two things keep the gearbox from hunting (shifting up and down again and again):

  1. Hysteresis in the maps. Every downshift speed is below the upshift speed of the gear below. After an upshift from 2nd to 3rd at 45 km/h (50 % pedal), the speed would have to drop to 32 km/h before the gearbox goes back to 2nd.
  2. A minimum time in each gear, after(min_gear_time): 100 samples of 10 ms = 1 s.

While a shift is in progress (shift_time = 0.3 s) the output shifting is 1 and the engine torque is cut. A real gearbox does this to synchronise the speeds of the shafts.

The TCU is an atomic subsystem with a 10 ms sample time, so it is one ECU task. Generate its C code with Code → Generate C on the selected tcu block, or:

from nervus.codegen import generate_c

code = generate_c(d.block("tcu"))

docs.title: The car
docs.text:
gearbox: the ratio of the current gear times the final drive, \(i = i_{gear}\,i_{final}\). The engine speed follows from the wheel speed, \(n = \frac{v}{r_{wheel}}\,i \cdot \frac{60}{2\pi}\) rpm. The clutch is locked, except below idle speed, where it slips (clutch_slip takes the maximum of the two).

engine: the torque is the pedal fraction times the full-load torque at the current speed, minus the friction torque. With the pedal released, the friction brakes the car (engine braking). While shifting, the torque is cut to zero.

body: Newton's second law along the road, with aerodynamic drag, rolling resistance and the grade \(\alpha = \arctan(\text{grade}/100)\):

\[ m\,\frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{T\,i\,\eta}{r_{wheel}} - \tfrac{1}{2}\rho\,c_d A\,v^2 - m g\,c_{rr}\cos\alpha - m g \sin\alpha \]

docs.title: Fuel consumption: why light-pedal upshifts save fuel
docs.text:
The engine has a brake-specific fuel consumption map (BSFC, in g/kWh) over speed and torque. The fuel flow is the map value times the power the engine delivers:

\[ \dot m_{fuel} = \frac{\mathrm{BSFC}(n, T)\cdot T\,\omega}{3.6\cdot 10^{6}} \quad [\text{g/s}] \]

The map is best (about 245 g/kWh, 33 % efficiency) at middle speed and high load, and poor at light load, where the throttle losses dominate. Cruising at 80 km/h needs the same power in every gear, but in 5th the engine runs at 2000 rpm with a high load, in 3rd at 3700 rpm with a light load. Over the cruise (12-22 s):

engine speed fuel 5th gear (the shift schedule) 2040 rpm 5.1 L/100 km held in 3rd (upshift_map row 3 = 999) 3720 rpm 7.6 L/100 km

Half as much fuel again, for the same speed. The model integrates the fuel (fuel_g) and the distance (distance); the whole drive with its full-throttle launch, kickdown and hill uses about 14 L/100 km.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Full-throttle launch (0–9 s): the upshifts come at 40 and 70 km/h, at almost 5000 rpm. Each upshift drops the engine speed, and the speed curve has a short flat step: the torque cut.
  • 20 % pedal (9–22 s): the thresholds fall below the current speed, so the gearbox shifts straight up to 5th and the engine settles at about 2100 rpm.
  • Kickdown (22 s): at 100 % pedal the downshift speeds of 5th (110 km/h) and 4th (85 km/h) are above the 76 km/h of the car. The gearbox drops to 4th, and one second later (the minimum gear time) to 3rd. The engine jumps to 3700 rpm and the car accelerates.
  • A 10 % hill at 60 % pedal (from 28 s): the car slows down and, below 76 km/h, the gearbox drops to 4th.

The four test cases in the Test Manager check each phase. The test in tests/test_examples.py also checks that no gear is held for less than a second, and that the C code of the TCU gives exactly the same gears as the simulation.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
To try one: change the value in the Model Workspace tab (double-click it), or for a block parameter select the block and edit it in Properties; press ▶ and compare with the previous run in the Data Inspector (Ctrl+I). Ctrl+Z undoes the change.

Try What you will see min_gear_time = 0 the kickdown goes from 5th to 3rd within 0.07 s, and the launch shifts 4 → 5 after only 0.2 s in 4th shift_time = 1.0 longer torque cuts: the car reaches 71 instead of 80 km/h at 9 s upshift_map 1 → 2 at full pedal = 60 (first row: 15, 25, 60) 1st gear tops out at 55 km/h, where the engine reaches 6400 rpm and its full-load torque runs out: the car is stuck in 1st until the pedal is released at 9 s. Shift maps must fit the gear ratios mass = 2500 the heavier car never reaches 5th: the kickdown drops one gear, and the hill pulls it down to 3rd gear_ratios = [4.0, 2.4, 1.6, 1.2, 1.0] shorter gears: 85 instead of 80 km/h at 9 s, but 2800 instead of 2100 rpm when cruising

docs.title: Tutorial: Idle speed control
docs.text:
You will learn how an ECU holds the idle speed: a mean-value engine model, a PI controller with feed-forward, requirements as test cases, C code Before this Your first model: a cruise control Level and time beginner, about 45 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/idle_speed_control.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Powertrain and engine control ▸ Engine management (all tutorials)

This tutorial walks through examples/idle_speed_control.py. It's a complete engine-control loop: a physical engine model, an ECU function that holds the idle speed, a calibration, requirement tests, and C code. Open examples/idle_speed_control.nervus in the editor to follow along.

docs.title: 1. The plant: a mean-value engine model
docs.text:
A mean-value engine model (MVEM) averages over the engine cycle. It ignores individual combustion events but captures how air, pressure and speed evolve, which is exactly what idle control needs.

Part Equation Block(s) Throttle flow \(\dot m_{th} = C_d A(\alpha) \frac{p_{amb}}{\sqrt{R T}} \Psi\left(\frac{p_{im}}{p_{amb}}\right)\) throttle_flow (Python Function) Intake manifold \(\dot p_{im} = \frac{R T}{V_{im}} (\dot m_{th} - \dot m_{cyl})\) manifold_net_flow, R_T_over_V, p_intake Cylinder air flow \(\dot m_{cyl} = \eta_{vol} \frac{p_{im} V_d \omega}{4 \pi R T}\) cylinder_flow Torque \(T = \eta_{th} Q_{LHV} \frac{\dot m_{cyl}/14.7}{\omega} - (T_{f0} + c_f \omega) - T_{load}\) net_torque Crankshaft \(J \dot\omega = T\) 1/J, omega

\(\Psi\) is the compressible-flow function. Below a pressure ratio of 0.528 the flow is choked (sonic) and no longer depends on the manifold pressure. At idle the throttle is almost closed and the manifold is at about 20 kPa, so the engine runs on choked flow: the air flow depends on the throttle angle only.

The manifold acts as a delay: when the throttle opens, the pressure (and therefore the torque) needs roughly a quarter of a second to follow. That makes idle control hard.

docs.title: 2. The ECU function
docs.text:
Double-click the ECU subsystem. It does what the idle speed controller in a real ECU does, every 10 ms:

  1. sample the engine speed (rpm_sample, a Zero-Order Hold at Ts = 0.01),
  2. compute the speed error to the target rpm_idle,
  3. run a discrete PI controller with clamping anti-windup (idle_pi),
  4. add a base throttle opening alpha_base (feed-forward for the nominal idle air demand),
  5. add alpha_ac when the air-conditioning is requested (AC feed-forward).

All gains are workspace variables, so they are calibration parameters with units and limits, and appear in the generated A2L file.

docs.title: 3. Why feed-forward?
docs.text:
At t = 5 s the AC compressor adds 12 N·m of load. Feedback alone can only react once the speed has already dropped, and the manifold delay makes the reaction slow, so the speed falls to about 685 rpm. Production ECUs receive the AC request about 200 ms before the compressor clutch engages, and open the throttle in advance. With alpha_ac = 3° the dip shrinks to about 775 rpm:

Try it: set alpha_ac to 0 in the Model Workspace and run again, or compare both in the Data Inspector.

docs.title: 4. Requirements as test cases
docs.text:
The model stores three test cases (Test Manager → Run all):

Test case Checks AC compressor on at 5 s 780–820 rpm before the event, never below 750 rpm, 780–820 rpm again after 9 s AC compressor on, no feed-forward alpha_ac = 0: between 600 and 900 rpm (no stall) higher idle target rpm_idle = 1000: settles at 1000 ± 15 rpm

docs.title: 5. C code for the ECU
docs.text: Select the ECU subsystem and press Code → Generate C Code. Run SIL check compiles the controller and compares it with the model step by step. The engine model stays in simulation; only the controller becomes code.

docs.title: Things to try
docs.text:
To try one: change the value in the Model Workspace tab (double-click it), or for a block parameter select the block and edit it in Properties; press ▶ and compare with the previous run in the Data Inspector (Ctrl+I). Ctrl+Z undoes the change.

  • Make the controller faster: increase Kp_idle. When does it start to oscillate, and why does the manifold delay limit it?
  • Replace the PI controller's feed-forward with a 2-D lookup table of base opening over coolant temperature and target speed. Real ECUs need more air when the engine is cold.
  • Add a State Chart that switches between crank, idle and drive modes and only enables idle control in idle.

docs.title: Tutorial: Ignition timing and knock control
docs.text:
You will learn spark advance from a speed/load map (2-D lookup table), knock and the knock limit, a knock controller that retards and recovers, noisy sensors Before this Idle speed control, Lambda control and fuel trims Level and time intermediate, about 30 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/ignition_knock.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Powertrain and engine control ▸ Engine management (all tutorials)

This tutorial follows examples/ignition_knock.py. It is the third part of the engine-control series, after idle speed control and lambda control.

uv run python examples/ignition_knock.py

docs.title: Spark advance
docs.text:
The flame needs time to burn through the charge, so the spark fires before top dead centre: the advance, in degrees of crank angle. The best torque comes at MBT (minimum advance for best torque); with less advance the pressure peaks too late. The torque efficiency in this model falls off quadratically:

\[ \eta_{spark} = 1 - 0.0011\,(\alpha - \alpha_{MBT})^2 \qquad (1\ \%\ \text{at}\ 3°,\ 11\ \%\ \text{at}\ 10°) \]

The ECU reads the base advance from a map over speed and load (advance_map, calibration data): more advance at high speed (less time per degree), less at high load.

docs.title: Knock
docs.text:
At high load, the last part of the charge can ignite by itself before the flame reaches it: knock, a sharp pressure wave that damages pistons and head gaskets. It starts at the knock limit, which is lower with low-octane fuel, hot intake air, a hot engine and high load. At full load the knock limit is below MBT, so the engine is knock limited: the calibration keeps 2-3° below the knock limit of the reference fuel.

A knock sensor (an accelerometer on the engine block) picks up the vibration. In the model, the knock intensity grows with the square of the advance beyond the limit, with cycle-to-cycle scatter (a Sensor Model with noise).

docs.title: Knock control
docs.text:
The ECU (10 ms task) counts a knock event when the sensor exceeds a threshold, and for each event retards the spark by 3°; the retard then recovers by 1°/s:

\[ r_{k+1} = \mathrm{clip}(r_k + 3°\cdot\text{knock}_k - 1°/\text{s}\cdot T_s,\ 0,\ 12°), \qquad \alpha = \alpha_{base}(n, \text{load}) - r \]

At 4 s the car gets low-octane fuel, and the knock limit drops by 6° to 12°. The first combustions knock hard; the ECU retards, and from then on the advance makes a sawtooth just around the new limit. It creeps up at 1°/s until a knock occurs, then steps back 3°. On average the spark is retarded by 5°, and the engine gives up 12 % torque (from 93 % to 81 %): the price of the cheaper fuel. Real ECUs do this per cylinder, and learn the retard into a map so the engine starts at the right timing.

The ECU subsystem generates C code; the test compares it back to back with the simulation.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
To try one: change the value in the Model Workspace tab (double-click it), or for a block parameter select the block and edit it in Properties; press ▶ and compare with the previous run in the Data Inspector (Ctrl+I). Ctrl+Z undoes the change.

Try What you will see knock_recover = 3 the advance creeps up faster: twice as many knock events, but less time far below the limit (82 % torque) knock_step = 1 smaller steps: the advance stays closer to the limit (3° average retard, 86 % torque) knock_threshold = 0.2 noise starts to count as knock: the ECU retards almost 12° and the torque falls to 57 %

docs.title: Tutorial: The injector driver power stage
docs.text:
You will learn a low-side switch driving a solenoid injector, opening delay versus battery voltage, freewheeling diode versus clamp, why injection needs a battery voltage correction Before this RC and RLC circuits Level and time intermediate, about 30 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/injector_driver.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Electrics and electronics ▸ ECU hardware and PCB (all tutorials)

A fuel injector is a solenoid valve, switched by a transistor on the ECU's circuit board. How long it is really open, and so how much fuel the engine gets, depends on that circuit and on the battery voltage, not only on the pulse the software commands. examples/injector_driver.py models the power stage and shows the two effects every injection software compensates.

uv run python examples/injector_driver.py

docs.title: The circuit
docs.text:
Part Value battery 9-15 V (V_bat), the injector's supply injector Fuel Injector block: 12 Ω, 10 mH, the needle lifts above 0.6 A and drops below 0.3 A, 3.5 g/s when open low-side switch the ECU's transistor between the injector and ground, 0.1 Ω when on clamp the transistor's avalanche clamp: limits its voltage to 60 V freewheeling diode optional (freewheel = 1): across the coil, from the transistor back to the battery

The software commands a 3 ms pulse. At 3.5 g/s that should be 10.5 mg of fuel.

docs.title: Opening: the battery voltage matters
docs.text:
When the transistor switches on, the coil current rises with the time constant \(\tau = L/R = 0.83\) ms towards \(V_{bat}/R\):

\[ i(t) = \frac{V_{bat}}{R}\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right) \]

The needle only starts to lift when the current passes the pull-in current (0.6 A), and then needs 0.5 ms to travel. At 14 V the injector is open (half lift) 0.96 ms after the command; at 9 V, where the current only just reaches 0.6 A (9/12.1 = 0.74 A at the end), it takes 1.71 ms.

docs.title: Closing: freewheeling diode or clamp
docs.text:
When the transistor switches off, the coil keeps driving its current:

  • With a freewheeling diode, the current circulates through the diode and decays slowly with τ; the voltage at the transistor stays near the battery voltage (14.7 V at 14 V). The needle closes 1.34 ms after the end of the pulse.
  • Without it, the current has nowhere to go; the transistor's voltage jumps until the clamp conducts at 60 V, and the high voltage drives the current down fast. The needle closes 0.50 ms after the end. That is why injector drivers use a clamp: a fast, repeatable closing. The price is a transistor rated for 60 V and the energy dissipated in it at every injection.

docs.title: What the engine gets
docs.text:
Battery Driver Opens after Closes after Fuel (3 ms command) 9 V clamp 1.71 ms 0.41 ms 6.0 mg 12 V clamp 1.12 ms 0.46 ms 8.2 mg 14 V clamp 0.96 ms 0.50 ms 8.9 mg 15 V clamp 0.90 ms 0.51 ms 9.2 mg 14 V freewheel diode 0.96 ms 1.34 ms 11.9 mg

The same command delivers 50 % more fuel at 15 V than at 9 V. An engine ECU therefore adds a battery voltage correction (the injector's "dead time", a table over the battery voltage) to every pulse, so a cold start on a weak battery still gets the fuel it needs. The table comes from exactly this kind of measurement, on the bench with the real injector and driver.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Try What you will see freewheel = 1 a slow, voltage-independent closing: more fuel, and a different dead-time table V_bat = 9 with freewheel = 0 the current barely reaches the pull-in level: a weak battery at a cold start the injector's L = 0.005 a faster coil: it opens earlier, and the voltage dependence shrinks the injector's I_pull = 0.75 at 9 V the current never reaches pull-in: the injector does not open at all

docs.title: Tutorial: Balancing an inverted pendulum with state feedback
docs.text:
You will learn an unstable plant, state-space models, LQR state feedback, non-minimum-phase behaviour, redesigning a gain in the Console Before this DC motor speed and position control Level and time advanced, about 45 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/inverted_pendulum.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Control engineering ▸ Classic lab experiments (all tutorials)

examples/inverted_pendulum.py is the classic advanced control lab: a pendulum hinged on a cart, balanced upright by moving the cart. Upright is unstable, a single PID loop cannot hold the pendulum and the cart at the same time, so the controller feeds back all four states with a gain designed by LQR (linear quadratic regulator). The dimensions are those of a common lab rig.

uv run python examples/inverted_pendulum.py

docs.title: The plant
docs.text:
A cart of 0.94 kg carries a pendulum rod (0.23 kg, 0.64 m) on a hinge; the motor pushes the cart with up to ±10 N. The state is \(x = [\,x_{cart},\ \theta,\ \dot x_{cart},\ \dot\theta\,]\) with \(\theta = 0\) upright. The model uses the full nonlinear equations of motion (the cart_pole Python Function block; its integrator holds the four states):

\[ (M + m)\ddot x + m l (\ddot\theta\cos\theta - \dot\theta^2 \sin\theta) = F - b\dot x, \qquad (J + m l^2)\ddot\theta + m l \ddot x \cos\theta = m g l \sin\theta - B\dot\theta \]

Linearized at upright, \(\dot x = A x + B F\) has the poles 0, −3.8, −6.7 and +4.9 rad/s: the pendulum falls with a time constant of 0.2 s. Set K_lqr to [0, 0, 0, 0] and run: it falls past 0.5 rad (29°) within 0.6 s.

docs.title: The controller: LQR state feedback
docs.text:
State feedback \(F = -K(x - x_{ref})\) places all four poles at once. LQR chooses the \(K\) that minimizes

\[ J = \int_0^\infty \left( x^T Q x + r F^2 \right) dt, \qquad Q = \mathrm{diag}(q_x, q_\theta, 0, 0) \]

so \(q_x\) and \(q_\theta\) say how much cart and angle errors cost, and \(r\) how much force costs. lqr_gain() in the example solves the Riccati equation (with SciPy) for the linear model; with \(q_x = 50\), \(q_\theta = 100\), \(r = 1\) it gives \(K = [-7.1,\ -57,\ -15,\ -11]\), stored in the workspace as K_lqr and used by the K gain block (matrix multiplication). The sensors are sampled every 2 ms.

Run the model: the controller catches the 3° start, rejects the tap at 3 s (5 N for 0.1 s) and moves the cart to 0.3 m at 5 s, settling within 2 % in 3.6 s, with the pendulum never more than 3° from upright and at most 4.3 N.

Look at the cart at 5 s, when the reference jumps to +0.3 m: it first moves backwards (from −17 to −26 mm, it was still recovering from the tap) and the pendulum leans 2° towards +x before the cart follows. To move right, the pendulum must first lean right, and the only way to tip it is to pull the cart left from under it. This non-minimum-phase behaviour (a zero in the right half plane) is why balancing systems react "backwards", and why they cannot be made arbitrarily fast.

docs.title: Redesign the gain in the Console
docs.text:
K_lqr is a workspace variable, so a new design is one line in the Console tab:

import sys

sys.path.insert(0, "examples")
from inverted_pendulum import lqr_gain

model.workspace["K_lqr"] = lqr_gain(q_x=200)

Then press ▶ and compare the runs in the Data Inspector.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Try What you will see lqr_gain(q_x=200) the cart is more important: it reaches 0.3 m in 2.1 s instead of 3.6 s, the pendulum leans up to 3.8° lqr_gain(r=10) force is expensive: gentle and slow, the cart has only reached 0.25 m after 5 s F_max = 3 a weaker motor still balances (it saturates for a moment during the tap) F_max = 1.5 too weak for the tap: the pendulum falls at 3.7 s m_pend = 0.35 the plant is heavier than the design model, and the LQR gain is robust enough to balance it anyway

docs.title: Tutorial: Lambda control and fuel trims
docs.text:
You will learn why petrol engines run at lambda = 1, closed-loop fuel control with a lambda sensor, short- and long-term fuel trims (as read over OBD-II), an ECU task in an atomic subsystem Before this Idle speed control Level and time intermediate, about 45 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/lambda_control.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Powertrain and engine control ▸ Engine management (all tutorials)

This tutorial follows examples/lambda_control.py. It shows how a petrol engine's ECU keeps the air-fuel ratio at the value the catalytic converter needs, and what the fuel trims that you can read from your car over OBD-II actually are.

uv run python examples/lambda_control.py      # simulates, saves lambda_control.nervus, runs the tests
uv run nervus examples/lambda_control.nervus  # open it in the editor

docs.title: Why lambda = 1
docs.text:
Burning petrol completely takes 14.7 kg of air per kg of fuel, the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio. The air-fuel equivalence ratio lambda compares the actual mixture with it:

\[ \lambda = \frac{m_{air}}{14.7\, m_{fuel}} \]

λ > 1 is lean (too much air), λ < 1 is rich. A three-way catalyst removes CO, HC and NOx at the same time only in a narrow window around λ = 1, so the ECU controls λ to 1 at part load all the time.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
Plant (the engine), top and bottom rows:

  • the air charge per cylinder stroke: 250 mg at part load, a tip-in to 400 mg from 4 s to 8 s;
  • from t = 12 s a vacuum leak: 6 % extra air that enters behind the MAF sensor, so the ECU doesn't see it;
  • the injectors: fuel mass = (injection time − dead time) × flow rate;
  • the exhaust gas needs \(n_{exh}\) = 8 samples × 10 ms to reach the lambda sensor, and the sensor itself has a time constant \(\tau\) = 0.1 s.

ECU: the ECU block is an atomic subsystem with sample_time = Ts (10 ms), the fuel task:

\[ m_{fuel,cmd} = \frac{m_{air,MAF}}{14.7}\,(1 + STFT + LTFT), \qquad t_{inj} = \frac{m_{fuel,cmd}}{q_{inj}} + t_{dead} \]
  • The base fuel comes from the measured air (feed-forward). If the sensors and injectors were perfect, this alone would give λ = 1.
  • The short-term fuel trim (STFT) is a discrete PI controller on the lambda error \(e = \lambda_{meas} - 1\), limited to ±25 %. Lean (e > 0) means more fuel.
  • The long-term fuel trim (LTFT) integrates the STFT slowly: \(LTFT[k+1] = LTFT[k] + K_{ltft}\,T_s\,STFT[k]\). It moves the average correction out of the STFT, which then returns to 0 and has its full ±25 % available again for fast disturbances.

docs.title: What happens
docs.text:
1. Up to 12 s λ stays at 1, even during the tip-in: the base fuel follows the measured air.
  2. At 12 s the leak makes the mixture 6 % lean. The lambda sensor sees it about 0.2 s later (exhaust delay and sensor lag); the STFT rises to about +5 % within three seconds and brings λ back to 1.
  3. Over the next 25 s the LTFT learns the leak: it rises to almost +6 % while the STFT falls back to 0.

A real ECU stores the LTFT, often per load and speed range, and keeps it when the engine is switched off. It also sets a trouble code when a trim reaches its limit, such as P0171 System too lean (see the OBD-II page).

docs.title: Compare with your car
docs.text:
Your car reports the same two numbers as OBD PIDs 06 (stft_b1) and 07 (ltft_b1):

uv run python -m nervus.obd record --port /dev/tty.usbserial-1110 \
    --pids rpm,maf,stft_b1,ltft_b1,o2_b1s1 --duration 300 --out my_drive.nervres
  • A healthy engine has an LTFT within about ±5 % and an STFT that keeps moving around 0.
  • An LTFT of +10 % or more at idle that gets smaller at higher load is the classic sign of a vacuum leak: the leak is a fixed amount of air, so it matters most when little air is flowing.
  • An LTFT that is high at all loads points more to fuel delivery (pump pressure, injectors) or the MAF sensor.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
To try one: change the value in the Model Workspace tab (double-click it), or for a block parameter select the block and edit it in Properties; press ▶ and compare with the previous run in the Data Inspector (Ctrl+I). Ctrl+Z undoes the change.

Change the workspace variables in the Model Workspace panel and run again:

Try What you will see injector_error = -0.05, leak = 0 clogged injectors: the LTFT learns about +5.3 % (= 1/0.95 − 1) K_ltft = 0.5 faster learning, but the trims overshoot: the STFT goes negative and λ dips rich (0.987) Ki_stft = 4 a faster STFT (peak after 0.7 s instead of 2.7 s), with some overshoot n_exh = 20 and Ki_stft = 4 a longer exhaust delay with a fast STFT: much more overshoot, λ dips to 0.98. The delay limits how fast the STFT can be

The test cases in the Test Manager check the leak and clogged-injector cases, and that λ stays at 1 during the tip-in. Generate C code for the ECU block (Code → Generate C) to get the fuel task as ECU code.

docs.title: Tutorial: Position control of a mass-spring-damper
docs.text:
You will learn what the P, I and D terms do, natural frequency and damping ratio, steady-state error, actuator limits and anti-windup Before this Your first model: a cruise control Level and time beginner, about 30 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/mass_spring_damper_pid.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Control engineering ▸ Classic lab experiments (all tutorials)

examples/mass_spring_damper_pid.py is the first experiment of many control lab courses: a mass on a spring, pushed by a force actuator, and a PID controller that moves it to a reference position. You will design the controller in the classic order, P, then PD, then PID, and see what each term does.

uv run python examples/mass_spring_damper_pid.py

docs.title: The plant
docs.text:
A mass \(m\) on a spring \(k\) with viscous damping \(c\), pushed by a force \(F\):

\[ m \ddot x + c \dot x + k x = F \]

With \(m = 1\) kg, \(c = 0.5\) N·s/m and \(k = 2\) N/m the open plant has the natural frequency \(\omega_n = \sqrt{k/m} = 1.41\) rad/s and the damping ratio \(\zeta = c / (2\sqrt{km}) = 0.18\): left alone it oscillates for a long time. In the model the equation is two Integrators (acceleration → velocity → position) with the spring and damper as feedback Gains, the way it is drawn in every textbook. The actuator is limited to ±50 N (the PID block's upper and lower).

docs.title: Step 1: P control
docs.text:
In the Model Workspace set Ki = 0 and Kd = 0, then press ▶ and open the scope. A P controller acts like an extra spring: the closed loop has the stiffness \(k + K_p\), so

\[ x_\infty = \frac{K_p}{k + K_p} = \frac{40}{42} = 0.952 \text{ m}, \qquad \omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{k + K_p}{m}} = 6.5 \text{ rad/s}, \qquad \zeta = \frac{c}{2\sqrt{m(k+K_p)}} = 0.04 \]

The mass shoots to 1.8 m and rings for many seconds around 0.952 m. A stiffer controller makes the error smaller but the oscillation worse: P alone cannot do both.

docs.title: Step 2: PD control
docs.text: Set Kd = 8. The derivative term acts like an extra damper: \(\zeta = (c + K_d) / (2\sqrt{m(k+K_p)}) = 0.66\). The overshoot drops to 5.5 % and the mass is settled within 1.4 s, but still at 0.952 m: the D term does nothing at standstill, so the steady-state error stays. The step makes the D term kick: the force jumps to the 50 N limit for a moment.

docs.title: Step 3: PID control
docs.text:
Set Ki = 30. The integral term keeps pushing while there is any error, so the mass ends exactly at 1 m. The price is a little more overshoot (12 %); the response settles within 2 % in 2.3 s.

Controller Highest position Final position Settled (2 %) P (Kp = 40) 1.80 m 0.952 m (still ringing at 10 s) > 10 s PD (Kd = 8) 1.00 m 0.952 m 1.4 s PID (Ki = 30) 1.12 m 1.000 m 2.3 s

The controller uses clamping anti-windup: while the force is at its limit, the integrator stops. With back-calculation anti-windup and Ki = 0, the integrator would still collect the saturation correction and leave a permanent offset (Simulink behaves the same way), so clamping is the right choice for a lab where the I term is switched off and on.

docs.title: Check it by hand, then with the tuner
docs.text: The PD loop's characteristic equation is \(m s^2 + (c + K_d) s + (k + K_p) = 0\), that is \(s^2 + 8.5 s + 42 = 0\), with the poles \(-4.25 \pm 4.9j\): \(\omega_n = 6.5\) rad/s and \(\zeta = 0.66\), as in step 2. For a systematic design open Analysis ▸ Linear Analysis ▸ PID Tuning, choose the block pid and a phase margin, and press Tune: it designs the gains from the plant the controller sees (see Linear analysis). Copy its gains into the workspace and compare its step response with yours in the Data Inspector: a large phase margin gives a calm but slower response.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Try What you will see Kp = 100 (PID) faster (settled in 1.3 s) but 20 % overshoot Ki = 100 the error disappears faster, but the overshoot grows to 33 % m = 3 (a heavier mass, same gains) 42 % overshoot: gains are tuned for one plant Kd = 20 more damping in the PD part, but the I term still overshoots (13 %) and settling takes longer (4.5 s)
