  • Glow Plug: A diesel glow plug: a heater whose resistance rises with its temperature, which limits its current as it
  • Alternator: An alternator with its voltage regulator, driven by the engine through a belt:

docs.title: CAN
docs.text:
• CAN Unpack: Decodes a CAN frame: the input is the frame's data bytes (a vector: 8 for classic CAN, up to 64 for CAN
  • CAN Pack: Encodes a CAN frame: one input per signal (physical units), output = the data bytes (uint8; 8 for
  • CAN Transmit: Sends a CAN message on a simulated bus: one input per signal (physical units), packed with the DBC file
  • CAN Receive: Receives a CAN message from a simulated bus: one output per signal (physical units, the last frame
  • CAN Bus: Settings of a simulated CAN bus, and its load: bitrate (125, 250, 500 kbit/s or 1 Mbit/s), and the
  • E2E Protect: Protects a frame AUTOSAR E2E style (like profile 1): writes an alive counter (0..14, one step per
  • E2E Check: Checks a frame protected by E2E Protect. Inputs: the 8 data bytes and new (from CAN Receive).
  • CAN Rest Bus: Rest-bus simulation: sends every message of the ECUs (nodes) that are not modelled, at their cycle
  • CAN Gateway: Forwards frames from one bus to another, like the central gateway between the powertrain and the body
  • XCP Slave: Makes the simulated ECU reachable for a calibration tool over XCP on CAN (INCA, CANape, or

docs.title: Continuous
docs.text:
• Integrator: Integrates its input:
  • Derivative: Approximate time derivative of the input.
  • Transfer Fcn: Continuous SISO transfer function
  • State-Space: Continuous linear state-space system

docs.title: Control
docs.text:
• PID Controller: Continuous PID controller (parallel form) with a filtered derivative:
  • Discrete PID Controller: Discrete PID controller (parallel form), as it would run on an ECU every sample_time seconds.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
• Diagnostic Monitor: A diagnostic monitor with a trouble code (DTC), like the diagnostic event manager of an engine ECU.
  • OBD Responder: Makes the model answer OBD-II requests like a car's engine ECU, while the simulation runs.

docs.title: Discontinuities
docs.text:
• Dead Zone: Zero output inside the dead zone [start, end]; outside, the input shifted by the zone edge.
  • Quantizer: Rounds the input to a multiple of interval, like an ADC or a fixed-resolution sensor.
  • Relay: Switch with hysteresis: turns on when the input rises to on_point and off when it falls to
  • Rate Limiter: Limits how fast the signal may change, e.g. torque or throttle ramps for drivability.
  • Saturation: Limits the input to the range [lower, upper]:

docs.title: Discrete
docs.text:
• Unit Delay: Delays its input by one sample period:
  • Zero-Order Hold: Samples its input every sample_time seconds and holds the value until the next sample:
  • Discrete-Time Integrator: Discrete-time integrator (accumulator).
  • Discrete Transfer Fcn: Discrete SISO transfer function
  • Integer Delay: Delays its input by delay samples: y[k] = u[k - N]. The first N outputs are initial.
  • Counter: Counts samples while the input is non-zero (true).
  • Edge Detect: Outputs 1 for one sample when the (boolean) input changes, otherwise 0.
  • Debounce: Debounces a boolean input: the output turns on only after the input has been true for on_samples
  • Discrete Filter (PT1): First-order low-pass filter, the workhorse for smoothing sensor signals in ECU software.
  • Moving Average: Average of the last length samples (including the current one).

docs.title: Electrical
docs.text:
• Electrical Reference: Ground: the node it is linked to is at 0 V. Every circuit needs one.
  • Resistor: An ideal resistor (Ohm's law):
  • Variable Resistor: A resistor whose resistance is the input signal (in Ω, at least R_min): a potentiometer, a sensor
  • Thermistor (NTC): An NTC thermistor, the sensing element of coolant, intake-air, oil and battery temperature sensors. The
  • Capacitor: An ideal capacitor; its voltage is a state:
  • Inductor: An ideal inductor; its current is a state:
  • Voltage Source: An ideal voltage source: \(v_p - v_n = V\). With controlled on, the voltage is the input signal (e.g. from
  • Current Source: An ideal current source: the current I flows out of its p port into the circuit (and back in at
  • Voltage Sensor: Measures the voltage \(v_p - v_n\) as a signal (ideal: no current flows into it).
  • Current Sensor: Measures the current flowing through it from p to n as a signal. Put it in series, like an
  • Switch: A switch controlled by a signal: closed (resistance R_on) while the input is ≥ 0.5, open (conductance
  • Ideal Diode: A piecewise-linear diode: conducts from p (anode) to n (cathode) when the voltage exceeds the
  • Battery: A battery: open-circuit voltage from its state of charge, and an internal resistance:
  • H-Bridge (PWM): An H-bridge driving a motor with PWM, as an average model: the output voltage is the duty cycle times
  • DC Motor: A permanent-magnet DC motor: electrical port p/n, mechanical port shaft:
  • Voltage-Controlled Voltage Source: A voltage-controlled voltage source (SPICE element E): \(v_p - v_n = gain\,(v_{cp} - v_{cn})\). No current
  • Voltage-Controlled Current Source: A voltage-controlled current source (SPICE element G): the current \(gm\,(v_{cp} - v_{cn})\) flows from

docs.title: Hydraulic
docs.text:
• Tank: The tank: the port linked to it is at 0 bar (ambient).
  • Flow Source (Pump): A pump with a given flow from a (suction) to b (outlet), whatever the pressure: the parameter
  • Pressure Source: Holds port a at a pressure above the tank: the parameter p or the input signal.
  • Orifice: A restriction with turbulent flow (an injector nozzle, a valve seat, a filter):
  • Relief Valve: A pressure relief (or pressure regulator) valve: closed below the cracking pressure, then opening in
  • Hydraulic Volume: A volume of fluid (a fuel rail, an accumulator, a hose): its pressure rises as fluid flows in,
  • Pressure Sensor: Measures the pressure of a port (above the tank) as a signal, in bar.
  • Flow Sensor: Measures the flow through it from a to b as a signal, in L/min.

docs.title: Logic and Bit Operations
docs.text:
• Relational Operator: Compares input 0 with input 1: y = (u0 OP u1), giving 1 when true and 0 when false.
  • Compare To Constant: Compares the input with a constant: y = (u OP constant), 1 when true, 0 when false.
  • Logical Operator: Boolean logic. Inputs are true when non-zero. The output is 1 (true) or 0 (false).

docs.title: Lookup Tables
docs.text:
• 1-D Lookup Table: 1-D lookup table (a calibration curve): maps the input through a table of points.
  • 2-D Lookup Table: 2-D lookup table (a calibration map), e.g. ignition advance over engine speed and load.
  • Prelookup: Breakpoint search on its own: finds the interval index k and the fraction f of the input.
  • Interpolation using Prelookup: Interpolates an n-D table (1 to 4 dimensions) at the index and fraction from Prelookup blocks.
  • Adaptive Map: A 2-D map that learns, like an ECU's long-term fuel trim or knock adaptation per load/speed cell.

docs.title: Math Operations
docs.text:
• Gain: Multiplies the input by a constant.
  • Sum: Adds and subtracts its inputs.
  • Product: Multiplies and divides its inputs elementwise.
  • Abs: Absolute value, |u|.
  • Math Function: Applies a mathematical function elementwise: exp, log, sqrt, square, sin, cos, tanh, sign, ...
  • MinMax: Smallest or largest value.
  • Bias: Adds a constant: y = u + bias.

docs.title: Ports & Subsystems
docs.text:
• FMU: Runs an FMU (Functional Mock-up Unit, FMI 2.0 co-simulation) from another tool: Simulink, Dymola,
  • Connection Port: A physical port of the subsystem it is in: what is linked to it inside is linked to whatever is linked
  • In: An input port.
  • Out: An output port. Inside a subsystem it is the subsystem's output number port; at the top level it is an
  • Subsystem: A block that contains its own diagram. Double-click it in the editor to open it.

docs.title: Rotational
docs.text:
• Rotational Reference: A fixed point: the port linked to it does not rotate (ω = 0), e.g. a housing.
  • Inertia: A rotating mass; its speed is a state:
  • Rotational Spring: A torsion spring between two flanges; its torque is a state:
  • Rotational Damper: Viscous friction between two flanges: \(\tau = d\,(\omega_a - \omega_b)\). Link b to a Rotational
  • Torque Source: A torque on a flange, against the reference: the parameter tau, or the input signal when
  • Speed Source: Drives a flange at a given speed, whatever the torque: the parameter w or the input signal.
  • Ideal Gear: A gear without losses or backlash, ratio n = ω_a / ω_b:
  • Speed Sensor: Measures the angular velocity of a flange (against the reference) as a signal, in rad/s.
  • Angle Sensor: Measures the angle of a flange (the integral of its speed) as a signal, in rad. phi0: the angle at
  • Torque Sensor: Measures the torque transmitted through it from a to b (a stiff shaft between the two).

docs.title: Semiconductors
docs.text:
• Diode: A diode with the Shockley equation, like SPICE's diode model:
  • Bipolar Transistor: A bipolar transistor (Ebers-Moll transport model), NPN or PNP. Ports c (collector), b (base),
  • MOSFET: A MOSFET (SPICE level 1, square law), N- or P-channel. Ports d (drain), g (gate), s (source);
  • Op-Amp: An operational amplifier: high gain, and the output limited to its supply rails:

docs.title: Sensors & Actuators
docs.text:
• Sensor Model: A real sensor between the physical value and the ECU's input, sampled every sample_time:
  • Actuator Model: A real actuator between the ECU's command and the physical effect, sampled every sample_time: a delay

docs.title: Signal Attributes
docs.text:
• Rate Transition: Passes a signal between two rates (two ECU tasks) in a way that is deterministic on an RTOS.
  • Data Type Conversion: Converts the input to another data type, e.g. a sensor value to int16 or a controller output to
  • Initial Condition: Outputs value at the start of the simulation, then passes its input through:

docs.title: Signal Routing
docs.text:
• Mux: Combines its inputs into one vector signal, in port order.
  • Demux: Splits a vector signal into num_outputs equally sized parts.
  • Switch: Passes input 0 when the control input (input 1) satisfies criterion, otherwise input 2:

docs.title: Sinks
docs.text:
• Scope: Plots its input signals. In scripts, read the data with result.inputs("scope_name").
  • To Workspace: Saves its input in the simulation result under variable, so result[variable] returns it.
  • Terminator: Terminates an unused output, so the diagram has no unconnected-output warnings.
  • Stop Simulation: Stops the simulation at the first major time step where the input is non-zero (true).
  • Assertion: Fails the simulation with an error if the input is zero (false) at a major time step.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Signal Builder: Test signals drawn as lines: one output per signal, several groups (scenarios) to choose from.
  • Constant: Outputs a constant value (scalar or vector).
  • Step: Steps from initial to final at time.
  • Ramp: A ramp starting at start_time:
  • Sine Wave: Sine wave:
  • Pulse Generator: Square pulse train. High (amplitude) for duty percent of each period, otherwise 0.
  • Clock: Outputs the simulation time t.
  • From Workspace: Plays back recorded data.
  • Ground: Outputs zero. Use it to connect an input you do not need, instead of leaving it unconnected.
  • Drive Cycle: A standard drive cycle as a speed profile (the target for a driver model):

docs.title: State Machines
docs.text: • State Chart: A state machine (chart) for operating modes, sequences and fault handling, like Simulink's Stateflow.

docs.title: Thermal
docs.text:
• Thermal Mass: A body that stores heat; its temperature is a state:
  • Thermal Resistance: Heat conduction or convection between two ports: \(Q = (T_a - T_b) / R\), with \(R = 1/(h A)\) for convection
  • Heat Source: Heat flowing into a port: the parameter Q or the input signal (e.g. a heater, or the losses of a
  • Temperature Source: Holds a port at a temperature, whatever the heat flow: the ambient air, a coolant at a fixed
  • Temperature Sensor: Measures the temperature of a port as a signal, in °C.
  • Heat Flow Sensor: Measures the heat flowing through it from a to b as a signal, in W.

docs.title: User-Defined
docs.text: • Python Function: Runs your own Python function, the equivalent of Simulink's MATLAB Function block.

docs.title: Solenoid
docs.text:
automotive.solenoid · Automotive Electrics

A solenoid (an actuator coil with an armature): the coil current builds up with τ = L/R; above the pull-in current the armature moves in, below the drop-out current it is released:

\[ L\,\frac{di}{dt} = v - R\,i, \qquad \tau\,\frac{dx}{dt} = x_{target} - x \]

Output: the armature position x (0 out, 1 in). For example a canister purge valve or a starter solenoid.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description R 12.0 Ω Coil resistance L 0.01 H Coil inductance I_pull 0.6 A Pull-in current I_drop 0.3 A Drop-out current tau 0.0005 s Armature travel time constant

Direct feedthrough: yes · no inputs

docs.title: Fuel Injector
docs.text:
automotive.injector · Automotive Electrics

A solenoid fuel injector: the needle opens when the coil current passes the pull-in current, so the injector opens a little after the ECU switches it on (the opening delay, which the ECU compensates with the battery voltage) and closes after the current has decayed. Outputs: needle lift (0..1) and fuel flow (lift × static flow, g/s). Typical port injector: R = 12 Ω, L = 10 mH, 3.5 g/s.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description R 12.0 Ω Coil resistance L 0.01 H Coil inductance I_pull 0.6 A Pull-in current I_drop 0.3 A Drop-out current tau 0.0005 s Armature travel time constant static_flow 3.5 g/s Flow when fully open

Direct feedthrough: yes · no inputs

docs.title: Relay
docs.text:
automotive.relay · Automotive Electrics

A relay: a coil (p, n) and a normally-open contact (a, b) that closes while the armature is pulled in. Output: 1 while the contact is closed. For example the main relay, the fuel pump relay or a starter relay.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description R 80.0 Ω Coil resistance L 0.1 H Coil inductance I_pull 0.08 A Pull-in current I_drop 0.03 A Drop-out current tau 0.002 s Armature travel time constant R_contact 0.005 Ω Contact resistance when closed

Direct feedthrough: yes · no inputs

docs.title: Glow Plug
docs.text:
automotive.glow_plug · Automotive Electrics

A diesel glow plug: a heater whose resistance rises with its temperature, which limits its current as it heats up (self-regulating):

\[ R(T) = R_0\,(1 + \alpha\,(T - 20)), \qquad C\,\frac{dT}{dt} = \frac{v^2}{R(T)} - \frac{T - T_{case}}{R_{th}} \]

Ports: p, n (electrical) and case (thermal: the cylinder head). Output: the tip temperature.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description R0 0.5 Ω Resistance at 20 °C alpha 0.006 1/K Temperature coefficient C 3.0 J/K Heat capacity of the tip R_th 25.0 K/W Thermal resistance to the cylinder head T0 20.0 °C Initial temperature

Direct feedthrough: yes · no inputs

docs.title: Alternator
docs.text:
automotive.alternator · Automotive Electrics

An alternator with its voltage regulator, driven by the engine through a belt:

\[ \tau_r\,\frac{dI}{dt} = \min(\max(K\,(V_{set} - v),\ 0),\ I_{max}(n)) - I \] \[ \tau_{shaft} = \frac{v\,I}{\eta\,\omega} \]

It delivers current I out of p to hold V_set; at low speed it can deliver less (zero below the cut-in speed, I_rated from rated_rpm). The current it delivers loads the engine: the torque on shaft (the crankshaft; ratio is the pulley ratio) is the electrical power divided by the efficiency. Output: the current I.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description V_set 14.2 V Regulated voltage I_rated 120.0 A Maximum current at rated speed cut_in_rpm 1000.0 rpm Alternator speed where it starts to deliver rated_rpm 6000.0 rpm Alternator speed for the full current ratio 2.5 Pulley ratio (alternator speed / engine speed) K 50.0 A/V Regulator gain tau_r 0.05 s Regulator and field time constant efficiency 0.6 Efficiency

Direct feedthrough: yes · no inputs

docs.title: CAN Unpack
docs.text:
can.unpack · CAN

Decodes a CAN frame: the input is the frame's data bytes (a vector: 8 for classic CAN, up to 64 for CAN FD), and there is one output per signal, in physical units (raw · factor + offset from the DBC file).

Intel (little-endian) and Motorola (big-endian) byte order, signed and unsigned signals are supported. Multiplexed signals are only in the frame when the multiplexer selects them; their outputs hold the last value received. The block can be generated as C code.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description dbc_file '' DBC file (relative paths are relative to the model file) message '' Message name in the DBC file signals '' Signals to use, comma separated (empty = all, in DBC order)

Direct feedthrough: yes

docs.title: CAN Pack
docs.text:
can.pack · CAN

Encodes a CAN frame: one input per signal (physical units), output = the data bytes (uint8; 8 for classic CAN, up to 64 for CAN FD).

Values are converted to the raw integer with rounding to nearest and saturated to the bit field, exactly as the generated C code does. Signals that are not selected are sent with their initial value from the DBC file (GenSigStartValue, else raw 0). Multiplexed signals are written only when the multiplexer value selects them.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description dbc_file '' DBC file (relative paths are relative to the model file) message '' Message name in the DBC file signals '' Signals to use, comma separated (empty = all, in DBC order)

Direct feedthrough: yes

docs.title: CAN Transmit
docs.text:
can.transmit · CAN

Sends a CAN message on a simulated bus: one input per signal (physical units), packed with the DBC file (with payload bytes: one input with the 8 data bytes, e.g. from CAN Pack and E2E Protect).

mode periodic sends at every sample: sample_time 0 takes the message's cycle time from the DBC file (GenMsgCycleTime; 10 ms if it has none); on_change sends only when the packed bytes change (event-triggered); on_trigger adds an input that sends on its rising edge. The frame competes for the bus with the other senders: the lowest identifier wins the arbitration, and it arrives after its transmission time (see the CAN Bus block).

Fault injection for tests: drop (probability of losing a frame), delay (extra queueing delay), corrupt (probability of a flipped data bit, which an E2E check detects) and bus_off (from fault_time this node sends nothing).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description dbc_file '' DBC file (relative paths are relative to the model file) message '' Message name in the DBC file signals '' Signals to use, comma separated (empty = all, in DBC order) bus 'can0' Name of the simulated CAN bus payload 'signals' Signals (packed with the DBC) or the raw 8 data bytes — one of signals, bytes mode 'periodic' When to send — one of periodic, on_change, on_trigger node '' Sending ECU (for the trace) drop 0.0 Probability of losing a frame (fault injection) delay 0.0 s Extra delay before the frame is queued (fault injection) corrupt 0.0 Probability of a flipped data bit (fault injection) bus_off 0.0 1: the node goes bus-off at fault_time (fault injection) fault_time 0.0 s When the faults start sample_time 0.0 s Send period; 0 = the message's cycle time in the DBC

Direct feedthrough: yes · no outputs

docs.title: CAN Receive
docs.text:
can.receive · CAN

Receives a CAN message from a simulated bus: one output per signal (physical units, the last frame received; with payload bytes one output with the 8 data bytes, e.g. for an E2E Check), then new (1 for the sample in which a new frame arrived) and age (seconds since the last frame; use it for a timeout monitor, e.g. with a Diagnostic Monitor for U-codes). Until the first frame the signals are 0 and the age counts from the start.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description dbc_file '' DBC file (relative paths are relative to the model file) message '' Message name in the DBC file signals '' Signals to use, comma separated (empty = all, in DBC order) bus 'can0' Name of the simulated CAN bus payload 'signals' Signals (packed with the DBC) or the raw 8 data bytes — one of signals, bytes sample_time 0.01 s Task period of the block

Direct feedthrough: no · no inputs

docs.title: CAN Bus
docs.text:
can.bus · CAN

Settings of a simulated CAN bus, and its load: bitrate (125, 250, 500 kbit/s or 1 Mbit/s), and the output is the bus load (0..1) over the last sample_time. A CAN bus should stay below about 50-70 % load, so the lowest-priority messages still get through in time.

With interface set (socketcan, pcan, kvaser, vector, ...; needs python-can and the driver), the bus is connected to real hardware: every frame the model transmits is also sent on the interface, and frames from the interface reach the CAN Receive blocks. Run the simulation in real time (Simulation ▸ Real-time pacing) for HIL-style tests against a real ECU.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description bus 'can0' Name of the simulated CAN bus bitrate 500000.0 bit/s Bit rate data_bitrate 2000000.0 bit/s CAN FD data-phase bit rate interface 'none' Real CAN interface (python-can); none = simulated only — one of none, socketcan, pcan, kvaser, vector, slcan, udp_multicast, virtual channel '' Interface channel, e.g. can0, PCAN_USBBUS1, 0 sample_time 0.1 s Window for the bus load

Direct feedthrough: no · no inputs

docs.title: E2E Protect
docs.text:
can.e2e_protect · CAN

Protects a frame AUTOSAR E2E style (like profile 1): writes an alive counter (0..14, one step per sample) into the low 4 bits of counter_byte and a CRC-8 (SAE J1850) over the data_id and the other bytes into crc_byte. Put it between CAN Pack and CAN Transmit (leave those two bytes free in the DBC). The receiver checks it with E2E Check, which detects corrupted, repeated, lost and out-of-order frames. Can be generated as C code.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description data_id 256 E2E data ID (16 bit, agreed between sender and receiver) crc_byte 0 Byte that holds the CRC counter_byte 1 Byte whose low 4 bits hold the alive counter sample_time -1 (inherited) s -1 = inherited

Direct feedthrough: yes

docs.title: E2E Check
docs.text:
can.e2e_check · CAN

Checks a frame protected by E2E Protect. Inputs: the 8 data bytes and new (from CAN Receive). Outputs: the status and valid (1 = use the data).

===== =============== ========================================================================== 0 ok new frame, CRC right, counter one step on (up to max_delta: some lost) 1 no_new_data no frame since the last sample 2 wrong_crc the bytes are corrupted (or the sender uses another data ID) 3 repeated the same counter again: a stuck sender 4 wrong_sequence the counter jumped more than max_delta: too many frames lost ===== =============== ==========================================================================

A receiver typically substitutes a safe value when valid is 0 for longer than a timeout, and sets a DTC. Can be generated as C code.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description data_id 256 E2E data ID (16 bit, agreed between sender and receiver) crc_byte 0 Byte that holds the CRC counter_byte 1 Byte whose low 4 bits hold the alive counter max_delta 2 Largest counter step accepted (1 = no frame may be lost) sample_time -1 (inherited) s -1 = inherited

Direct feedthrough: yes

docs.title: CAN Rest Bus
docs.text:
can.rest_bus · CAN

Rest-bus simulation: sends every message of the ECUs (nodes) that are not modelled, at their cycle times from the DBC file, so the ECU under test sees a complete bus. Signal values default to 0 (or to the DBC's initial value); set others with values, e.g. CoolantTemp=90, VehicleSpeed=50. nodes empty = every sender in the DBC file.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description dbc_file '' DBC file nodes '' Sending ECUs to simulate, comma separated (empty = all) values '' Signal values, e.g. CoolantTemp=90, VehicleSpeed=50 bus 'can0' Name of the simulated CAN bus sample_time 0.001 s Scheduler tick (a divisor of the cycle times)

Direct feedthrough: yes · no inputs, no outputs

docs.title: CAN Gateway
docs.text:
can.gateway · CAN

Forwards frames from one bus to another, like the central gateway between the powertrain and the body CAN. ids: the identifiers to route (e.g. 0x100, 0x200; empty = all). A frame is forwarded at the gateway's next task (sample_time), so routing adds up to one period of latency plus the transmission time on the second bus.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description from_bus 'can0' Bus to read from to_bus 'can1' Bus to send on ids '' Identifiers to route, comma separated (empty = all) sample_time 0.001 s Gateway task period

Direct feedthrough: yes · no inputs, no outputs

docs.title: XCP Slave
docs.text:
can.xcp_slave · CAN

Makes the simulated ECU reachable for a calibration tool over XCP on CAN (INCA, CANape, or nervus.xcp.XcpMaster): the inputs are measurements that the tool can read, the outputs are calibration values that the tool can change while the simulation runs (like the ECU's calibration RAM). Use the outputs where the model needs the tunable value, e.g. as the gain of a controller.

calibrations lists workspace variables (scalars); each output starts at the variable's value. measurements names the inputs. The memory map (8-byte IEEE doubles, Intel byte order): calibration k at 0x10000 + 8·k, measurement k at 0x20000 + 8·k; write_a2l writes the matching A2L file.

Requests arrive on request_id, answers go out on response_id (both on bus). With an interface on the CAN Bus block and real-time pacing, a real tool on a real CAN adapter can connect.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description bus 'can0' Name of the simulated CAN bus request_id 2032 CAN identifier of the requests (master → slave) response_id 2033 CAN identifier of the answers (slave → master) measurements '' Names of the measured inputs, comma separated calibrations '' Workspace variables to calibrate (one output each) sample_time 0.001 s Task period: requests are answered at this rate

Direct feedthrough: no

docs.title: Integrator
docs.text:
continuous.integrator · Continuous

Integrates its input:

\[ y(t) = y_0 + \int_0^t u(\tau)\,d\tau \]

where y₀ is initial.

The output is limited to [lower, upper]. At a limit the integration stops (no wind-up). A vector initial gives a vector integrator; a scalar initial expands to the input width.

external_reset adds a second input, reset. When it fires, the state jumps back to initial and the solver restarts from there: rising (reset goes from ≤ 0 to > 0), falling, either, or level (held at initial while reset ≠ 0). Variable-step solvers stop exactly at the edge (zero crossing). Typical use: restart an integral when a mode starts, e.g. the fuel consumed since the engine started.

initial_source external adds an input x0 (the last port): the initial value comes from that signal at the start and at every reset, e.g. a temperature that starts at the measured ambient temperature. saturation_port adds a second output: +1 at the upper limit, −1 at the lower limit, 0 in between (e.g. to tell a controller that its integral is saturated).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description initial 0.0 Initial condition upper inf Upper saturation limit lower -inf Lower saturation limit external_reset 'none' Add a reset input that sets the state back to the initial value — one of none, rising, falling, either, level initial_source 'internal' Where the initial value comes from: the parameter, or an extra input x0 — one of internal, external saturation_port False Add an output: +1 at the upper limit, -1 at the lower

Direct feedthrough: only some inputs (see above)

docs.title: Derivative
docs.text:
continuous.derivative · Continuous

Approximate time derivative of the input.

An exact derivative cannot be simulated robustly, so this block uses the filtered derivative

\[ Y(s) = \frac{s}{\tau s + 1} U(s) \]

with a small time_constant τ. Smaller τ is more exact but noisier and stiffer. The filter starts at rest, so a non-zero input at t = 0 gives an initial spike.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description time_constant 0.001 s Filter time constant τ

Direct feedthrough: yes

docs.title: Transfer Fcn
docs.text:
continuous.transfer_function · Continuous

Continuous SISO transfer function

\[ G(s) = \frac{b_0 s^m + \dots + b_m}{a_0 s^n + \dots + a_n} \]

numerator and denominator are coefficient lists in descending powers of s, e.g. [1] and [0.5, 1] for 1 / (0.5 s + 1). The initial state is zero.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description numerator [1.0] Numerator coefficients (descending powers of s) denominator [1.0, 1.0] Denominator coefficients (descending powers of s)

Direct feedthrough: depends on parameters

docs.title: State-Space
docs.text:
continuous.state_space · Continuous

Continuous linear state-space system

\[ \dot x = A x + B u, \qquad y = C x + D u \]

The input width must equal the number of columns of B; the output width is the number of rows of C.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description A [[-1.0]] State matrix (n×n) B [[1.0]] Input matrix (n×m) C [[1.0]] Output matrix (p×n) D [[0.0]] Feedthrough matrix (p×m) initial 0.0 Initial state (scalar or n-vector)

Direct feedthrough: depends on parameters

docs.title: PID Controller
docs.text:
control.pid · Control

Continuous PID controller (parallel form) with a filtered derivative:

\[ u = P\,e + I \int e\,dt + D \frac{N s}{s + N} e \]

The input is the control error e. The output is limited to [lower, upper]. When the output saturates, the integral term keeps growing ("winds up") and causes overshoot. anti_windup prevents that:

  • clamping stops integrating while the output is saturated and the error would push it further out.
  • back_calculation feeds the excess Kb·(y - u_unsat) back into the integrator. It is smooth, which variable-step solvers handle well.

With variable-step solvers, zero-crossing detection locates the moments the output saturates exactly. With clamping, the integrator then slides along the limit: it integrates just enough to keep the output there (a thin boundary layer of 0.1 % of the limit, instead of switching the integrator on and off, which would chatter). With a fixed-step solver the integrator is switched off in every step that would push the output further out.

docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description P 1.0 Proportional gain I 0.0 1/s Integral gain D 0.0 s Derivative gain N 100.0 rad/s Derivative filter coefficient initial_integrator 0.0 Initial value of the integral term upper inf Output upper limit lower -inf Output lower limit anti_windup 'none' Anti-windup method used while the output is saturated — one of none, clamping, back_calculation Kb 1.0 1/s Back-calculation gain

Direct feedthrough: yes

docs.title: Discrete PID Controller
docs.text:
control.discrete_pid · Control

Discrete PID controller (parallel form), as it would run on an ECU every sample_time seconds.

The integral and the derivative filter use forward Euler:

\[ u[k] = P\,e[k] + x_i[k] + D N (e[k] - x_f[k]) $$ $$ x_i[k+1] = x_i[k] + I\,T\,e[k], \qquad x_f[k+1] = x_f[k] + N\,T\,(e[k] - x_f[k]) \]

The derivative filter is stable only when N·T < 2. See PID for the anti-windup options; clamping works well here because the controller is discrete.

docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description P 1.0 Proportional gain I 0.0 1/s Integral gain D 0.0 s Derivative gain N 100.0 rad/s Derivative filter coefficient initial_integrator 0.0 Initial value of the integral term upper inf Output upper limit lower -inf Output lower limit anti_windup 'none' Anti-windup method used while the output is saturated — one of none, clamping, back_calculation Kb 1.0 1/s Back-calculation gain sample_time 0.01 s Sample period

Direct feedthrough: yes

docs.title: Diagnostic Monitor
docs.text:
diagnostics.monitor · Diagnostics

A diagnostic monitor with a trouble code (DTC), like the diagnostic event manager of an engine ECU.

Input fault is the raw test result of a monitor (≥ 0.5 = the test failed this sample), e.g. rpm_variation > limit for a misfire monitor. It is debounced with a counter, so a short glitch does not set a code:

\[ c_k = \begin{cases} \min(c_{k-1} + \mathrm{fail\_step},\ T) & \text{fault} \\ \max(c_{k-1} - \mathrm{pass\_step},\ -T) & \text{no fault} \end{cases} \]

The test has failed when the counter reaches T (threshold) and passed when it reaches −T. Like OBD-II, the code is then handled over operation cycles (drive cycles):

  • the first failure makes the code pending at once;
  • after confirm_cycles operation cycles in a row with a failure (2: "two-trip" detection) it is confirmed, and the MIL (check-engine lamp) comes on if mil is set;
  • after heal_cycles cycles in a row that passed without failure, the MIL goes off again (the code stays stored as confirmed, so a workshop can still read it); a cycle without failure also clears pending.

Optional inputs (parameters): enable (the test conditions are met, e.g. engine warm; the counter holds while it is 0), cycle (a rising edge starts a new operation cycle, e.g. key on), and clear (a rising edge clears the code like OBD mode 04: also the readiness).

Outputs: mil, pending, confirmed, ready (the monitor has completed, passed or failed, since the code was last cleared: the OBD readiness of this monitor) and status: the UDS status byte (bit 0 test failed, 1 failed this cycle, 2 pending, 3 confirmed, 4 not completed since clear, 5 failed since clear, 6 not completed this cycle, 7 warning indicator). Outputs change one sample after the input that causes them. Runs at its sample time.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description dtc 'P0300' Trouble code, e.g. P0171 (system too lean) threshold 10.0 Debounce threshold T: failed at +T, passed at -T fail_step 1.0 Counter step up for each failed sample pass_step 1.0 Counter step down for each passed sample jump_down True A failure after passing restarts counting from 0 confirm_cycles 2 Operation cycles in a row with a failure to confirm heal_cycles 3 Passed cycles in a row before the MIL goes off mil True A confirmed code switches the MIL on enable_input False Add an input: the test conditions are met cycle_input False Add an input: a rising edge starts a new operation cycle clear_input False Add an input: a rising edge clears the code (mode 04) sample_time 0.01 s Sample period

Direct feedthrough: no

docs.title: OBD Responder
docs.text:
diagnostics.obd_responder · Diagnostics

Makes the model answer OBD-II requests like a car's engine ECU, while the simulation runs.

Its inputs are the values of the PIDs in pids (e.g. rpm, speed, coolant_temp; see python -m nervus.obd pids), then the status bytes of the trouble codes in dtcs (wire the status output of a Diagnostic Monitor to each). Every sample they are published to the simulated ECU named ecu, which answers requests from a diagnostic tool:

  • mode 01: the PIDs, and PID 01 with the MIL and the number of confirmed codes;
  • modes 03 / 07 / 0A: confirmed, pending and permanent codes;
  • mode 04 (clear codes): the output clear is 1 for one sample; wire it to the clear input of the Diagnostic Monitors so the model really clears them;
  • mode 09: the VIN.

Run the model with python -m nervus.obd simulate model.nervus: it runs in real time and offers the ECU as an ELM327 adapter on a serial port (a pseudo-terminal) for any OBD program, or on a CAN bus. This block is part of the test setup: it has no C code.

docs.text:

docs.title: Relay
docs.text:
discontinuities.relay · Discontinuities

Switch with hysteresis: turns on when the input rises to on_point and off when it falls to off_point. In between it keeps its previous state.

\[ s[k] = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } u[k] \geq \mathrm{on\_point} \\ 0 & \text{if } u[k] \leq \mathrm{off\_point} \\ s[k-1] & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

The output is on_value when \(s = 1\) and off_value when \(s = 0\). Use it for thermostats, fan control or any on/off decision that must not chatter. The relay is evaluated at its sample time, so it needs a discrete rate (set sample_time, or drive it from a discrete block).

\[ y[k] = u[k-1], \qquad y[0] = \mathrm{initial} \]

docs.text:
discrete.zero_order_hold · Discrete

Samples its input every sample_time seconds and holds the value until the next sample:

\[ y(t) = u(kT) \quad \mathrm{for}\ kT \leq t < (k+1)T \]

This is how a continuous signal (e.g. a sensor) enters a discrete controller.

docs.title: Discrete-Time Integrator
docs.text:
discrete.integrator · Discrete

Discrete-time integrator (accumulator).

forward_euler (no direct feedthrough):

\[ y[k] = x[k], \qquad x[k+1] = x[k] + K\,T\,u[k] \]

backward_euler:

\[ y[k] = x[k] + K\,T\,u[k], \qquad x[k+1] = y[k] \]

The state is limited to [lower, upper].

external_reset adds a second input, reset. When it fires, the state goes back to initial before the output of that step is computed: rising (reset goes from ≤ 0 to > 0), falling (> 0 to ≤ 0), either, or level (every step while reset ≠ 0). Typical use: clear an accumulated error or an on-time counter when a mode changes.

docs.text:

electrical.thermistor · Electrical

An NTC thermistor, the sensing element of coolant, intake-air, oil and battery temperature sensors. The input is its temperature in °C; the resistance falls with temperature (β model):

\[ R(T) = R_{25}\, e^{\beta \left( 1/T - 1/(298.15\,\mathrm{K}) \right)} \]

Typical automotive sensors have \(R_{25}\) = 2 to 3 kΩ and β = 3400 to 4000 K, so the resistance goes from about 50 kΩ at −30 °C to 150 Ω at 120 °C.

docs.text:

A battery: open-circuit voltage from its state of charge, and an internal resistance:

\[ v_p - v_n = \mathrm{OCV}(SOC) - R_i\, i_{out}, \qquad \frac{dSOC}{dt} = -\frac{i_{out}}{3600\, Q} \]

Q is the capacity in Ah, i_out the current delivered from p. The OCV is a table over SOC (0..1); the default is a 12 V lead-acid battery. Output: the state of charge (0..1).

An H-bridge driving a motor with PWM, as an average model: the output voltage is the duty cycle times the supply voltage, and the supply delivers the same power (no losses):

\[ v_a - v_b = d\,(v_+ - v_-), \qquad i_{supply} = d\, i_{out}, \qquad -1 \le d \le 1 \]

docs.text:

A permanent-magnet DC motor: electrical port p/n, mechanical port shaft:

k is both the torque constant (N·m/A) and the back-EMF constant (V·s/rad). The torque acts on the shaft against the reference (the motor housing); add an Inertia for the rotor and a Rotational Damper for its friction. The armature current is a state.

Boolean logic. Inputs are true when non-zero. The output is 1 (true) or 0 (false).

operator output is true when AND all inputs are true OR any input is true NOT the (single) input is false XOR an odd number of inputs is true NAND not all inputs are true NOR no input is true

docs.title: 1-D Lookup Table
docs.text:
lookup.table_1d · Lookup Tables

1-D lookup table (a calibration curve): maps the input through a table of points.

For an input between breakpoints \(x_i\) and \(x_{i+1}\) with linear interpolation:

\[ y = t_i + \frac{u - x_i}{x_{i+1} - x_i}\,(t_{i+1} - t_i) \]
  • interpolation: linear; nearest (closest point); flat (value of the breakpoint at or below the input, a staircase).
  • extrapolation: clip holds the end values; linear extends the first/last segment.

Each element of a vector input is looked up separately.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description breakpoints [0.0, 1.0, 2.0] Input values (strictly increasing) table [0.0, 1.0, 4.0] Output value at each breakpoint interpolation 'linear' Between breakpoints — one of linear, nearest, flat extrapolation 'clip' Outside the breakpoints — one of clip, linear output_type 'double' Output data type: inherit, double, single, boolean, int8…uint32, fixdt(signed, bits, fraction)

Direct feedthrough: yes

docs.title: 2-D Lookup Table
docs.text:
lookup.table_2d · Lookup Tables

2-D lookup table (a calibration map), e.g. ignition advance over engine speed and load.

Input 0 selects the row (row_breakpoints) and input 1 the column (column_breakpoints). table has one row per row breakpoint and one column per column breakpoint. With linear interpolation the result is bilinear between the four surrounding points:

\[ y = (1-f_r)(1-f_c)\,T_{i,j} + (1-f_r) f_c\,T_{i,j+1} + f_r (1-f_c)\,T_{i+1,j} + f_r f_c\,T_{i+1,j+1} \]

where \(f_r\) and \(f_c\) are the fractions within the row and column intervals. Interpolation and extrapolation work as in the 1-D table.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description row_breakpoints [0.0, 1.0] Breakpoints for input 0 (rows) column_breakpoints [0.0, 1.0] Breakpoints for input 1 (columns) table [[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]] Table: rows × columns interpolation 'linear' Between breakpoints — one of linear, nearest extrapolation 'clip' Outside the breakpoints — one of clip, linear output_type 'double' Output data type: inherit, double, single, boolean, int8…uint32, fixdt(signed, bits, fraction)

Direct feedthrough: yes

docs.title: Prelookup
docs.text:
lookup.prelookup · Lookup Tables

Breakpoint search on its own: finds the interval index k and the fraction f of the input.

For an input between breakpoints \(x_k\) and \(x_{k+1}\):

\[ f = \frac{u - x_k}{x_{k+1} - x_k} \]

Output 0 is k (0-based), output 1 is f. Feed both into one or more Interpolation blocks. ECUs calibrate many maps over the same axes (engine speed, load); searching the axis once and sharing the result saves time on the processor, and the A2L file can declare the axis as a shared axis.

With clip extrapolation, f stays in [0, 1]; with linear it continues outside.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description breakpoints [0.0, 1.0, 2.0] Axis points (strictly increasing) extrapolation 'clip' Outside the breakpoints — one of clip, linear

Direct feedthrough: yes

docs.title: Interpolation using Prelookup
docs.text:
lookup.interpolation · Lookup Tables

Interpolates an n-D table (1 to 4 dimensions) at the index and fraction from Prelookup blocks.

Inputs: k1, f1 (1-D), k1, f1, k2, f2 (2-D, rows then columns), and so on: one Prelookup per dimension. In 2-D the result is the same as a 2-D Lookup Table with linear interpolation over the same breakpoints:

\[ y = (1-f_1)(1-f_2)\,T_{k_1,k_2} + (1-f_1) f_2\,T_{k_1,k_2+1} + f_1 (1-f_2)\,T_{k_1+1,k_2} + f_1 f_2\,T_{k_1+1,k_2+1} \]

With more dimensions the same rule weights all \(2^n\) corners of the cell around the input. ECUs use 3-D maps for example for a base value over speed × load, with a third axis such as coolant temperature or the camshaft position. A 3-D table is a nested list: table[i][j][k].

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description dimensions 1 Number of table dimensions (1 to 4) table [0.0, 1.0, 4.0] Table values (1-D: one per breakpoint; 2-D: rows × columns) output_type 'double' Output data type: inherit, double, single, boolean, int8…uint32, fixdt(signed, bits, fraction)

Direct feedthrough: yes

docs.title: Adaptive Map
docs.text:
lookup.adaptive_map · Lookup Tables

A 2-D map that learns, like an ECU's long-term fuel trim or knock adaptation per load/speed cell.

Output: the table interpolated at (x, y), like a 2-D Lookup Table with clipped axes. Every sample while learn is ≥ 0.5 the table moves towards the correction input e at the cells around (x, y), each by its interpolation weight:

\[ T_{ij} \leftarrow \mathrm{clip}(T_{ij} + r\,T_s\,w_{ij}\,e,\ -L,\ L) \]

with the learning rate r (1/s) and the limit L. So each operating region gets its own correction: a lean error that only exists at idle is learned in the idle cells and does not disturb full load. The learned table is a state (it would be kept in the ECU's non-volatile memory).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description row_breakpoints [0.0, 1.0] Breakpoints for x (rows) column_breakpoints [0.0, 1.0] Breakpoints for y (columns) initial 0.0 Initial table (rows × columns, or one value for all cells) rate 0.1 1/s Learning rate limit inf Largest sample_time 0.01 s Sample period

Direct feedthrough: only some inputs (see above)

docs.title: FMU
docs.text:
fmi.fmu · Ports & Subsystems

Runs an FMU (Functional Mock-up Unit, FMI 2.0 co-simulation) from another tool: Simulink, Dymola, OpenModelica, SimulationX, AMESim, CANoe, or Nervus itself (Code ▸ Export FMU). The block's ports are the FMU's real-valued inputs and outputs, in the order of its model description.

The FMU is a co-simulation slave: every sample_time (the communication step; 0 = the FMU's default step) the block sets the inputs, lets the FMU advance by one step, and reads the outputs, which it holds until the next step. The outputs therefore lag the inputs by one communication step, as in every co-simulation. parameters sets the FMU's parameters before it starts, e.g. Kp = 2.0, Ki = 30. Needs fmpy (uv sync --extra fmi).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description fmu_file '' FMU file (relative paths are relative to the model file) parameters '' Parameter values for the FMU, e.g. Kp = 2.0, Ki = 30 sample_time 0.0 s Communication step; 0 = the FMU's default step

Direct feedthrough: no

docs.title: Subsystem
docs.text:
ports.subsystem · Ports & Subsystems

A block that contains its own diagram. Double-click it in the editor to open it.

A subsystem can be masked: it then has its own parameters (e.g. displacement) that the blocks inside use in their expressions, so several copies of the same component can have different values.

A subsystem can have variants: alternative implementations with the same inputs and outputs, e.g. a petrol and a diesel engine model. Each variant can have a condition such as ENGINE == 2 on workspace variables; the one whose condition is true is simulated and turned into C code.

With a sample_time the subsystem is an atomic task, like one task of an ECU's operating system: every block inside that inherits its sample time runs at that period. Its inputs are sampled at the start of each period and its outputs held until the next one. Blocks with continuous states are not allowed inside.

With enable_port the subsystem gets an extra last input, enable. While it is ≤ 0 nothing inside runs: outputs and discrete states are held and continuous states stop. With when_enabled = reset the discrete states return to their initial values each time the subsystem is enabled again.

With trigger the subsystem gets a last input, trigger, and runs only when that signal has an edge (rising: from ≤ 0 to > 0, falling: from > 0 to ≤ 0, or either). Between triggers its outputs and states are held. The trigger is checked each time the blocks inside would execute, so drive it with a discrete signal of the same rate. Blocks with continuous states are not allowed inside.

With trigger = function_call the subsystem runs once every time the trigger value changes. A State Chart (or any logic) calls it by incrementing a counter output, e.g. calls = calls + 1 in a state's entry action: the subsystem then runs in the same time step, after the chart.

Its inputs and outputs are the In and Out blocks inside, in the order of their port numbers. Subsystems structure a model the way functions structure code: one subsystem per ECU function (e.g. "idle control", "fuel", "ignition"). Parameters inside can use the model workspace.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description sample_time -1 (inherited) s Task period for the blocks inside that inherit theirs (-1 = no own rate) enable_port False Add an enable input: the subsystem only runs while it is > 0 when_enabled 'held' Discrete states when the subsystem is enabled again — one of held, reset trigger 'none' Add a trigger input: the subsystem only runs when it has this kind of edge — one of none, rising, falling, either, function_call function_name '' C code: generate this subsystem as a reusable function with this name (empty = inline)

Direct feedthrough: yes

docs.title: Diode
docs.text:
semiconductors.diode · Semiconductors

A diode with the Shockley equation, like SPICE's diode model:

\[ i = I_s\left(e^{v/(N V_T)} - 1\right) - I_{BV}\, e^{-(v + BV)/(N V_T)} \]

The second term is the reverse breakdown (a Zener diode): set BV to the Zener voltage. Ports p (anode) and n (cathode). Typical values:

Device Is [A] N BV [V] 1N4148 small-signal 2.5e-9 1.75 100 1N4007 rectifier 7e-9 1.8 1000 red LED (≈ 1.9 V at 20 mA) 1e-18 1.9 5 Zener 5.1 V 1e-14 1 5.1

docs.title: Bipolar Transistor
docs.text:
semiconductors.bjt · Semiconductors

A bipolar transistor (Ebers-Moll transport model), NPN or PNP. Ports c (collector), b (base), e (emitter):

\[ I_C = I_s\left(e^{V_{BE}/V_T} - e^{V_{BC}/V_T}\right) - \frac{I_s}{\beta_R}\left(e^{V_{BC}/V_T} - 1\right), \qquad I_B = \frac{I_s}{\beta_F}\left(e^{V_{BE}/V_T} - 1\right) + \frac{I_s}{\beta_R}\left(e^{V_{BC}/V_T} - 1\right) \]

In the active region the collector current is β_F times the base current; as a switch (a relay driver) the transistor saturates with a small collector-emitter voltage. A small NPN like the 2N2222: Is = 1e-14, β_F = 200.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description type 'NPN' Polarity — one of NPN, PNP Is 1e-14 A Saturation current BF 100.0 Forward current gain β_F BR 1.0 Reverse current gain β_R

Direct feedthrough: yes · no inputs, no outputs

docs.title: MOSFET
docs.text:
semiconductors.mosfet · Semiconductors

A MOSFET (SPICE level 1, square law), N- or P-channel. Ports d (drain), g (gate), s (source); no current flows into the gate:

\[ I_D = \begin{cases} 0 & V_{GS} \le V_{th} \\ K\left((V_{GS} - V_{th})V_{DS} - V_{DS}^2/2\right)(1 + \lambda V_{DS}) & V_{DS} < V_{GS} - V_{th} \\ \frac{K}{2}(V_{GS} - V_{th})^2 (1 + \lambda V_{DS}) & \text{saturation} \end{cases} \]

K = μC_ox·W/L. A logic-level switch like a 2N7000: Vth = 2 V, K = 0.1 A/V²; a power MOSFET driving a motor: Vth = 3 V, K = 20 A/V². The device is symmetric: with V_DS < 0 drain and source swap roles.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:

Direct feedthrough: yes · no inputs, no outputs

docs.title: Op-Amp
docs.text:
semiconductors.opamp · Semiconductors

An operational amplifier: high gain, and the output limited to its supply rails:

\[ v_{out} = v_{mid} + v_{half} \tanh\left(\frac{A\,(v_+ - v_-)}{v_{half}}\right) \]

with \(v_{mid} = (V_{pos} + V_{neg})/2\) and \(v_{half} = (V_{pos} - V_{neg})/2\).

No current flows into the inputs plus and minus; the output out is referenced to ground and can deliver any current. With negative feedback it is an amplifier or an active filter; without, a comparator.

docs.text:

docs.title: Sensor Model
docs.text:
sensors.sensor · Sensors & Actuators

A real sensor between the physical value and the ECU's input, sampled every sample_time:

\[ y = \mathrm{quantize}(\mathrm{clip}(g\,u(t - d) + o + \sigma\,n,\ y_{min},\ y_{max})) \]

with gain error g (1 = exact), offset o, white noise of standard deviation σ (reproducible: the same every run for the same seed), a delay d of whole samples (filtering, a slow bus), limits of the measuring range and the resolution of the A/D converter (0 = none).

fault injects a failure from fault_time: stuck (the last good value), open_circuit (the lower rail, y_min), short_to_supply (the upper rail, y_max), drift (an offset growing by drift_rate per second). Use it to test the ECU's plausibility checks and diagnostic monitors.

docs.title: Rate Transition
docs.text:
discrete.rate_transition · Signal Attributes

Passes a signal between two rates (two ECU tasks) in a way that is deterministic on an RTOS.

Set sample_time to the slower of the two rates. For slow_to_fast, also set output_sample_time to the fast rate, so that the blocks after it inherit the fast rate.

  • fast_to_slow: the slow task gets the fast signal sampled at its own start: \(y = u\) at every slow sample (like a Zero-Order Hold).
  • slow_to_fast: the fast task gets the slow signal one slow period late: \(y[k] = u[k-1]\) at the slow rate (like a Unit Delay), held in between.

Why the delay? On an ECU the fast task interrupts the slow one. If the fast task read the slow task's output directly, it would sometimes see the old and sometimes the new value, depending on timing. With the delay it always sees the value the slow task finished one period ago, in the simulation and on the target. C code generated with one function per task (generate_c(..., tasks=True)) requires a Rate Transition on every signal that crosses between rates.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description direction 'fast_to_slow' From a faster to a slower rate, or from slower to faster — one of fast_to_slow, slow_to_fast initial 0.0 Output before the first slow sample has arrived (slow_to_fast) sample_time 0.1 s Sample period (-1 = inherit from input) output_sample_time -1 (inherited) s slow_to_fast: the fast rate that the blocks after it inherit (-1 = the sample time)

Direct feedthrough: depends on parameters

docs.title: Data Type Conversion
docs.text:
routing.datatype_conversion · Signal Attributes

Converts the input to another data type, e.g. a sensor value to int16 or a controller output to fixed point.

The real-world value is kept as well as the type allows:

\[ Q = \mathrm{round}\left(\frac{u - \mathrm{bias}}{\mathrm{slope}}\right), \qquad y = \mathrm{slope} \cdot Q + \mathrm{bias} \]

rounding: nearest (half away from zero), floor, ceil or zero (truncate). overflow: saturate limits to the type's range; wrap wraps around like C integer arithmetic. For example int8 turns 3.6 into 4, and 200 into 127 (saturate) or -56 (wrap).

docs.text:
routing.switch · Signal Routing

Passes input 0 when the control input (input 1) satisfies criterion, otherwise input 2:

\[ y = \begin{cases} u_0 & \text{if } u_1 \geq \mathrm{threshold} \\ u_2 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

Criteria: u1 >= threshold, u1 > threshold or u1 != 0. The control input must be scalar.

docs.title: Signal Builder
docs.text:
sources.signal_builder · Sources

Test signals drawn as lines: one output per signal, several groups (scenarios) to choose from.

Double-click the block to draw the signals in the signal editor: drag a point, double-click to add one, select it and press Delete to remove it. The group chooses the scenario the simulation uses, e.g. a tip-in or a panic stop.

The signals are stored as text in definition, one line per signal: pedal: 0 0, 1 0, 1 80, 10 80 (pairs of time and value). Two points at the same time make a jump; after the last point the value is held. Variable-step solvers stop exactly at every point, so jumps are sharp.

docs.title: Drive Cycle
docs.text:
sources.drive_cycle · Sources

A standard drive cycle as a speed profile (the target for a driver model):

  • wltc3b: WLTC class 3b (WLTP, the European type approval since 2017), 1800 s, 23.3 km, up to 131 km/h;
  • ftp75: FTP-75, the US city cycle, 1874 s, 17.8 km;
  • ece15: ECE-15, the urban part of the old NEDC, 195 s, 1 km;
  • csv_file: your own: two columns, time [s] and speed [km/h].

Output 0 is the speed (km/h or m/s, unit), output 1 the acceleration [m/s²] (the slope of the profile, useful as a feed-forward for a driver model). After the end of the cycle the speed stays 0. The WLTC and FTP-75 tables are the official second-by-second values.

docs.title: State Chart
docs.text:
charts.state_chart · State Machines

A state machine (chart) for operating modes, sequences and fault handling, like Simulink's Stateflow.

The chart is written in a short text language in definition:

input rpm, key
output mode = 0, fuel = 0

state off
  entry: mode = 0; fuel = 0
state cranking
  entry: mode = 1
  during: fuel = 1
state running
  entry: mode = 2

transition off -> cranking: key > 0.5
transition cranking -> running: rpm > 600
transition cranking -> off: after(300) / fuel = 0
transition running -> off: key < 0.5 or rpm < 300

Inputs and outputs become the block's ports, in the order they are declared; with state_output an extra last output gives the active state's number (0, 1, ... in the order the states are written). Every sample period the transitions leaving the active state are checked in the order written; the first true guard fires (exit → transition action → entry). Otherwise the state's during actions run. after(n) is true after n periods in the state, and t_in_state is the time in the state in seconds. The initial state is entered in the first sample (its entry actions see the inputs of that sample), and its clock starts there.

The chart runs at a discrete rate, and can be generated as C code.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description definition (code) The chart: inputs, outputs, states and transitions state_output True Add an output with the number of the active state sample_time -1 (inherited) s Sample period (-1 = inherit)

Direct feedthrough: yes

docs.title: Python Function
docs.text:
user.python_function · User-Defined

Runs your own Python function, the equivalent of Simulink's MATLAB Function block.

code must define a function f(t, u0, u1, ...) with one argument per input. It returns one value per output (a tuple if there are several). Values may be scalars or arrays. np (NumPy) and math are available.

parameters is a vector of values the code reads as p[0], p[1], ... Like any numeric parameter it can be an expression of workspace or mask variables, e.g. [eta_vol, displacement], so the same code can be reused with different values (and calibrated).

The function must be stateless: its output may only depend on t and the inputs. Use Unit Delay or Integrator blocks for memory.

Warning

The code runs with full Python privileges. Only open model files from sources you trust.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Default Unit Description code (code) Python source defining f(t, u0, ...) num_inputs 1 Number of inputs num_outputs 1 Number of outputs output_width -1 Width of each output (-1 = same as input 0, or 1) parameters [] Values available in the code as p[0], p[1], ...

Direct feedthrough: yes

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
nervus/
  core/      Block, ports, Param, SampleTime, Diagram, SimulationSettings, errors   (pure Python)
  blocks/    the block library and the registry (type_id -> class)
  sim/       compiler (diagram -> CompiledModel), simulator loop, SimResult
  solvers/   fixed-step (Euler, RK4) and variable-step (SciPy solve_ivp) integration
  io/        model file load/save, schema migration
  codegen/   C code generation (generator, per-block templates) and software-in-the-loop testing
  help.py    block help / reference generation
  gui/       PySide6 desktop editor, Model-View-Controller
    models/       DiagramModel, SimulationModel: Qt wrappers that emit change signals
    views/        canvas, library, properties, diagnostics, scope, help (render and forward input)
    controllers/  EditorController (undoable commands), FileController, SimulationController (worker thread)

Rule: nothing outside nervus.gui imports Qt. The engine must run headless in scripts, tests and CI.

docs.title: Data flow
docs.text:
Diagram ──compile_diagram()──▶ CompiledModel ──simulate()──▶ SimResult
 (editable)                    (sorted, sized, states        (time + logged signals)
                                allocated; executable)

docs.title: Compilation (nervus.sim.compiler)
docs.text:
1. Diagram.check(): every input connected, no dangling ports.
  2. Width propagation: repeatedly ask each block output_widths(input_widths) until nothing changes. Blocks with state (Integrator, Unit Delay) give a provisional width so feedback loops resolve.
  3. configure(in_widths, out_widths) on each block, which validates sizes.
  4. Sorting: a topological sort over direct-feedthrough edges. A cycle is an algebraic loop.
  5. Sample times: inherited (-1) times are resolved from the drivers.
  6. States: the continuous states of all blocks are packed into one vector for the solver. Discrete states are kept per block.

The CompiledModel is also where C code generation will start: it holds a sorted list of blocks with known sizes, rates and states.

docs.title: Simulation (nervus.sim.simulator)
docs.text:
The simulator owns all state. Blocks are pure: outputs, derivatives and update get the state passed in and return new values. This lets variable-step solvers evaluate trial points and throw them away, and it maps directly onto generated C (model_step() with a state struct).

Discrete rates are scheduled with integer counters (offset + k·period), so sample hits never drift.

docs.title: GUI (Model-View-Controller)
docs.text:
user ──▶ View ──intent──▶ Controller ──command──▶ Model ──signal──▶ View
        (canvas,          (EditorController,      (DiagramModel   (scene adds/moves
         panels)           QUndoStack)             wraps Diagram)  items, panels refresh)
  • Models (gui/models): DiagramModel wraps the core Diagram. Its methods are primitive edits (add_block, set_params, add_connection, ...), and each emits a Qt signal (blockAdded, paramsChanged, connectionAdded, ...). SimulationModel holds the run state and the latest SimResult.
  • Views (gui/views): DiagramScene/DiagramView (canvas), LibraryBrowser, PropertyPanel, DiagnosticsPanel, ScopeWindow, HelpBrowser. Views never change a model directly. A finished drag becomes controller.move_blocks(...), a drawn wire becomes controller.connect_ports(...), and so on.
  • Controllers (gui/controllers): EditorController turns every edit into a QUndoCommand (see commands.py), so everything is undoable. FileController handles new/open/save and recent files. SimulationController compiles on the GUI thread and simulates on a worker QThread; editing is locked while a run is active.

Commands catch their own exceptions and mark themselves obsolete, because an exception raised in a Python redo() does not propagate out of QUndoStack.push().

docs.title: Help, equations and figures
docs.text:
Block help comes from the block docstrings (nervus.help). The same Markdown feeds:

  • the MkDocs block reference (scripts/gen_block_reference.py), where $$...$$ is rendered by MathJax, and
  • the in-app HelpBrowser, where $$...$$ is typeset to images with matplotlib's math engine (gui/views/math_render.py), since Qt's Markdown renderer has no math support.

Figures referenced as figures/<name>.png are generated by scripts/gen_figures.py. They go into gui/resources/figures (bundled with the app) and docs/images/blocks (docs). Screenshots in the docs are generated by scripts/screenshots.py.

docs.title: Code generation
docs.text:
nervus.codegen.generate_c(target) compiles the target (a model or a subsystem's system) with the normal compiler, so the generated code uses exactly the simulation's execution order, widths and sample times. CGenerator then asks each block's template (codegen/templates.py, registered with @template) for its output and update statements. An Emitter gives templates access to input and output signals, parameters (registered in <name>_P) and states (in <name>_DW).

The C step function mirrors one major step of the simulator: outputs in execution order (discrete blocks only at their rate's hits), then state updates, then the rate counters. codegen.sil.run_python() steps the compiled Python model the same way, and back_to_back() compares the two. The test suite runs this for every block with a template.

docs.title: Writing a block
docs.text:
A block is a subclass of nervus.core.Block. Here is a first-order low-pass filter \(\tau \dot x = u - x,\ y = x\):

from collections.abc import Sequence

import numpy as np

from nervus.blocks import register
from nervus.core import CONTINUOUS, Block, Param, ParameterError, ParamKind
from nervus.core.types import Array


@register
class LowPass(Block):
    """First-order low-pass filter with time constant *tau*: ``tau·y' = u - y``."""

    type_id = "mylib.low_pass"  # stable id used in model files
    label = "Low-Pass Filter"
    category = "My Blocks"
    DEFAULT_SAMPLE_TIME = CONTINUOUS
    DIRECT_FEEDTHROUGH = False  # y depends only on the state
    PARAMS = (
        Param("tau", 0.1, ParamKind.FLOAT, "Time constant", "s", min=0.0),
        Param("initial", 0.0, ParamKind.FLOAT, "Initial output"),
    )

    def validate_params(self) -> None:
        if self.params["tau"] <= 0:
            raise ParameterError("tau must be > 0")

    def initial_continuous_state(self) -> Array:
        return np.full(self.out_widths[0], self.params["initial"])

    def outputs(self, t: float, u: Sequence[Array], xc: Array, xd: Array) -> list[Array]:
        return [xc.copy()]

    def derivatives(self, t: float, u: Sequence[Array], xc: Array, xd: Array) -> Array:
        return (u[0] - xc) / self.params["tau"]

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Pure functions. Never store simulation state on self. Use xc (continuous) or xd (discrete).
  • Direct feedthrough: set DIRECT_FEEDTHROUGH = False only if outputs does not read u. Getting this wrong breaks the execution order. If only some inputs feed through (an Integrator's x0 input, but not u), override feedthrough_ports() to return those port indices.
  • State jumps: major_step() may return a new continuous state at a major step (an integrator reset); the solver restarts from it. self.t_start is the simulation start time.
  • Never constant: set CAN_BE_CONSTANT = False if the output changes over time even with constant inputs (like Initial Condition); otherwise the block is computed once.
  • Widths: override output_widths if the output width is not "broadcast of the inputs". Override configure to validate widths, and raise ValueError with a clear message.
  • Discrete blocks need a sample_time parameter (ParamKind.SAMPLE_TIME) and implement update.
  • Discontinuities: return their times from breakpoints() (like Step) so variable-step solvers hit them.
  • Ports: set NUM_INPUTS/NUM_OUTPUTS, or override num_inputs()/num_outputs() if they depend on parameters.
  • Docs: the class docstring is the help text, in the app and in the docs. Write the equation in LaTeX between $$ ... $$ (use \\ for backslashes in a normal docstring). If a picture helps, add a figure function to scripts/gen_figures.py and reference it as ![description](figures/<name>.png). Then run scripts/gen_figures.py and scripts/gen_block_reference.py.
  • Tests: check against an analytical solution.

docs.title: Stateflow sample models (needs MATLAB)
docs.text:
To import Simulink models with Stateflow charts, the tests need real files saved by Simulink, with what Simulink computes for them. If you have MATLAB with Simulink and Stateflow:

  1. In MATLAB, go to the folder scripts/matlab of the Nervus repository (cd <the nervus folder>/scripts/matlab).
  2. Run make_stateflow_samples. It builds two small models (a lamp with three states; a gearbox with states inside states, parallel states, timers and a junction), simulates them, and saves both models and Simulink's results in a new folder, stateflow_samples.
  3. Open a pull request with that folder, or attach it as a zip file to an issue.

If the script stops with an error, report the error message (releases differ in small ways). The README in scripts/matlab also explains how to build the lamp model by hand.

docs.title: Logs from your scanner app

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
35 tutorials, grouped by topic. Each one uses a finished model in examples/: open it in the editor, run it, read why it behaves as it does, then change it. They are built around problems from the automotive industry and the classic experiments of engineering lab courses.

Every tutorial has the same parts:

  • At a glance: what you will learn, what to do first, the level and the time it takes.
  • Follow along: which model to open, and what to run and look at.
  • Experiments: changes to try, each with the effect you should see.
  • Next: the next tutorial on the same topic.

New to Nervus? Start with Your first model: a cruise control: it builds a model from scratch in the editor, step by step, with a screenshot for each step. Then pick a topic.

docs.title: Tips for every tutorial
docs.text:
• Running the Python version: each model is built by a script, e.g. uv run python examples/truck.py. It runs the model's tests and prints the key numbers quoted in the tutorial.
  • Getting lost: File ▸ Open the example again to start over; your changes are only saved if you save.
  • Looking inside: double-click a subsystem to open it, Ctrl+↑ to go back up. Press F1 on any block for its help page with the equations.
  • Comparing: every run is kept in the Data Inspector (Ctrl+I). Tick two runs and a signal to overlay them.
  • Scripting: the Console tab runs Python on the open model, e.g. res["speed"].max().

docs.title: Tutorial: Anti-lock braking (ABS)
docs.text:
You will learn braking slip and the tyre's friction peak, a quarter-car model, hydraulic pressure modulation, a threshold ABS as a State Chart, stopping distances on dry, wet and icy roads Before this Tyre slip and traction control Level and time intermediate, about 35 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/abs_braking.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Vehicle dynamics and energy ▸ Chassis control (all tutorials)

examples/abs_braking.py brakes a car as hard as possible from 100 km/h, with and without ABS. Without it the wheels lock: the car slides further and cannot be steered. With it, an ECU modulates the brake pressure dozens of times a second to keep the tyres at the slip where they grip best.

uv run python examples/abs_braking.py

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
A quarter car: one wheel carrying a quarter of a 1600 kg car (400 kg), with a 0.31 m tyre and a wheel inertia of 1.2 kg·m². The tyre force depends on the slip between the car and the wheel,

\[ s = \frac{v - \omega r}{v} \qquad (0: \text{rolling freely},\ 1: \text{locked}) \]

through Pacejka's magic formula, as in the traction control tutorial: on this tyre the friction peaks at 15 % slip and a locked wheel keeps only 71 % of the peak. The car decelerates by the tyre force; the wheel by the brake torque minus the tyre's torque.

The brake is a torque that the hydraulic unit changes at a limited rate (8000 N·m/s up, 16000 N·m/s down). The driver asks for 2500 N·m from 0.5 s: much more than the tyre can transmit (about 1200 N·m), so the wheel would lock.

The ABS ECU is a State Chart running every 5 ms, the classic threshold algorithm:

State Valves Leave when build inlet open: the pressure rises towards the driver's demand slip > 10 % → hold, > 20 % → release hold both closed: the pressure stays slip > 20 % → release, < 10 % → build release outlet open: the pressure falls slip < 10 % → build

Below 7 km/h the ABS stops controlling, as in real cars.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Without ABS the wheel locks 0.14 s after the driver brakes: it stops turning while the car slides on. With ABS the wheel speed dips and recovers six times a second, the slip oscillates between 3 and 23 %, and the brake torque saws up and down; that is the pulsing you feel in the pedal.

Road mu_road Stopping distance with ABS without ABS dry 1.0 45.7 m 54.9 m wet 0.5 97.0 m 110.2 m ice 0.15 276 m 367 m

The physical limit on the dry road is \(v^2 / (2 \mu g) = 39\) m: the ABS reaches 86 % of the tyre's best grip. The shorter distance is a bonus; the main purpose of ABS is that a rolling wheel can still produce side force, so the driver can steer around the obstacle.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Try What you will see abs_on = 0 the wheel locks (slip 100 %) and the car slides 9 m further on a dry road slip_hold = 0.05, slip_release = 0.10 too careful: the tyre never reaches its peak, 49.3 m slip_hold = 0.2, slip_release = 0.4 too late: the slip reaches 61 %, past the peak, 54.2 m release_rate = 4000 slower release: 43.4 m, but the slip peaks at 29 %; a trade-off between distance and steerability T_driver = 1500 a gentler driver still locks the wheel without ABS: 1200 N·m is all the tyre can take

docs.text: That was the last tutorial on vehicle dynamics and energy. Continue with electrics and electronics: RC and RLC circuits, or pick another one from the tutorial overview.

docs.title: Tutorial: A vehicle network (CAN)
docs.text:
You will learn ECUs on simulated CAN buses: DBC files, arbitration and bus load, a gateway, rest-bus simulation, E2E protection, fault injection and timeouts, the bus trace Before this Your first model: a cruise control; read CAN communication first Level and time advanced, about 40 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/can_network.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic ECU software, communication and diagnostics ▸ Vehicle networks (all tutorials)

examples/can_network.py connects ECUs over two simulated CAN buses: an engine ECU (ECM) on the powertrain CAN (500 kbit/s), an instrument cluster on the body CAN (125 kbit/s), a gateway between them, and a rest-bus simulation for the ECUs that are not modelled. Then it breaks things.

uv run python examples/can_network.py

docs.title: The network
docs.text:
• ECM (a subsystem, 10 ms): CAN Pack (EngineSpeed, CoolantTemp of EngineData, DBC file examples/data/vehicle.dbc) → E2E Protect (CRC in byte 6, alive counter in byte 7) → CAN Transmit on powertrain.
  • Rest bus: the GATEWAY node's VehicleData every 20 ms, from the DBC's cycle times.
  • Gateway: routes 0x100 and 0x200 to body every 1 ms.
  • Cluster (10 ms): CAN Receive (bytes) → E2E Check → CAN Unpack. A frame that fails the check is ignored and the needle holds its last good value. A counter measures the time since the last valid frame; after comm_timeout = 100 ms the needle drops to 0 and the U0100 monitor (lost communication with the ECM) sets its code.

The run prints the bus loads (powertrain 3.7 %, body 14.6 %: the same frames take four times as long at 125 kbit/s) and the gateway latency (about 1 ms: up to one gateway period plus the frame time). Tools ▸ CAN Bus Trace shows every frame after a run in the app.

docs.title: Faults
docs.text:
From 1 s, 20 % of the ECM's frames get a flipped data bit (corrupt_rate). The CAN CRC would catch a bit error on the wire, so this models a fault behind it, in a gateway's memory or the sender's software. Only the E2E CRC can see it:

The check reports wrong CRC for each corrupted frame; after two corrupted frames in a row the counter has jumped by 3 and it reports wrong sequence (max_delta = 2). The needle never shows a corrupted value, it just holds for 10 to 20 ms. The third test case switches the ECM bus-off: after 100 ms the needle drops to 0 and U0100 is pending.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
To try one: change the value in the Model Workspace tab (double-click it), or for a block parameter select the block and edit it in Properties; press ▶ and compare with the previous run in the Data Inspector (Ctrl+I). Ctrl+Z undoes the change.

Try What you will see corrupt_rate = 0.6 many frames in a row fail: the needle lags, and eventually the timeout fires E2E Check removed (CAN Unpack straight after CAN Receive) corrupted engine speeds reach the needle body CAN bitrate = 50 kbit/s the body bus load rises to about 37 % and the latency grows comm_timeout = 0.03 with corrupted frames the timeout fires after three samples without a valid frame: too sensitive

docs.title: Tutorial: The 12 V charging system and energy management
docs.text:
You will learn the power balance of battery, alternator and loads, alternator output versus engine speed, an electrical energy management function (idle boost and load shedding) as a State Chart Before this Starter motor and electronic throttle Level and time intermediate, about 35 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/charging_system.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Electrics and electronics ▸ Vehicle electrical system (all tutorials)

Every car's electrical system is a balance between the alternator, the battery and the loads. On a cold, dark winter evening the loads are high and the alternator, turning slowly at idle, cannot keep up; the battery makes up the difference, and a long traffic jam drains it. examples/charging_system.py models this balance and the ECU function that manages it.

uv run python examples/charging_system.py

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
Part Block Values battery Battery 60 Ah, 75 % charged, 12 mΩ internal resistance alternator Alternator 120 A at full speed (6000 rpm), nothing below 1000 rpm, 2.5:1 belt, regulator 14.2 V loads Variable Resistor 45 A always on (ECUs, ignition, fuel pump, headlights, blower) + 25 A comfort (heated rear window, seat heaters) engine controlled Speed Source idle in the traffic jam, 2000 rpm when driving battery sensor Current Sensor the battery current (positive: charging), like an intelligent battery sensor

The alternator's maximum current grows with its speed. At 800 rpm idle the alternator turns at 2000 rpm and delivers at most 24 A, while the loads draw about 70 A: the battery has to deliver almost 40 A.

docs.title: Energy management
docs.text:
The engine ECU has an energy management function, a State Chart running every 200 ms on the battery current:

State When Action normal idle at 800 rpm boost discharging by more than 10 A for 3 s idle at 1100 rpm: the alternator delivers about 42 A shed_loads still discharging after 5 s in boost also switch off the heated rear window and seat heaters (25 A) back to normal charging by more than 10 A

Its outputs go through a Unit Delay, so they act one task later, like the outputs of a real ECU (and the loop from the battery current back to the circuit is not instantaneous).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Without energy management the battery delivers 38 A for the whole traffic jam: 2.5 Ah, the state of charge falls from 0.75 to 0.71 and the voltage to 11.95 V. Repeat this on every trip in winter and the car will not start one morning.

With energy management the chart raises the idle speed after 3.0 s and sheds the comfort loads at 8.0 s; from then on the alternator covers the remaining 45 A and the battery is in balance (0.03 Ah in the whole jam). When the car drives off, the alternator can deliver 96 A, the battery charges with 30 A, the loads come back on at once, and the battery ends the trip fuller than it started (0.78).

Note that the voltage stays near 12.8 V even while charging at 2000 rpm: a partly discharged battery takes all the current the alternator has left, and the voltage only rises to the regulator's 14.2 V when the battery is nearly full.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Try What you will see energy_mgmt = 0 the traffic jam costs the battery 2.5 Ah idle_boost = 1300 the higher idle covers most of the load by itself: the comfort loads stay on, and the battery gives 0.7 Ah in the jam; the trade-off is fuel I_comfort = 40 (more comfort loads) still balanced after shedding: 0.06 Ah soc0 = 0.4 (a weak battery) the same balance, but the voltage drops to 11.7 V before the management acts
