docs.title: Tutorial: Balancing an inverted pendulum with state feedback
docs.text:
You will learn an unstable plant, state-space models, LQR state feedback, non-minimum-phase behaviour, redesigning a gain in the Console Before this DC motor speed and position control Level and time advanced, about 45 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/inverted_pendulum.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Control engineering ▸ Classic lab experiments (all tutorials)

examples/inverted_pendulum.py is the classic advanced control lab: a pendulum hinged on a cart, balanced upright by moving the cart. Upright is unstable, a single PID loop cannot hold the pendulum and the cart at the same time, so the controller feeds back all four states with a gain designed by LQR (linear quadratic regulator). The dimensions are those of a common lab rig.

uv run python examples/inverted_pendulum.py

docs.title: The plant
docs.text:
A cart of 0.94 kg carries a pendulum rod (0.23 kg, 0.64 m) on a hinge; the motor pushes the cart with up to ±10 N. The state is \(x = [\,x_{cart},\ \theta,\ \dot x_{cart},\ \dot\theta\,]\) with \(\theta = 0\) upright. The model uses the full nonlinear equations of motion (the cart_pole Python Function block; its integrator holds the four states):

\[ (M + m)\ddot x + m l (\ddot\theta\cos\theta - \dot\theta^2 \sin\theta) = F - b\dot x, \qquad (J + m l^2)\ddot\theta + m l \ddot x \cos\theta = m g l \sin\theta - B\dot\theta \]

Linearized at upright, \(\dot x = A x + B F\) has the poles 0, −3.8, −6.7 and +4.9 rad/s: the pendulum falls with a time constant of 0.2 s. Set K_lqr to [0, 0, 0, 0] and run: it falls past 0.5 rad (29°) within 0.6 s.

docs.title: The controller: LQR state feedback
docs.text:
State feedback \(F = -K(x - x_{ref})\) places all four poles at once. LQR chooses the \(K\) that minimizes

\[ J = \int_0^\infty \left( x^T Q x + r F^2 \right) dt, \qquad Q = \mathrm{diag}(q_x, q_\theta, 0, 0) \]

so \(q_x\) and \(q_\theta\) say how much cart and angle errors cost, and \(r\) how much force costs. lqr_gain() in the example solves the Riccati equation (with SciPy) for the linear model; with \(q_x = 50\), \(q_\theta = 100\), \(r = 1\) it gives \(K = [-7.1,\ -57,\ -15,\ -11]\), stored in the workspace as K_lqr and used by the K gain block (matrix multiplication). The sensors are sampled every 2 ms.

Run the model: the controller catches the 3° start, rejects the tap at 3 s (5 N for 0.1 s) and moves the cart to 0.3 m at 5 s, settling within 2 % in 3.6 s, with the pendulum never more than 3° from upright and at most 4.3 N.

Look at the cart at 5 s, when the reference jumps to +0.3 m: it first moves backwards (from −17 to −26 mm, it was still recovering from the tap) and the pendulum leans 2° towards +x before the cart follows. To move right, the pendulum must first lean right, and the only way to tip it is to pull the cart left from under it. This non-minimum-phase behaviour (a zero in the right half plane) is why balancing systems react "backwards", and why they cannot be made arbitrarily fast.

docs.title: Redesign the gain in the Console
docs.text:
K_lqr is a workspace variable, so a new design is one line in the Console tab:

import sys

sys.path.insert(0, "examples")
from inverted_pendulum import lqr_gain

model.workspace["K_lqr"] = lqr_gain(q_x=200)

Then press ▶ and compare the runs in the Data Inspector.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Try What you will see lqr_gain(q_x=200) the cart is more important: it reaches 0.3 m in 2.1 s instead of 3.6 s, the pendulum leans up to 3.8° lqr_gain(r=10) force is expensive: gentle and slow, the cart has only reached 0.25 m after 5 s F_max = 3 a weaker motor still balances (it saturates for a moment during the tap) F_max = 1.5 too weak for the tap: the pendulum falls at 3.7 s m_pend = 0.35 the plant is heavier than the design model, and the LQR gain is robust enough to balance it anyway

docs.title: Tutorial: Lambda control and fuel trims
docs.text:
You will learn why petrol engines run at lambda = 1, closed-loop fuel control with a lambda sensor, short- and long-term fuel trims (as read over OBD-II), an ECU task in an atomic subsystem Before this Idle speed control Level and time intermediate, about 45 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/lambda_control.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Powertrain and engine control ▸ Engine management (all tutorials)

This tutorial follows examples/lambda_control.py. It shows how a petrol engine's ECU keeps the air-fuel ratio at the value the catalytic converter needs, and what the fuel trims that you can read from your car over OBD-II actually are.

uv run python examples/lambda_control.py      # simulates, saves lambda_control.nervus, runs the tests
uv run nervus examples/lambda_control.nervus  # open it in the editor

docs.title: Why lambda = 1
docs.text:
Burning petrol completely takes 14.7 kg of air per kg of fuel, the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio. The air-fuel equivalence ratio lambda compares the actual mixture with it:

\[ \lambda = \frac{m_{air}}{14.7\, m_{fuel}} \]

λ > 1 is lean (too much air), λ < 1 is rich. A three-way catalyst removes CO, HC and NOx at the same time only in a narrow window around λ = 1, so the ECU controls λ to 1 at part load all the time.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
Plant (the engine), top and bottom rows:

  • the air charge per cylinder stroke: 250 mg at part load, a tip-in to 400 mg from 4 s to 8 s;
  • from t = 12 s a vacuum leak: 6 % extra air that enters behind the MAF sensor, so the ECU doesn't see it;
  • the injectors: fuel mass = (injection time − dead time) × flow rate;
  • the exhaust gas needs \(n_{exh}\) = 8 samples × 10 ms to reach the lambda sensor, and the sensor itself has a time constant \(\tau\) = 0.1 s.

ECU: the ECU block is an atomic subsystem with sample_time = Ts (10 ms), the fuel task:

\[ m_{fuel,cmd} = \frac{m_{air,MAF}}{14.7}\,(1 + STFT + LTFT), \qquad t_{inj} = \frac{m_{fuel,cmd}}{q_{inj}} + t_{dead} \]
  • The base fuel comes from the measured air (feed-forward). If the sensors and injectors were perfect, this alone would give λ = 1.
  • The short-term fuel trim (STFT) is a discrete PI controller on the lambda error \(e = \lambda_{meas} - 1\), limited to ±25 %. Lean (e > 0) means more fuel.
  • The long-term fuel trim (LTFT) integrates the STFT slowly: \(LTFT[k+1] = LTFT[k] + K_{ltft}\,T_s\,STFT[k]\). It moves the average correction out of the STFT, which then returns to 0 and has its full ±25 % available again for fast disturbances.

docs.title: What happens
docs.text:
1. Up to 12 s λ stays at 1, even during the tip-in: the base fuel follows the measured air.
  2. At 12 s the leak makes the mixture 6 % lean. The lambda sensor sees it about 0.2 s later (exhaust delay and sensor lag); the STFT rises to about +5 % within three seconds and brings λ back to 1.
  3. Over the next 25 s the LTFT learns the leak: it rises to almost +6 % while the STFT falls back to 0.

A real ECU stores the LTFT, often per load and speed range, and keeps it when the engine is switched off. It also sets a trouble code when a trim reaches its limit, such as P0171 System too lean (see the OBD-II page).

docs.title: Compare with your car
docs.text:
Your car reports the same two numbers as OBD PIDs 06 (stft_b1) and 07 (ltft_b1):

uv run python -m nervus.obd record --port /dev/tty.usbserial-1110 \
    --pids rpm,maf,stft_b1,ltft_b1,o2_b1s1 --duration 300 --out my_drive.nervres
  • A healthy engine has an LTFT within about ±5 % and an STFT that keeps moving around 0.
  • An LTFT of +10 % or more at idle that gets smaller at higher load is the classic sign of a vacuum leak: the leak is a fixed amount of air, so it matters most when little air is flowing.
  • An LTFT that is high at all loads points more to fuel delivery (pump pressure, injectors) or the MAF sensor.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
To try one: change the value in the Model Workspace tab (double-click it), or for a block parameter select the block and edit it in Properties; press ▶ and compare with the previous run in the Data Inspector (Ctrl+I). Ctrl+Z undoes the change.

Change the workspace variables in the Model Workspace panel and run again:

Try What you will see injector_error = -0.05, leak = 0 clogged injectors: the LTFT learns about +5.3 % (= 1/0.95 − 1) K_ltft = 0.5 faster learning, but the trims overshoot: the STFT goes negative and λ dips rich (0.987) Ki_stft = 4 a faster STFT (peak after 0.7 s instead of 2.7 s), with some overshoot n_exh = 20 and Ki_stft = 4 a longer exhaust delay with a fast STFT: much more overshoot, λ dips to 0.98. The delay limits how fast the STFT can be

The test cases in the Test Manager check the leak and clogged-injector cases, and that λ stays at 1 during the tip-in. Generate C code for the ECU block (Code → Generate C) to get the fuel task as ECU code.

docs.title: Tutorial: Position control of a mass-spring-damper
docs.text:
You will learn what the P, I and D terms do, natural frequency and damping ratio, steady-state error, actuator limits and anti-windup Before this Your first model: a cruise control Level and time beginner, about 30 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/mass_spring_damper_pid.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Control engineering ▸ Classic lab experiments (all tutorials)

examples/mass_spring_damper_pid.py is the first experiment of many control lab courses: a mass on a spring, pushed by a force actuator, and a PID controller that moves it to a reference position. You will design the controller in the classic order, P, then PD, then PID, and see what each term does.

uv run python examples/mass_spring_damper_pid.py

docs.title: The plant
docs.text:
A mass \(m\) on a spring \(k\) with viscous damping \(c\), pushed by a force \(F\):

\[ m \ddot x + c \dot x + k x = F \]

With \(m = 1\) kg, \(c = 0.5\) N·s/m and \(k = 2\) N/m the open plant has the natural frequency \(\omega_n = \sqrt{k/m} = 1.41\) rad/s and the damping ratio \(\zeta = c / (2\sqrt{km}) = 0.18\): left alone it oscillates for a long time. In the model the equation is two Integrators (acceleration → velocity → position) with the spring and damper as feedback Gains, the way it is drawn in every textbook. The actuator is limited to ±50 N (the PID block's upper and lower).

docs.title: Step 1: P control
docs.text:
In the Model Workspace set Ki = 0 and Kd = 0, then press ▶ and open the scope. A P controller acts like an extra spring: the closed loop has the stiffness \(k + K_p\), so

\[ x_\infty = \frac{K_p}{k + K_p} = \frac{40}{42} = 0.952 \text{ m}, \qquad \omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{k + K_p}{m}} = 6.5 \text{ rad/s}, \qquad \zeta = \frac{c}{2\sqrt{m(k+K_p)}} = 0.04 \]

The mass shoots to 1.8 m and rings for many seconds around 0.952 m. A stiffer controller makes the error smaller but the oscillation worse: P alone cannot do both.

docs.title: Step 2: PD control
docs.text: Set Kd = 8. The derivative term acts like an extra damper: \(\zeta = (c + K_d) / (2\sqrt{m(k+K_p)}) = 0.66\). The overshoot drops to 5.5 % and the mass is settled within 1.4 s, but still at 0.952 m: the D term does nothing at standstill, so the steady-state error stays. The step makes the D term kick: the force jumps to the 50 N limit for a moment.

docs.title: Step 3: PID control
docs.text:
Set Ki = 30. The integral term keeps pushing while there is any error, so the mass ends exactly at 1 m. The price is a little more overshoot (12 %); the response settles within 2 % in 2.3 s.

Controller Highest position Final position Settled (2 %) P (Kp = 40) 1.80 m 0.952 m (still ringing at 10 s) > 10 s PD (Kd = 8) 1.00 m 0.952 m 1.4 s PID (Ki = 30) 1.12 m 1.000 m 2.3 s

The controller uses clamping anti-windup: while the force is at its limit, the integrator stops. With back-calculation anti-windup and Ki = 0, the integrator would still collect the saturation correction and leave a permanent offset (Simulink behaves the same way), so clamping is the right choice for a lab where the I term is switched off and on.

docs.title: Check it by hand, then with the tuner
docs.text: The PD loop's characteristic equation is \(m s^2 + (c + K_d) s + (k + K_p) = 0\), that is \(s^2 + 8.5 s + 42 = 0\), with the poles \(-4.25 \pm 4.9j\): \(\omega_n = 6.5\) rad/s and \(\zeta = 0.66\), as in step 2. For a systematic design open Analysis ▸ Linear Analysis ▸ PID Tuning, choose the block pid and a phase margin, and press Tune: it designs the gains from the plant the controller sees (see Linear analysis). Copy its gains into the workspace and compare its step response with yours in the Data Inspector: a large phase margin gives a calm but slower response.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Try What you will see Kp = 100 (PID) faster (settled in 1.3 s) but 20 % overshoot Ki = 100 the error disappears faster, but the overshoot grows to 33 % m = 3 (a heavier mass, same gains) 42 % overshoot: gains are tuned for one plant Kd = 20 more damping in the PD part, but the I term still overshoots (13 %) and settling takes longer (4.5 s)

docs.title: Tutorial: From model to ECU C code
docs.text:
You will learn an ECU software component with an interface, generated C code and its structure, calibration parameters and the A2L file, a back-to-back (SIL) test of the code, a MISRA C check Before this Your first model: a cruise control; read C code generation first Level and time intermediate, about 40 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/throttle_ecu.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic ECU software, communication and diagnostics ▸ From model to ECU code (all tutorials)

examples/throttle_ecu.py takes a throttle position controller from the model to C code that can run on an ECU: the controller as a software component, the generated code, its calibration file, and a back-to-back test that proves the C code computes the same as the model.

uv run python examples/throttle_ecu.py    # simulates, runs the tests, generates examples/generated/ECU/

docs.title: Step 1: the ECU as a software component
docs.text:
Open throttle_ecu.nervus. Everything that runs on the ECU is inside the subsystem ECU; the throttle body (an actuator lag and the plate angle) is outside, because it is hardware. The ECU's In and Out blocks are its software interface:

Port Signal Unit In 1 target_deg requested throttle angle (from the pedal map) ° In 2 tps_deg measured angle (throttle position sensor) ° Out 1 duty_pct H-bridge duty cycle %

Inside, the sensor is sampled every Ts = 10 ms (Zero-Order Hold), and a Discrete PID (P and I) with clamping anti-windup computes the duty cycle, limited to 0-100 %. The gains Kp and Ki are workspace variables. Run the three test cases in the Test Manager: the throttle reaches 59° within 80 ms of the step to 60° and overshoots to 62.7°.

docs.title: Step 2: generate the code
docs.text:
Select the ECU block and choose Code ▸ Generate C Code (Ctrl+B). Nervus writes:

File What it is ECU.h the interface: input, output, parameter and state structs, ECU_initialize(), ECU_step() ECU.c the step function: every block as a few lines of C, in execution order ECU.a2l the calibration description for INCA or CANape: parameters and measurements with their addresses main_example.c a template showing how to call the code from a 10 ms task report an HTML page linking each block to its code

The interface in ECU.h:

#define ECU_BASE_PERIOD (0.01) /* seconds between calls to ECU_step() */

typedef struct { real_T target_deg[1]; real_T tps_deg[1]; } ECU_U_t;   /* inputs  */
typedef struct { real_T duty_pct[1]; } ECU_Y_t;                         /* outputs */
typedef struct { real_T Kp[1]; real_T Ki[1]; /* ... */ } ECU_P_t;      /* calibration parameters */

and the PI controller in ECU_step():

/* error (Sum) */
ECU_B.error[0] = ECU_B.target_deg[0] - ECU_B.tps_sample[0];
/* throttle_pi (Discrete PID Controller) */
real_T unsat = ECU_P.Kp[0] * err + ECU_DW.throttle_pi_x[0] + d_term;
real_T y = fmin(fmax(unsat, ECU_P.throttle_pi_lower[0]), ECU_P.throttle_pi_upper[0]);

The code uses only static memory, no dynamic allocation and no operating system: a timer interrupt or an RTOS task calls ECU_step() every 10 ms after writing the inputs, as main_example.c shows.

docs.title: Step 3: calibration
docs.text: Kp and Ki stay parameters in RAM (ECU_P), so a calibration tool can change them on the running ECU through the A2L file, the same way as in the XCP tutorial. In the Model Workspace, untick Cal. for Kp: it becomes a constant in ROM (ECU_C) and disappears from the A2L file, which is what production code does with values that must never change.

docs.title: Step 4: back-to-back test (software in the loop)
docs.text:
How do you know the C code does what the model does? The script compiles the generated code with the system C compiler (gcc or clang), feeds it the same 300 input samples as the model, and compares every output:

Back-to-back test, 300 steps: PASSED
  duty_pct: max |C - Python| = 1.42e-14

The difference is in the last digits of a double: the C code computes the same numbers. In the editor, the code generation dialog offers the same check (Run SIL check). Run it after every change to the model, and after updating the compiler.

docs.title: Step 5: MISRA C
docs.text: ECU code is written to a coding standard, in the automotive industry nearly always MISRA C. Click MISRA check in the code generation dialog (it needs cppcheck: brew install cppcheck or apt install cppcheck): the throttle controller's code has no findings. C code generation lists what the generated code does for the rules, and the three documented deviations.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Try What you will see Ts = 0.02 (a 20 ms task) the loop gets slower and overshoots to 66°; the tip-in tests fail: the gains were tuned for 10 ms Ts = 0.05 79° overshoot: a controller tuned for one rate does not work at another untick Cal. for Kp, generate again Kp moves from ECU_P (RAM) to ECU_C (ROM) and leaves the A2L file

docs.title: Tutorial: An NTC temperature sensor interface
docs.text:
You will learn a thermistor in a voltage divider, the ECU's pull-up, input filter and ADC, a conversion table, resolution over the range, why software and hardware must match Before this Your first model: a cruise control Level and time intermediate, about 35 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/ntc_sensor.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Electrics and electronics ▸ ECU hardware and PCB (all tutorials)

Coolant, intake air, oil, fuel and battery temperatures are all measured the same way: an NTC thermistor in a voltage divider, read by the ECU's analog-to-digital converter. examples/ntc_sensor.py models the whole chain, from the component on the engine to the number in the software, so you can see the design decisions an ECU hardware engineer makes.

uv run python examples/ntc_sensor.py

docs.title: The circuit
docs.text:
Part Where Value NTC thermistor in the engine 2 kΩ at 25 °C, β = 3600 K (the Thermistor block) harness the wiring 0.5 Ω (a Variable Resistor, used for fault injection) sensor supply ECU board 5 V reference pull-up resistor ECU board 2.49 kΩ input filter ECU board 10 kΩ and 100 nF (τ = 1 ms): protection against noise and transients ADC microcontroller 12 bits on 0-5 V (4096 counts), read every 100 ms

The NTC's resistance falls steeply with temperature, \(R = R_{25}\, e^{\beta (1/T - 1/298\,\mathrm{K})}\): 30.7 kΩ at −30 °C, 2.0 kΩ at 25 °C, 230 Ω at 90 °C. With the pull-up it forms a divider:

\[ V_{sig} = 5\,\mathrm{V} \cdot \frac{R_{NTC}}{R_{NTC} + R_{pull}} \]

The software turns the ADC counts back into a temperature with a lookup table (23 points from −40 to 150 °C, computed from the divider, the way a sensor supplier's data sheet gives it), every 100 ms.

docs.title: Accuracy depends on the temperature
docs.text:
The divider is nonlinear, so one ADC count means a different temperature step at each temperature. With the 2.49 kΩ pull-up:

Temperature NTC Signal Resolution −30 °C 30.7 kΩ 4.62 V 0.06 °C per count 20 °C 2.46 kΩ 2.48 V 0.02 °C per count 90 °C 230 Ω 0.42 V 0.12 °C per count 120 °C 108 Ω 0.21 V 0.26 °C per count

The pull-up is chosen so the sensor is most accurate where it matters (here 20-100 °C) and the signal stays inside the diagnostic window of 0.1-4.9 V over the whole range. Run the model: over the warm-up from −10 to 95 °C the ECU reads the temperature within 0.3 °C. (At the very first sample, at power-up, the filter capacitor is still empty and the ADC reads 0 V; real ECUs wait a few milliseconds before the first reading.)

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
Try What you will see R_pull = 470 the ECU reads 41.5 °C at 95 °C: the table still describes the 2.49 kΩ circuit. Software and hardware must match R_pull = 470 and the table for it: in the Console, import sys; sys.path.insert(0, "examples"); from ntc_sensor import table, then model.workspace["adc_counts_axis"], model.workspace["adc_temp_table"] = table(470) accurate again (0.4 °C) and better at high temperatures, but −30 °C would give 4.92 V, above the 4.9 V open-circuit limit: a false code on a cold morning C_filter = 100e-6 (τ = 1 s) a slower filter: the reading lags by about a second and the error grows to 0.9 °C during the warm-up

The same circuit with a short or an open wire is the subject of the next tutorial, Sensor fault diagnosis.

docs.title: Tutorial: On-board diagnostics and trouble codes
docs.text:
You will learn diagnostic monitors: debouncing, enable conditions, pending and confirmed codes, two-trip detection, the MIL, readiness; reading the codes with an OBD tool Before this Engine operating modes; read OBD-II live data first Level and time intermediate, about 35 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/obd_ecu.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic ECU software, communication and diagnostics ▸ Diagnostics (all tutorials)

Every engine ECU watches itself: monitors test the misfire rate, the fuel trims, the catalyst, the sensors, and store a diagnostic trouble code (DTC) and switch on the check-engine lamp (MIL) when a test fails. A workshop reads the codes over the OBD-II port. examples/obd_ecu.py is such an ECU with two monitors, and it can answer a real OBD tool.

uv run python examples/obd_ecu.py

docs.title: The monitors
docs.text:
Code Monitor Raw test Enable condition P0302 cylinder 2 misfire misfires in a counting window ≥ misfire_limit coolant above 40 °C (a cold engine misfires more) P0171 system too lean long-term fuel trim ≥ ltft_limit (+20 %) always

From 20 s, cylinder 2 misfires. The fuel trim stays at +4 %, so P0171 passes. A key cycle (key off and on) happens every 30 s.

Each monitor is a Diagnostic Monitor block, which implements what the OBD rules require:

  • debouncing: a counter goes up while the raw test fails and down while it passes; only at the threshold (10 samples of 0.1 s) is the test failed, so a glitch does not set a code;
  • pending: the first failure stores the code as pending at once;
  • confirmed and MIL: failing in two key cycles in a row ("two-trip detection") confirms the code and switches on the MIL; three cycles without a failure switch it off again (the code stays stored);
  • readiness: the monitor reports complete once it has run, passed or failed. An inspection station checks that the monitors are ready before it trusts "no codes".

docs.title: Follow the scenario
docs.text: Open examples/obd_ecu.nervus and run it (90 s). The engine is warm (40 °C) at 8.5 s; the misfire monitor then runs and is ready at 9.5 s (it has completed without a failure). The misfire starts at 20 s: after 10 failed samples the code is pending at 21.6 s. At the key cycle at 30 s the code fails again in the new cycle: it is confirmed and the MIL comes on at 31.1 s. The Test Manager has the same story as two test cases; run them with Ctrl+T.

docs.title: Read the codes with an OBD tool
docs.text:
The OBD Responder block publishes four PIDs (rpm, speed, coolant temperature, load) and both codes. Run the model in real time as a simulated car with an ELM327 adapter on a serial port (macOS and Linux):

uv run python -m nervus.obd simulate examples/obd_ecu.nervus
#   ECU 'ecu': ELM327 on /dev/ttys007
uv run python -m nervus.obd dtc --port /dev/ttys007        # in another terminal, after 31 s

The dtc command shows P0302 (Cylinder 2 misfire detected) as stored and pending, and the MIL. Any OBD program that talks to an ELM327 can connect to that port, also one that clears the codes (mode 04): the responder's clear output then resets the monitors, and their readiness drops back to not complete, exactly as after clearing codes in a real car. See OBD-II live data.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Try What you will see coolant_tau = 100 (slow warm-up) the monitor is enabled only at 35 s: the code is pending at 35.1 s and the MIL comes on in the third cycle (60.9 s) misfire_limit = 1.5 the raw test can never fail: no code, but the monitor reports ready. A wrong threshold hides the fault and still passes the inspection: why monitors are calibrated and tested against faults threshold = 30 on P0302_monitor slower debouncing (the raw test fails in only 75 % of the windows, so the counter also goes down): pending at 25.0 s instead of 21.6 s

docs.title: Tutorial: Starter motor and electronic throttle
docs.text:
You will learn physical modelling (circuits, shafts, springs connected by links instead of signals): cranking an engine on a weak battery, a drive-by-wire throttle servo Before this Your first model: a cruise control; read Physical modelling first Level and time intermediate, about 45 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/starter_motor.nervus, examples/electronic_throttle.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Electrics and electronics ▸ Vehicle electrical system (all tutorials)

Two physical models that mix circuits, mechanics and control: cranking an engine with the starter motor, and the drive-by-wire throttle. Both are built from physical blocks (see Physical modelling).

uv run python examples/starter_motor.py
uv run python examples/electronic_throttle.py

docs.title: Cranking: why ECUs must survive 8 V
docs.text:
The key switches the starter relay; the relay connects the starter motor to the battery. At standstill the motor has no back-EMF, so the current is limited only by the resistances of the battery (10 mΩ), the motor (20 mΩ) and the contact:

\[ I_0 \approx \frac{12.6\ \text{V}}{0.010 + 0.020 + 0.002\ \Omega} \approx 390\ \text{A} \]

The simulation peaks at 378 A (the inductance and the first movement take a little off), and the battery voltage falls to 9 V: \(12.6 - 378 \cdot 0.010\). With a cold, weak battery it falls much further, which is why ECUs and sensors are specified to keep working down to 6-8 V while cranking.

The motor drives the flywheel through the pinion (12:1). Each compression stroke resists, so speed, current and voltage ripple twice per revolution (four cylinders). The engine settles at about 300 rpm, with 160 A from the battery. The rotor's inertia is lumped with the crankshaft's (\(J_{engine} + 12^2 J_{rotor}\)): a stiff gear between two separate inertias has no unique solution.

docs.title: Electronic throttle: a position servo
docs.text:
The ECU reads the throttle position sensor every millisecond and sets the H-bridge's duty cycle; the motor turns the plate through a 20:1 gear against a return spring, whose preload closes the throttle if the motor is off (the limp-home safety requirement). Signal blocks (the ECU) and physical blocks (battery, H-bridge, motor, gear, spring) are linked through the H-bridge's duty input and the angle sensor's output.

The controller was designed with Linear Analysis → PID Tuning: it opens the loop at the PID block, linearizes the plant from the duty cycle to the angle through the motor, gear and spring (third order, after the battery's charge and the angle sensor's integrator are cancelled), and shapes the loop for 60° phase margin at 100 rad/s:

P I D tuned 0.081 2.05 0.0008 in the model 0.08 2.0 0.0008

Small steps follow the target closely. A big step (5° → 60°) saturates the duty cycle at 100 % for the first 40 ms: the plate reaches 90 % in 45 ms and overshoots by 6.6° before the integral (with clamping anti-windup) recovers. A feed-forward of the spring torque helps the integral at part throttle, where the error goes to zero within 0.15 s. The ECU subsystem generates C code (generate_c(d.block("ECU"))), which the tests check back to back against the simulation.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
To try one: change the value in the Model Workspace tab (double-click it), or for a block parameter select the block and edit it in Properties; press ▶ and compare with the previous run in the Data Inspector (Ctrl+I). Ctrl+Z undoes the change.

Try What you will see starter: battery R_internal = 0.03 the battery collapses to 4.5 V while cranking: an ECU without enough reserve resets throttle: Kd_etc = 0 10° of overshoot and 0.25 s to settle: the derivative damps the motor throttle: R_motor = 3 a weaker motor: 56 ms instead of 45 ms to 90 %, and more overshoot

docs.title: Tutorial: Scripting and testing models from Python
docs.text:
You will learn loading and running a model from a script, changing parameters for one run or for good, parameter sweeps, running a model's test cases in pytest, building a model in code Before this Your first model: a cruise control Level and time beginner, about 25 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/cruise_control.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Getting started (all tutorials)

Everything the editor does, a Python script can do too: load a model, change its parameters, run it, sweep a gain, check the results. Scripts make studies repeatable, and they put models into CI, where every change is tested. We take the cruise control of the first tutorial and drive it from Python.

The whole script is examples/scripting.py; it prints every number quoted here:

uv run python examples/scripting.py          # add --plot to see the speed curves

You can type the same lines into the editor's Console tab, where the open model is already loaded as model.

docs.title: Step 1: load and run a model
docs.text:
from nervus import load, simulate

model = load("examples/cruise_control.nervus")
print({v.name: v.value for v in model.workspace.variables})
# {'m': 1500.0, 'c_drag': 8.0, 'Kp': 300.0, 'Ki': 30.0}

res = simulate(model)
print(res["speed"][-1], res["speed"].max())  # 99.97 99.97

simulate returns a SimResult. res.t is the time vector; res["speed"] is the output of the block named speed, as a NumPy array with one value per time step. A block with several outputs is res["block:1"], and a named wire is reached by its signal name. res.names() lists them all.

The stop time, the solver and the step come from the model's settings, as in the editor. Override them per run: simulate(model, t_final=60.0, solver="rk4", step=0.01).

docs.title: Step 2: change parameters
docs.text:
There are two ways, and the difference matters.

For one run only, pass workspace values with params. The model is not changed:

p_only = simulate(model, params={"Ki": 0.0})
print(p_only["speed"][-1])  # 97.40: P control alone leaves a steady error
print(model.workspace["Ki"])  # still 30

In the model itself, set the workspace value or a block parameter. This is what the Properties panel does:

model.block("cruise_control").set_param("anti_windup", "none")
print(simulate(model)["speed"].max())  # 138.57 km/h: integrator windup
model.workspace["Kp"] = 400.0

Block parameters accept the same expressions as in the editor, e.g. set_param("gain", "3.6 / m"). Save the changed model with save(model, "my_cruise.nervus").

Prefer params in studies

A study that changes the model in place has to remember to change it back. With params, every run starts from the saved model, so runs cannot leak into each other.

docs.title: Step 3: sweep a gain
docs.text:
nervus.sweep runs a model once per parameter combination and reduces each run to a few numbers, the metrics:

from nervus.sweep import metric, sweep


def overshoot(res):
    return max(0.0, res["speed"].max() - 100.0)


table = sweep(
    model, {"Kp": [100.0, 300.0, 1000.0]}, metrics={"overshoot": overshoot, "max_speed": metric("speed", "max")}
)
for row in table.rows:
    print(row["Kp"], row["overshoot"])
Kp Overshoot 100 9.73 km/h 300 0 1000 0

A smaller proportional gain gives more overshoot here. With Ki fixed, a small Kp leaves the integral term in charge, and the integral overshoots. Sweeps like this one find such surprises quickly.

table.to_csv("sweep.csv") saves the table. Pass several variables to get every combination, and use monte_carlo for random tolerances (see Robustness and tolerances with Monte Carlo). Pass keep_results=True to keep the full results for plotting:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

for row in sweep(model, {"Kp": [100.0, 300.0, 1000.0]}, keep_results=True).rows:
    plt.plot(row["result"].t, row["result"]["speed"], label=f"Kp = {row['Kp']:g}")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

docs.title: Step 4: run the model's test cases
docs.text:
The test cases you see in the editor's Test Manager are saved with the model. Run them from Python:

from nervus.testing import run_tests

for r in run_tests(model):
    print(r.summary())

PASS  reaches the set speed without overshoot
    ✓ -inf ≤ speed ≤ 101.0: min 0, max 99.9738
    ✓ 99.0 ≤ speed ≤ 101.0 for 20 ≤ t ≤ end: min 99.7148, max 99.9738

That makes a model a regression test. Put this in tests/test_cruise.py and pytest runs it in CI on every push:

from pathlib import Path

import pytest

from nervus import load
from nervus.testing import run_tests

MODEL = load(Path(__file__).parent.parent / "examples" / "cruise_control.nervus")


@pytest.mark.parametrize("case", MODEL.tests, ids=lambda c: c.name)
def test_model(case):
    (result,) = run_tests(MODEL, [case])
    assert result.passed, result.summary()

Each test case becomes one pytest test, and a failure prints which check failed and by how much. Plain asserts on a result work too: assert simulate(model)["speed"].max() < 101.

docs.title: Step 5: build a model in code
docs.text:
Models can also be built without the editor. That suits generated models, such as a filter bank with one block per frequency, and small models inside unit tests. A first-order lag, \(\dot y = (u - y)/\tau\):

from nervus import Diagram, simulate
from nervus.blocks import Gain, Integrator, Scope, Step, Sum

d = Diagram("first_order")
u = d.add(Step(time=0.0, final=1.0), name="u")
err = d.add(Sum(signs="+-"), name="err")
k = d.add(Gain(gain=1 / 0.5), name="1/tau")
y = d.add(Integrator(), name="y")
d.connect(u, err.in_port(0))
d.connect(y, err.in_port(1))
d.chain(err, k, y)  # err -> 1/tau -> y

res = simulate(d, t_final=3.0)
print(res["y"][-1])  # 0.9975 = 1 - exp(-6)

d.add places a block, d.connect wires an output to an input, and d.chain wires a row of single-port blocks. save(d, "first_order.nervus") writes a file the editor opens. Blocks get no position in code, and the editor lays them out when it opens the file. Every example in examples/ is built this way, so they are a good reference: examples/cruise_control.py builds the model of the first tutorial, test case included.

The block classes and their parameters are listed in the block reference. In the Console, help(Gain) shows the same text.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Try What you will see sweep Ki over [0, 10, 30, 100] with Kp = 300 0 leaves a steady error of 2.6 km/h; 10 is still 0.8 km/h short after 40 s; 100 overshoots to 101.6 km/h model.workspace["m"] = 2500.0, then run_tests(model) a heavier car is still at 95.7 km/h after 20 s: the test case fails, and the summary says where res.to_csv("run.csv"), then open the file one column per signal, ready for a spreadsheet in pytest, change the check to upper: 99.5 the test fails, and the message shows the maximum speed that broke it

docs.title: Tutorial: RC and RLC circuits
docs.text:
You will learn time constant and step response, cut-off frequency and the Bode plot, resonance, damping and the quality factor, physical circuit blocks and linear analysis Before this Your first model: a cruise control Level and time beginner, about 30 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/rc_filter.nervus, examples/rlc_circuit.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Electrics and electronics ▸ Circuit fundamentals (all tutorials)

The first lab of every electronics course: charge a capacitor through a resistor, then add an inductor and watch the circuit ring. examples/rc_rlc.py builds both circuits from physical blocks, and you measure their step response in the time domain and their frequency response with Linear Analysis, and compare with the formulas.

uv run python examples/rc_rlc.py      # builds rc_filter.nervus and rlc_circuit.nervus

docs.title: The RC low-pass
docs.text:
Open examples/rc_filter.nervus: an In block (5 V) drives a controlled voltage source, through \(R = 1\) kΩ into \(C = 1\) µF; a voltage sensor measures the capacitor and feeds the Out block. The capacitor starts empty, so pressing ▶ shows the classic charging curve:

\[ v_C(t) = V \left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right), \qquad \tau = RC = 1 \text{ ms} \]

After one time constant the capacitor is at 63 % (3.16 V), after five at 99 %. The model's test case checks both.

Now Analysis ▸ Linear Analysis (Ctrl+L), from v_in to v_out: the transfer function is \(G(s) = 1 / (\tau s + 1)\), a first-order low-pass. The Bode plot is flat at low frequencies and falls by 20 dB per decade above the cut-off frequency

\[ f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi RC} = 159 \text{ Hz}, \]

where the gain is −3.01 dB (half the power) and the phase −45°.

docs.title: The RLC circuit
docs.text:
Open examples/rlc_circuit.nervus: the same source, 1 V, through \(R = 10\) Ω, \(L = 10\) mH and \(C = 10\) µF in series. The capacitor voltage is now a second-order system:

\[ G(s) = \frac{1}{LC s^2 + RC s + 1}, \qquad f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} = 503 \text{ Hz}, \qquad \zeta = \frac{R}{2}\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}} = 0.16 \]

With so little damping the step response overshoots by 60 % and rings at about 500 Hz before settling, and the Bode plot has a resonance peak of +10 dB at \(f_0\): the quality factor \(Q = 1/(2\zeta) = 3.2\), the voltage across the capacitor at resonance is 3.2 times the input.

The resistance decides the damping. Critical damping (\(\zeta = 1\)) needs \(R = 2\sqrt{L/C} = 63\) Ω: the fastest response without overshoot. More resistance makes it overdamped: no overshoot, but slower.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
Change the values in the Model Workspace, run, and compare in the Data Inspector or Linear Analysis:

Try What you will see RC: C = 10e-6 τ = 10 ms: ten times slower, and the cut-off moves to 15.9 Hz RLC: R = 63.2 critical damping: no overshoot, settled in about 2 ms RLC: R = 200 overdamped: slow, like a first-order circuit RLC: R = 1 ζ = 0.016: Q = 32, a 30 dB resonance peak and a ringing that lasts many milliseconds RLC: L = 2.5e-3 f₀ doubles to 1007 Hz, ζ doubles to 0.32

From here, the circuits tutorial goes on to diodes, transistors and switching converters.

docs.title: Tutorial: Requirements-based testing and coverage
docs.text:
You will learn requirements imported from a CSV file, traceability from requirements to blocks and tests, model coverage to find untested behaviour, closing the gap, review reports Before this Idle speed control Level and time intermediate, about 40 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/idle_requirements.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Testing and verification (all tutorials)

In the automotive industry a function is finished when every requirement is verified by a test, and the tests exercise the whole function (coverage). This tutorial takes the idle speed controller of the idle speed tutorial through that process: import its requirements, link them to the model and the tests, find the gap, close it, and write the reports a review asks for.

uv run python examples/idle_requirements.py   # the finished result: idle_requirements.nervus and two reports

docs.title: Step 1: import the requirements
docs.text:
The requirements of the function are in examples/data/idle_requirements.csv, as exported from a requirements tool or a spreadsheet (;-separated, with id, title, text and source columns):

Id Title Requirement IDLE-01 Idle speed With the engine warm and no load change, the idle speed stays within 800 ± 20 rpm. IDLE-02 Load rejection When the AC compressor switches on, the speed drops by less than 50 rpm and is back within ± 20 rpm after 4 s. IDLE-03 Stall protection Even without the AC feed-forward the engine must not stall: the speed stays above 600 rpm. IDLE-04 Calibratable target The idle target is a calibration parameter; the engine reaches a new target within ± 15 rpm. IDLE-05 Limited correction The correction is limited to 15° of throttle, and a large target change still settles without windup.

Open examples/idle_speed_control.nervus, go to the Requirements tab and press Import CSV…. All five appear as not implemented: nothing in the model claims them yet.

docs.title: Step 2: link the model and the tests
docs.text:
• Right-click the ECU subsystem ▸ Requirements… and tick all five: the ECU implements them. They change to not tested.
  • In the Test Manager, open each test case and fill in Requirements: AC compressor on at 5 s verifies IDLE-01 and IDLE-02, AC compressor on, no feed-forward IDLE-03, higher idle target IDLE-04.
  • Press Run All (Ctrl+T). Four requirements are now verified, and IDLE-05 is still not tested: no test checks the limit.

docs.title: Step 3: find what the tests miss
docs.text:
Requirements tell you what to test; coverage tells you whether the tests reached every decision in the model. The Test Manager measures it with every Run All: the line under the results shows the coverage, and Coverage report lists what was missed (in Python: run_tests(model, coverage=Coverage()), as in the example):

Decision coverage: 4/8 outcomes (50 %) in 3 run(s)
  ECU/idle_pi: never output at upper limit
  p_intake: never at upper limit, at lower limit
  omega: never at lower limit

The controller idle_pi never reached its upper limit, exactly the behaviour IDLE-05 is about. The other three outcomes are limits of the plant (the manifold pressure and a stopped engine): physically impossible or a stall, so they are justified in the review rather than tested.

docs.title: Step 4: close the gap
docs.text:
Add a test case in the Test Manager:

Field Value Name large target change: correction limited Parameter overrides rpm_idle = 1500 Requirements IDLE-05 Checks bounds on ECU/idle_pi (lower −2, upper 15); final_value of engine_rpm = 1500 ± 20

Run all tests again: the controller now saturates at 15°, the engine still settles at 1500 rpm, IDLE-05 is verified, and the controller's decisions are fully covered (5 of 8 outcomes, the rest being the plant).

docs.title: Step 5: the reports
docs.text: Report… in the Requirements tab writes the traceability matrix (requirement → blocks → tests → status) as an HTML page; the coverage report lists every decision outcome. The example writes both to examples/generated/. Together with the test results they are what a design review or an ISO 26262 assessment asks for. The Model Advisor (Analysis ▸ Model Advisor) adds the static checks: it warns about requirements without blocks or tests, and about links to unknown ids.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Try What you will see Kp_idle = 0.01 (a weak controller), run the tests the two AC tests fail: IDLE-01, IDLE-02 and IDLE-03 show failed, IDLE-04 and IDLE-05 still pass rename IDLE-05 to IDLE-06 in the table the links in the ECU block and the new test follow the rename delete the link from the ECU to IDLE-03 IDLE-03 becomes not implemented, even though its test still passes

docs.title: Tutorial: Robustness and tolerances with Monte Carlo
docs.text:
You will learn parameter spread in a vehicle range, Monte Carlo studies in the editor and in Python, custom metrics, why the average hides the failures Before this Your first model: a cruise control Level and time intermediate, about 30 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/cruise_control.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Testing and verification (all tutorials)

A controller is tuned on one car, but it is built into thousands, and every one is different: the mass changes with passengers and luggage, the drag with tyres and roof boxes. A Monte Carlo study runs the model many times with random parameters to see the spread, and checks the requirement for every one. This tutorial does it for the cruise control of the first tutorial.

uv run python examples/cruise_tolerance.py

docs.title: The question
docs.text:
The cruise control was tuned for 1500 kg. The model range weighs 1200 to 2000 kg (a uniform distribution), and the drag coefficient varies by about ±10 % (a normal distribution, mean 8 N/(km/h), standard deviation 0.8). The requirement:

After the step to 100 km/h, the speed is within ±1 km/h of the set speed within 20 s, for every car.

docs.title: Step 1: in the editor
docs.text: Open examples/cruise_control.nervus and choose Analysis ▸ Parameter Sweep / Monte Carlo… (Ctrl+Shift+W). Choose Monte Carlo, add the parameters m = uniform(1200, 2000) and c_drag = normal(8, 0.8), 200 runs, signal speed, statistic max, and press Run. The Signal tab draws all 200 responses on top of each other: a band instead of a line. The Metric tab shows the histogram of the highest speed: never more than 0.3 km/h above the set speed. The table can be exported as CSV.

docs.title: Step 2: the settling time in Python
docs.text:
The settling time needs a little logic (the last time the speed was more than 1 km/h off), so the example computes it as a metric with nervus.sweep.monte_carlo:

from nervus.sweep import monte_carlo


def settling_time(res):
    v = res["speed"]
    off = np.where(np.abs(v - 100) > 1)[0]
    return res.t[off[-1]] - 1.0


table = monte_carlo(
    model,
    {"m": ("uniform", 1200, 2000), "c_drag": ("normal", 8, 0.8)},
    runs=200,
    seed=1,
    metrics={"settling_s": settling_time},
)

With the original Ki = 30 every car settles between 12.1 and 18.4 s: the requirement is met with margin. The settling time follows the mass closely (correlation 0.94); the drag hardly matters.

docs.title: Step 3: the trap of the average
docs.text:
Someone proposes Ki = 60 to make the cruise control faster. On the nominal car it is faster, and the average settling time drops from 15.2 to 14.5 s. But the Monte Carlo study shows the spread getting wider: the heavy cars now overshoot and need up to 22.5 s, and only 83 % of the cars meet the requirement. A test on one nominal car would have passed.

Ki settling time (range) mean cars meeting 20 s 15 15.4-29.2 s 22.0 s 17 % 30 (original) 12.1-18.4 s 15.2 s 100 % 45 11.1-17.3 s 14.1 s 100 % 60 10.5-22.5 s 14.5 s 83 %

Ki = 45 is faster for every car and still meets the requirement everywhere: that is the robust choice.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
Try What you will see m = uniform(1200, 2600) (a van version) the heaviest vans need longer; check whether 20 s still holds runs = 20 the statistics change from seed to seed: too few runs miss the rare cases a third parameter, Kp = normal(300, 30) (a controller calibrated with a tolerance) the spread widens a little

See Test cases and results for sweeps over a grid and the dialog's options.

docs.title: Tutorial: Sensor fault diagnosis and substitute values
docs.text:
You will learn range checks on a sensor signal, open circuit and short to ground (P0117/P0118), debouncing, substitute values for limp-home, fault injection in a test Before this An NTC temperature sensor interface Level and time intermediate, about 30 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/ntc_sensor.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic ECU software, communication and diagnostics ▸ Diagnostics (all tutorials)

Sensors and their wiring fail: a connector corrodes open, a chafed wire touches the engine block. The ECU must notice, store a trouble code, and keep the engine running with a sensible substitute value. This tutorial uses the coolant temperature sensor of the NTC tutorial (examples/ntc_sensor.py) and breaks it.

uv run python examples/ntc_sensor.py

docs.title: Range checks
docs.text:
A healthy sensor never produces every voltage: the divider keeps the signal between 0.11 V (150 °C) and 4.79 V (−40 °C). The ECU uses the rest as a diagnostic window:

Signal Meaning Code below 0.1 V the signal wire is shorted to ground P0117 engine coolant temperature circuit low above 4.9 V open circuit: broken wire or connector, the pull-up pulls the signal to 5 V P0118 engine coolant temperature circuit high

Each check is a Compare to Constant on the measured voltage, followed by a Diagnostic Monitor that debounces it (5 samples of 100 ms) and stores the code. While either code is pending, a Switch gives the rest of the ECU the substitute value T_substitute = 80 °C instead of the measurement: the fan runs, and the engine is fuelled as if warm, which is safe for driving to a workshop.

docs.title: Break the wire
docs.text:
The fault_injection block (a Python Function) sets the harness resistance to 100 MΩ (open circuit) or the signal wire's resistance to ground to 0.05 Ω (short) at fault_time = 200 s. Set fault = 1 and run:

The voltage jumps to 5.0 V; the raw measurement reads −40 °C (the end of the table), which would make the engine run very rich if the ECU believed it. After 5 samples the code P0118 is pending (200.6 s) and the ECU uses 80 °C. The MIL comes on in the same drive cycle (confirm_cycles = 1: electrical faults are usually confirmed at once). With fault = 2 the voltage drops to 0 V, the raw reading is 150 °C, and P0117 is pending at 200.6 s.

The model's three test cases check the normal warm-up and both faults; run them in the Test Manager.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Try What you will see fault = 1, fault_time = 50 the open circuit during the warm-up: P0118 at 50.6 s, and from then on the ECU uses 80 °C threshold = 50 on P0118 5 s of debouncing: the wrong −40 °C reading is used for 5 s V_high = 4.5 the window is too narrow: below about −25 °C a healthy sensor already gives more than 4.5 V, so a cold start sets a false P0118 T_substitute = 20 a cold substitute: the ECU would run the engine rich, as if it were cold; why the substitute is chosen per function

docs.title: Tutorial: Tyre slip and traction control
docs.text:
You will learn tyre slip and Pacejka's magic formula, wheel and vehicle dynamics, a traction control ECU on dry, wet and snowy roads Before this Your first model: a cruise control Level and time intermediate, about 30 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/traction_control.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Vehicle dynamics and energy ▸ Chassis control (all tutorials)

This tutorial follows examples/traction_control.py: a car launching at full throttle on dry, wet and snowy roads, and a traction control (TCS) ECU that keeps the driven wheels from spinning.

uv run python examples/traction_control.py

docs.title: Slip and the magic formula
docs.text:
A tyre transmits force only through slip: the driven wheel turns a little faster than the car moves,

\[ \lambda = \frac{\omega r - v}{\max(\omega r,\ v)} \]

The force rises steeply with slip, peaks at about 10 %, then falls slowly; a spinning tyre also loses its side grip, so the car can no longer be steered. Pacejka's magic formula fits this curve:

\[ F_x = \mu\,F_z\,\sin\!\big(C \arctan(B\lambda - E(B\lambda - \arctan B\lambda))\big) \]

with B = 10, C = 1.9, E = 0.97 here, and the road's friction μ (dry 1.0, wet 0.5, snow 0.2) scaling it.

The car: the engine torque at the wheels turns the driven wheels (their inertia includes the engine's, reflected through 1st gear: 30 kg·m²); the tyre force pushes the car and brakes the wheels.

docs.title: Traction control
docs.text:
Every 10 ms the TCS ECU compares the driven wheels' speed with the non-driven wheels' (which turn with the car) and computes the slip. Above the 10 % target, a PI controller reduces the engine torque (0 = none, 1 = all).

Road TCS off TCS on dry (μ = 1.0) 8 % slip, 0-50 km/h in 2.7 s the same: the tyres grip, TCS does nothing wet (μ = 0.5) the wheels spin at 86 % slip, 0-50 in 5.4 s 10 % slip, 0-50 in 5.2 s snow (μ = 0.2) 96 % slip 10 % slip (13 % at the start)

On the wet road the car is only a little faster with TCS (the magic formula's force falls slowly past its peak), but its wheels keep their side grip: that is the main point of traction control. In the first 0.2 s the controller oscillates: at walking pace the slip changes very fast compared with the 10 ms task, and real systems use the brakes and an engine torque model for the start.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
To try one: change the value in the Model Workspace tab (double-click it), or for a block parameter select the block and edit it in Properties; press ▶ and compare with the previous run in the Data Inspector (Ctrl+I). Ctrl+Z undoes the change.

Try What you will see slip_target = 0.2 20 % slip and a little faster (60 instead of 58 km/h after 6 s): this tyre's peak is broad J_wheels = 2.5 (the wheels alone) the wheels spin up much faster than the 10 ms task: slip peaks at 67 % mu_road = 0.2, T_wheel_max = 500, tcs_enable = 0 below the 550 N·m the snowy tyres can carry: little slip even without TCS

docs.title: Tutorial: A truck on a mountain road
docs.text:
You will learn heavy-duty vehicles: a diesel's narrow torque band, a 12-speed automated gearbox (State Chart), cruise control, an exhaust brake on a descent Before this A car on a drive cycle, Gear-shift logic Level and time intermediate, about 30 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/truck.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic Powertrain and engine control ▸ Transmission and driveline (all tutorials)

examples/truck.py puts a 40-tonne truck on a 6 % climb and a 6 % descent: a heavy-duty diesel engine, a 12-speed automated manual gearbox (AMT) with its shift logic as a State Chart, cruise control and an exhaust brake.

uv run python examples/truck.py

docs.title: The climb
docs.text: The engine (2600 N·m from 1000 to 1400 rpm) is small for 40 tonnes: on a 6 % climb the gravity alone is \(40\,000 \cdot 9.81 \cdot 0.06 \approx 23.5\) kN. The truck slows from 80 to under 40 km/h, and the AMT shifts down one gear at a time whenever the engine falls below 1050 rpm, so it stays in its narrow band of full torque. Each shift interrupts the torque for 0.8 s (the clutch opens and the gearbox synchronises), which on a steep climb costs speed: that is why truck gearboxes have many closely spaced gears.

docs.title: The descent
docs.text: Downhill the same 23.5 kN push the truck. The service brakes would overheat on a long descent, so the truck uses an auxiliary brake: the exhaust flap closes and the engine works as a compressor, braking more the faster it turns. The ECU closes it above the set speed + 4 km/h, and the TCU holds a lower gear so the engine turns fast. Here the exhaust brake holds the truck at 98 km/h; without it the truck would run away. To hold 84 km/h on this descent it needs more braking power, which is why trucks for mountain roads also have a hydraulic retarder. The chart's param values (shift speeds, hold speed, shift time) are calibration data in the workspace.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
To try one: change the value in the Model Workspace tab (double-click it), or for a block parameter select the block and edit it in Properties; press ▶ and compare with the previous run in the Data Inspector (Ctrl+I). Ctrl+Z undoes the change.

Try What you will see exhaust_brake = 0 the truck runs away on the descent shift_time = 2.0 longer interruptions: the truck loses more speed with every downshift on the climb down_rpm = 900 later downshifts: the engine labours below its torque band

docs.text: That was the last tutorial on powertrain and engine control. Continue with vehicle dynamics and energy: A car on a drive cycle, or pick another one from the tutorial overview.

docs.title: Tutorial: Live calibration over XCP
docs.text:
You will learn how calibration tools work: XCP on CAN, A2L files, measuring and changing values in a running ECU, a command-line calibration tool, real-time simulation Before this Your first model: a cruise control Level and time intermediate, about 35 minutes Follow along start the editor (uv run nervus), File ▸ Open examples/xcp_calibration.nervus, press ▶ and double-click the scopes; the figures below come from the same model Topic ECU software, communication and diagnostics ▸ Vehicle networks (all tutorials)

Calibration engineers tune an ECU while the car drives: a tool such as INCA or CANape reads signals and changes parameters in the ECU's memory over XCP, using the ECU's A2L file to know where each variable is. In this tutorial the "ECU" is a running model: the cruise control of the first tutorial with an XCP Slave block, on a virtual CAN bus, and the tool is a small command-line program in another terminal.

uv run python examples/xcp_calibration.py    # a scripted session: model and tool in one program, at 8× real time

docs.title: The ECU side
docs.text:
Open examples/xcp_calibration.nervus. Compared with the cruise control there are three new blocks:

  • xcp (XCP Slave): its inputs are measurements the tool can read (speed, force, and time, the ECU's clock); its outputs are calibration values the tool can change: set_speed_cal (100 km/h) and gain_trim (1.0), which start at their workspace values.
  • The set speed now comes from set_speed_cal, and gain_trim multiplies the speed error before the PI controller, which scales both its P and I terms.
  • can (CAN Bus): interface udp_multicast, python-can's virtual CAN bus shared by all programs on this computer. With a real CAN adapter you would choose pcan, kvaser, vector or socketcan.

The model's Simulation Settings have pacing 1: it runs in real time, like an ECU, so a person or a tool can follow it. The XCP Slave answers on CAN identifier 0x7F1 to requests on 0x7F0.

The A2L file tells the tool where the values are; examples/xcp_calibration.py writes examples/xcp_calibration.a2l:

/begin CHARACTERISTIC set_speed_cal "Set speed (calibrated over XCP)"
  VALUE 0x10000 RL_FLOAT64 0 CM_IDENTICAL 0.0 180.0
  PHYS_UNIT "km/h"
/end CHARACTERISTIC
/begin MEASUREMENT speed ""
  FLOAT64_IEEE CM_IDENTICAL 0 0 -1e12 1e12
  ECU_ADDRESS 0x20000
/end MEASUREMENT

docs.title: Step 1: run the ECU
docs.text:
Start the editor with the model and press ▶ (the stop time is 60 s; it now takes 60 s):

uv run nervus examples/xcp_calibration.nervus

docs.title: Step 2: measure and calibrate from another terminal
docs.text:
While it runs, use the tool in a second terminal:

uv run python examples/xcp_tool.py watch speed time       # measure twice a second (Ctrl+C to stop)
uv run python examples/xcp_tool.py write set_speed_cal 60  # calibrate: a new set speed

The tool connects (XCP CONNECT), reads each value by address (SHORT_UPLOAD / UPLOAD) and writes calibration values (DOWNLOAD). After the write the car slows to 60 km/h: the next watch shows the speed falling, and the scope in the editor shows it too. This is exactly how an engineer works with a real ECU; only the transport differs. For a real ECU on a PCAN adapter:

uv run python examples/xcp_tool.py --interface pcan --channel PCAN_USBBUS1 --bitrate 500000 --a2l ecu.a2l read engine_rpm

docs.title: The scripted session
docs.text: uv run python examples/xcp_calibration.py runs the same thing in one program, 8× faster than real time: a script plays the calibration engineer, following the ECU's clock. At 20 s it raises the set speed to 120 km/h, at 35 s it triples the controller gain, and at 40 s it lowers the set speed to 100 km/h again. With three times the gain, the car comes down faster (it brakes harder), as the calibrator wanted:

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
Try What you will see xcp_tool.py write gain_trim 0.3 while running a sluggish controller: the next set speed change takes much longer xcp_tool.py write set_speed_cal 200 a full calibration tool would refuse this (the A2L limit is 180 km/h); this small tool does not check, and the car accelerates at the full 4000 N towards 200 km/h xcp_tool.py read speed when the model is not running no ECU answers: XCP needs a running slave

Polled measurement (reading values one by one) is what this tool does; production tools also use DAQ lists, where the ECU sends measurements on its own every task cycle. See CAN communication for the protocol details and how to make your own models measurable.
